44.
* 1

# On Easter.

## The First Sermon.

->How we are to die with Christ and kill within us all sensuality, desire, natural<-
->powers, and mental images, and how we are to rise in Christ and be<-
->transformed.<-
-><note>original Latin: "Exivi a patre et veni in mundum, iterum relinquo mundum."</note> I came from the Father and have come into the world; again, I am leaving the world and going to the Father. John 16:28.<-

Our most beloved Lord Jesus Christ said: "I have gone out from the Father and have come into the world; I leave it again and go to the Father." And Saint Paul says: "Christ has risen from the dead through the glory of the Father, so that we should walk in a new life; for if we become like Christ in his death, so shall we also be like him in his resurrection." <note>A reference to Romans 6:4-5.</note>

Children, this is the purest, truest, and most essential doctrine one can have; it is the most direct, shortest, safest, and simplest path—interpret it how you will, without any extra <term>glosses</term><note>Interpretive commentaries or explanations often added to biblical texts.</note>—this is the path that the dear Lord himself walked, if we wish to arrive where he is, and if we wish to be perfectly united with him. He came from the Father's heart, from the Father's womb, and came into the world, and suffered beyond all measure in the world all his days; he never gained comfort nor pleasure; he was ruined, killed, and buried. After that, he arose truly free from suffering, in radiance, entirely free from death, and ascended again into the Father's heart, in complete, true, and equal <term>blessedness</term><note>The German "Seligkeit" refers to a state of eternal happiness or salvation.</note>.

---

\*) <note>Bibliographic references for this sermon:</note> 1543. f. 85; 1565. f. 68; 1548. p. 121; 1552. p. 188; Author: Heinrich Suso. The 1621 edition and the editions by <note>Philipp Jakob</note> Spener do not contain it.

<summary>This page introduces an Easter sermon attributed to Heinrich Suso, focusing on the mystical necessity of "dying" to worldly desires to be resurrected with Christ. It emphasizes a direct, unadorned spiritual path modeled on Christ's own journey from the Father into the world and back again.</summary>

--- Page 10 ---
<meta>This page continues the Easter sermon attributed to Heinrich Suso, expanding on the necessity of "dying to the self" to achieve union with God. It transitions from the scriptural basis of the resurrection to the practical, mystical steps required for spiritual perfection.</meta>

Whichever person would still walk this path and had died within themselves in Christ, they could and must, without any doubt, also rise with him. If you are buried with Christ, you will surely rise with him. As Saint Paul says: You are dead, and your life is hidden with Christ in God. <note>A reference to Colossians 3:3.</note> In truth, such a person becomes, in a sense, free from suffering and free from death; they ascend with him to heaven, in complete and true union with the Son into the Father, into the Fatherly heart, in full possession of true, equal, and united <term>blessedness</term><note>The German "Seligkeit" implies both happiness and the state of being saved in the afterlife.</note>. What God has by nature, you have by grace. <note>This is a central theme in Rhineland mysticism: through grace, the soul participates in the very nature of God.</note> But this must be pursued. The person who walks this path is elevated above other common people, as a noble human is over a beast. He who does not wish to be un-made with Christ, how shall he be made with him? <note>The original uses a wordplay between "verwerden" (to perish or be un-made) and "gewerden" (to become or be created anew).</note> He who does not wish to die, how shall he rise? Saint Paul says: If you have risen with Christ, then taste the things that are above, and not those on earth. <note>A reference to Colossians 3:1-2.</note> One finds people who, when they hear of great things, would like to achieve them; they make a beautiful start and wish to live for the Spirit and for God, but if things do not go easily for them right away, they soon settle back down into their [fallen] nature. These are just like students: they would all like to be great <term>priests</term><note>The original "Pfaffen" was a common term for clerics, sometimes used disparagingly, but here referring to the rank of the learned.</note>, yet some hardly learn "sickly" Latin and poor grammar, while others persevere and become great masters. Likewise, there are some dear people for whom things go easily, and they are quite steady and diligent, but nothing will ever come of the others.

Whoever now wishes to attain high perfection must also overcome great things. He must overcome nine things, of which we will explain only the four lowest and least here. First, he must rise above the senses and sensuality, and step beyond all sensory things. Second, you must rise above your bodily and natural powers. Third, above all desire. Fourth, above all images and <term>formation</term><note>The German "Bildung" here refers to the mental process of creating concepts or "pictures" of God, which the mystic must move beyond to find the formless Reality.</note>.

Regarding the first, we say: rise above all senses. Here we do not mean the people who live according to sensory pleasures, willingly in mortal sins, but rather those who wish to rise with Christ and ascend to heaven. One finds people who can speak of great things and yet know nothing except from hearsay or from reading, all of which is brought in through the senses. One finds "Knights of Faithfulness" <note>likely referring to those who are loyal in outward practice but lack inner experience</note>, and people

<summary>Suso explains that spiritual resurrection requires a total "death" of the self and the ego. He outlines the first steps of mystical ascent, specifically the need to transcend the physical senses and intellectual "images" to reach true union with God.</summary>

<keywords>resurrection, self-denial, mystical union, grace vs nature, sensuality, spiritual perfection, Rhineland mysticism, Saint Paul</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on spiritual perfection through the "death" of the senses. It moves from the previous page's focus on rising with Christ to the practical inward turn (introversion) and the physical toll of mystical practice.</meta>

...of word, of sensory blossoming and breaking forth, you must die and pass over it, if you are to become perfect.

A person desired greatly to know from God what His dearest will might be; then our Lord appeared to him and said:
> You shall constrain your mind, bind your tongue, overcome your heart, and suffer all adversity joyfully for my sake; that is my dearest will.
Turn away from sensory images into your inward image; there it is: *The light of your countenance, O Lord, is signed upon us* <note>original: "Signatum est super nos lumen vultus tui, domine"</note>, Lord, you have marked the light of your countenance upon us. Some people have a great deal of sensory activity <note>Referring to religious practices that rely on the physical senses or external rituals.</note> with good intentions, and yet they hardly ever find rest. What should they do? When they become idle for an hour, they should sink themselves so deeply into God—and so much so—that in one hour they powerfully press back forty years of time which they lost through the senses; thus they do more to become pious. They should not be like those who cannot come to God except through sensory images or with learned, read, or composed words; rather, they should seek God's Spirit from the ground <note>The "Ground" (Grund) is a central term in German mysticism, referring to the deepest point of the soul where it meets God.</note>, from the innermost part, from the spirit—Spirit with Spirit, heart to heart. As the dear Lord said:
> God is a spirit, and those who worship Him must worship Him in spirit and in truth. <note>A reference to John 4:24.</note>
God understands the language of the heart and the intention of the soul—a profound, inward, and <term>essential</term><note>The German "wesentlich" here implies an address from the very "essence" or "being" of the person, rather than just words.</note> address. Mary’s mind and her presence prayed more holily and deeply in the ears of Christ than everything Martha could say or complain about. <note>The author uses the sisters Mary and Martha to represent the "contemplative life" versus the "active life."</note>

Secondly, one should go beyond all natural strength, both inwardly and outwardly. If any person could work properly in this way, so that they understood this and yet remained within their natural strength and vigor, that would be a miracle! I have never seen such a person; whoever they are, let them step forward and show themselves. Saint Bernard <note>Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153), a Cistercian abbot and mystic.</note> did not have this, for he complained that he had ruined his body (the servant of God) <note>Referring to how extreme fasting and asceticism damaged his physical health.</note>. Neither did Saint Gregory <note>Gregory the Great (c. 540–604), a Pope and influential theologian.</note>, who was a light of Christendom. Therefore, let no one deceive themselves or imagine that they are or have that which is distant and foreign to them, for it must cost something; what costs nothing is worth nothing. He who wishes to have love must let go of love. A disciple asked his master:
> "Dear Master, we eat and drink, and it does not seem so to us;"
then the Master said:
> "Dear son, that is no wonder, we consume everything..."

<summary>This page emphasizes the necessity of inward contemplation over outward religious "busyness" and warns that true spiritual growth requires physical and emotional sacrifice. It uses the examples of Mary of Bethany and great saints to show that the spirit must be prioritized over natural strength.</summary>
<keywords>inwardness, sensory images, Holy Spirit, Mary and Martha, Saint Bernard, Saint Gregory, asceticism, the Ground of the soul</keywords>

--- Page 12 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion on the inward journey of the soul, moving from the requirement of "worshipping in spirit" (mentioned on the previous page) to the specific internal "powers" or faculties that a person must transcend to reach spiritual perfection.</meta>

...with inward exercises; everything goes a different way. All outward strength is too small to achieve this, yet God can indeed give a new strength. If the grain of wheat dies, it brings forth new grain and much fruit; truly, if it does not die, it remains alone; it must first die to its own self. One must also go beyond another power, beyond the **common sense** <note>The "common sense" (*sensus communis*) was understood in medieval psychology as the faculty that organizes various sensory inputs—sight, sound, etc.—into coherent mental images.</note>. A person finds this even when they see and hear nothing externally; they then find all kinds of images within themselves, and there is much of what is inside them, and they turn one image here, another there; now this way, now that way, and there is much unrest within. This should be turned entirely into **simplicity** <term>Simplicity: (German: *Einfalt*) In mystical thought, this is a state of being "un-folded" or "single," where the soul is stripped of all complex thoughts and images to focus only on the one-ness of God.</term>, into the pure Good, which is God. A master <note>Referring to a master craftsman or sculptor.</note> saw a rough block lying there and said: "Oh, what a beautiful, delightful image is inside; if only the chips were hewn away and peeled off." Our Lord said: "If you separate the good from the evil, you will be just like my mouth" <note>original: "Scheidest du das Gute von dem Bösen, so wirst du recht wie mein Mund." A reference to Jeremiah 15:19.</note>; oh, whoever would part, peel, and separate everything would find God bare and pure within themselves.

The third power is the **rational power**. A person must move beyond this power. One finds people who have much rational activity and "flowering" with their reason, just as if they wanted to traverse the heavens, yet they stand only upon their bare nature—like Aristotle and Plato, who understood many wonders and also lived quite virtuously, and yet it was only nature <note>The author distinguishes between "nature" (human effort and intellect) and "grace" (divine gift). Even the greatest philosophers are seen as limited because they rely on human reason alone.</note>. These people must suppress their nature with great diligence and guard themselves carefully against their own pride. One also finds other people who are quite simple, and they remain simple, and thus receive all things; it happens for them inwardly and easily, like a wave in which an image of a ship is easily impressed, but also soon collapses and passes away; but into a stone, the image comes only with great labor, yet it remains hard and firm within and does not soon vanish. So it is also with these rational people.

Thirdly, one must come beyond all desire and beyond the **desirous power**. Here we do not mean the people who desire transitory things (for such things are a hundred thousand miles distant and foreign to this path, as they desire wealth, honor, and other temporal things); we mean certain good people who have much desire with **attachment** <term>Attachment: (German: *Eigenschaft*) A central concept in German mysticism referring to "self-ownership" or the ego's claim over its own religious experiences and desires.</term> and life, wishing from morning until night: "Oh, if only God would do this and that for me, and give me this grace and..."

<summary>This page describes how a seeker must transcend the mental faculties of sensory imagination (common sense), human reason, and spiritual desire to find God. It uses the famous analogy of a sculptor "peeling away" stone to reveal the divine image already hidden within the soul.</summary>

<keywords>inner exercises, common sense, simplicity, rational power, Aristotle, Plato, nature vs grace, desirous power, attachment, detachment</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the powers of the soul that must be transcended. Having previously discussed common sense and the rational power, the text now addresses the total surrender of the will and the abandonment of mental images.</meta>

...the revelation, or "if only it were with me as it is with that person," or "if I were this way or that." No, not like that! One should leave oneself entirely to God, and faithfully desire Him alone, and commit all things to Him entirely and faithfully, saying with Christ: Father, not as I will, but as You will <note>original: "fiat voluntas tua"</note>—not just with the mouth, but from the depths of the heart, out of heartfelt devotion and inner intention. Oh, that would be a delightful thing in all suffering, in all **releasement** <term>Releasement: (German: *Gelassenheit*) A central concept in German mysticism, referring to a state of perfect detachment and the letting go of one's own will to become a vessel for God's will.</term>, in every way: to be able to sink oneself into the Depths, just as the dear Lord let Himself sink so groundlessly. He was entirely released, more than any **created being** <note>original: "Creatur"</note> ever was; He cried out: "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me!" He released Himself until everything was accomplished and said: "It is finished" <note>original: "Consumatum est"</note>. In exactly this way, a person should leave themselves entirely to God in all suffering and in all lack of consolation. Do not think that suffering should not hurt you; if it did not hurt, how would one earn anything? Had our Lord Jesus Christ stuck His finger into a fire, it would have hurt Him; therefore, in all your suffering and desires, leave yourself to God. He who desires something that is outside of Him, or he who is vexed by something that is within him, is not yet in this state; he has not yet released himself.

A person was once shown in a revelation how they should leave themselves: they should act as if they were sitting on their cloak in the middle of the deep sea, and for a mile around there was no land, neither near nor far. What could he do? He could neither call out, nor swim, nor wade; he had to leave himself to God. In this same way, a person should always leave themselves to God if they truly wish to be a "released" person. Now I say, one should not desire; you should desire nothing else except that the dear God take away all **means** <note>In mystical theology, "means" (*Mittel*) are any intermediate things—like icons, specific prayers, or even holy thoughts—that stand between the soul and a direct, unmediated experience of God.</note> and unite you entirely with Himself without any means. With this, all sins fall away, and all good and all blessedness enter in.

Fourthly, you must move beyond all **images and mental forms** <term>Images and Mental Forms: (German: *Bilde und Bildung*) This refers to the psychological process of forming mental representations. Mystics argued that to find the "formless" God, one must clear the mind of all created images.</term>. Now, we do not mean those people who willfully take into themselves or carry the image of some mortal creature, whoever they may be or whatever they are called; such people are entirely far and foreign to this state. One also finds people who suffer from this and are good people, yet they have many intrusive notions and imaginings; a person must let go of these, so that they may carry all such "forming" simply into God, confessing and lamenting their failings to Him, and wishing to...

<summary>This page explores the core mystical concept of Gelassenheit (releasement), urging total surrender to God's will through the example of Christ's suffering and a metaphor of a person stranded at sea. It also introduces the necessity of transcending mental images to achieve a direct, unmediated union with the Divine.</summary>

...if it then does not pass away, let him bear with God in this and release himself. There are also people who have many fantasies and dreams; they see such beautiful things and future events in their sleep, or they see the saints or the souls. I do not deny this—for the angel appeared to Joseph in his sleep—nor do I affirm it, for such things also happen naturally, as Boethius <note>Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius (c. 477–524 AD), a philosopher whose works on logic and theology were foundational for medieval thought.</note> says: He who occupies himself with pure things dreams of pure things by nature; he who occupies himself with folly dreams of folly. One also finds such people who have many visions and revelations; and even if all were well for ten years, the **angel of false light** <note>original: "Engel des falschen Lichts." A reference to 2 Corinthians 11:14, where Satan disguises himself as an angel of light to deceive the faithful.</note> could mix himself in at any time to deceive and mislead. In these revelations, all your effort should be directed toward finding the testimony of Holy Scripture in all things. Run to the Holy Gospel and to the teachers of the Holy Church; if you find that it accords with them, let it be; if it does not, trample it down—as dear as God and your eternal **salvation** <note>original: "Seligkeit"</note> are to you—do not follow or heed it, but cast it away from you.

By this path, you should come into yourself in such a way that you do not fix your mind on any particular manner or revelation of God or the saints. Place yourself in the divine will in all things: in having, in wanting, in something, in nothing, in comfort, in lack of comfort, according to the most lovely example of Christ. Let Him be manifest always in the **ground** <term>Ground: (German: *Grund*) A central term in German mysticism referring to the deepest, innermost part of the soul where the human meets the Divine.</term> of your heart and soul, so that you form Him within you and look upon Him without ceasing—how high the perfection of His life, His walk, and His mind was; how **released** <term>Released: (German: *gelassen*) Related to "Gelassenheit," meaning a state of perfect detachment and surrender of the ego.</term>, how simple, how modest, humble, patient, and full of all virtues He was. Abandon yourself to Him; also take Him to yourself as a companion in all things. If you eat a mouthful, think that your dearest Lord sits across from you and eats with you; if you sit, He sits by you and looks at you; if you walk, never walk alone, let Him be your companion; if you sleep, lie down in Him; and thus in all places, in all ways, among all people. I know a person who, for the sake of perfect likeness to our Lord and His ways, went from one corner to another like one going on a pilgrimage for an **indulgence** <term>Indulgence: (German: *Ablaß*) In the medieval church, a way to reduce the punishment for sins, often through specific acts of devotion or pilgrimages.</term>, meditating on the works of Christ. St. Bernard <note>Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153), a Cistercian monk and influential mystic.</note> writes to the beginner that he should set a well-ordered person before his eyes and think upon his deeds and omissions. If you would and...

<meta>This page continues the spiritual advice regarding the internal state of the soul. The previous page cautioned against over-reliance on external visions and dreams, urging the reader to test all revelations against Holy Scripture and the teachings of the Church, while maintaining a state of surrender to the divine will.</meta>

...would you dare to say or do this if this good person saw it? How much more should one imprint within oneself the lovely image of our Lord, which is truly and essentially in us and closer to us than we are to ourselves; for in Him is all comfort, all goodness, all joy, *full of grace and truth* <note>original Latin: "plenus gratiae et veritatis," a reference to John 1:14.</note>; all grace and truth is in Him.

Your inner spiritual self <term>geistlicher Mensch: literally "spiritual person," referring to the inward, divine-oriented part of the soul as opposed to the physical or worldly self.</term> should not let this escape for a single moment; it should possess a rational awareness of the hours <note>original Latin: "horae," likely referring to the Canonical Hours or the specific times set aside for prayer and meditation.</note> and an internal observation and vigilance regarding how one stands before God during those hours. This should be a necessity for those whom God has redeemed from the evil, false world, and who have no need to worry or think about household or children, but only how they might please God and live for Him alone. It is difficult to advise and act for those who must bear the cares of the world, for one can hardly be in the mill without being covered in dust, or in the fire without being burned. Yet you should know that I have found people amidst all their troubles who possess such high purity <note>original: "Lauterkeit," meaning a state of being unmixed with worldly intentions; sincerity of soul.</note> and perfection <note>original: "Vollkommenheit"</note> that spiritual people <note>Referring to members of religious orders or those dedicated to a contemplative life.</note> might well feel ashamed.

The lovely image of our Lord is received, and one can receive it in a figurative way and also in a living way. In a figurative way, one should receive it nobly, divinely, and rationally—not in a creaturely or sensory way. Some people, when they are meant to think of God, think of Him as a creature, like a dear man who has done them much good and suffered for them, and they feel a natural mercy and compassion for Him—no, not so! A person should have learned a divine conception <note>original: "Einbildung," which in this context refers to the mental formation of an image or a spiritual visualization, rather than "fantasy."</note> of the lovely man Jesus Christ, as of the Son of God and the God-man <term>Gott-Mensch: a theological term for the dual nature of Christ as both divine and human.</term> and man-God—not a creaturely conception, but a divine, supernatural one, so that he never thinks of the most beloved image of Christ except as God. Thus thought of and received, one is never without God. Wherever anything of God is, there God is entirely. In this way, one may never miss out on the very best.

One also receives the image of Christ in a living way; that is, that a person does not rest until he becomes like the image in conformity <note>original: "Gleichförmigkeit," the mystical practice of aligning one's will and nature with the likeness of Christ.</note>, according to his own manner, as much as is possible for him. It should not seem like a small thing to him that he merely keeps the commandments,

<summary>This page explores how the "spiritual person" should internalize the image of Christ, moving beyond simple human pity for Jesus's suffering toward a divine, supernatural understanding of the God-man. The author also notes that even those living in the busy world can achieve higher spiritual purity than those in religious orders.</summary>

<keywords>inner life, image of Christ, divine nature, spiritual purity, conformity to Christ, God-man, contemplation vs. worldly cares</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the spiritual instruction on maintaining an internal focus on the divine. The previous page emphasized the "lovely image" of Christ as a source of grace and truth, distinguishing the spiritual person from those entangled in worldly cares. This page moves deeper into the concept of "transcending images" to achieve union with God.</meta>

rather, all the counsels <term>Rathschlüsse: the divine decrees, purposes, or designs of God</term> of our Lord should be delightful, desirable, and blissful to him. Our Lord has spoken:
> You shall love your enemies,
this love is so lovely that it is not enough for it to speak kindly to enemies, but one can and should love them from the whole heart, and out of heartfelt favor wish them all good and honor, speak well of them, and favorably excuse them of all guilt. Do not think that the person should be unresponsive <note>The original German "unfügsam" suggests being stiff or unyielding; here it means a person shouldn't be a stone—they still feel favor or disfavor, but they choose to transcend those feelings.</note>; he can indeed recognize favor or disfavor, but he should not regard it, nor wish to know it, after the image of Christ, so that he may become completely like Him.

Now we have spoken of this, that a person should and must transcend all images <term>Bilde: mental representations or concepts; in mystical thought, "images" are sensory or intellectual tools that must eventually be left behind to experience God directly.</term>. Should we then reject the lovely image of our Lord, of whom we have spoken much? No, truly that would be a perilous thing, for if we go to Him ourselves and ask His own words, He speaks:
> It is better for you that I go away from you, for if I do not go away from you, the Holy Spirit will not come to you. <note>original: John 16:7</note>
Is this image hereby rejected? It is rejected in a creaturely, sensory, and pictorial way, as the disciples possessed Him, and thus they had to let Him go; but in a lovely, divine, and supernatural way, they never let Him go. For as He departed from them physically and presentially, He took with Him all their disposition <term>Gemüth: the heart, mind, and spiritual soul combined</term>, all their senses, and all their love. Thus should we also do! He has ascended into heaven, into the Fatherly heart where He is, into the Father’s bosom; we want to travel with Him with all our senses, love, and intention, especially into the Fatherly heart. He is there a life, an essence, a shining mirror of His clarity and an image of His Fatherly countenance, not alone in the manner of an image, but in an essential manner, in perfect equality with the Fatherly person, in the divine outpouring of the eternal birth <note>A core concept in Rhineland Mysticism referring to the eternal generation of the Son by the Father, which is also meant to take place within the soul of the believer.</note>, One with the Father. Thither we should go with all our disposition and love, and there be united with Him and become a shining mirror. There we shall dwell and walk in the three persons, and can then at all times speak with Saint Paul:
> Our citizenship is in heaven, <note>original: Philippians 3:20</note>
that is, in the three persons of the Godhead. According to this, a person should strive with all his desires, senses, and powers, so that this may be his. If it does not happen to him during his life, then God gives it to him at his end. If it happens to him then—

## 45. a
### The Second Sermon.

How we must depart from and die to all things, including our own will and knowledge, and thus rise with Christ and become one.

> I pray, Father, that they may be one, just as we also are one. John XVII. v. 20 — 23. <note>original Latin: "Rogo Pater ut sint unum, sicut et nos unum sumus."</note> **)
> Father, I pray that they may be one, as you and I are one, that they may be perfected into one.

St. Paul received this when he wrote: I live, but not I, but Christ lives in me. How then shall we also come to this, that we become one with God? Not until we lose and forget ourselves, and are transformed <term>übergeformt: a mystical term meaning to be "reshaped" or "molded over" into the likeness of God</term> into God,

...through the Spirit of God. For as long as a person possesses himself, finds himself, and knows himself in God, and God in himself, he is not one; for he possesses and knows two, that is, God and himself. This is multiplicity <term>Mannigfaltigkeit: the state of being many or divided; in mystical thought, this is the opposite of divine oneness</term> and not perfect unity; for in unity, one loses all multiplicity. But that is true unity, where one finds oneself entirely in the One (which is called and is God), so that one does not love, nor intend, nor know, nor outwardly work for oneself, nor for God, nor for any creature, because he has lost himself in God. In the person united with God, this is all one essence and one life, and he knows of no other things. All creatures chase after this unity; all multiplicity intends <insert>strives toward</insert> this unity; it seeks nothing but unity.

Every creature comes without mediation <term>ohne Mittel: directly from God, without any intervening tools, saints, or physical processes</term> from the One, and desires to return to the undivided One, according to the capacity of its own essence. And therefore all works, all love, all restlessness are for the sake of rest, and this rest is nowhere but in the one, unique, simple God. All outflows <term>Ausfluss: a Neoplatonic term for creation "flowing out" from God</term> are for the sake of the inflow. The outflow intends nothing but the return-inflow <term>Wiedereinfluß: the soul’s mystical journey back into its divine origin</term> into our origin, which is God; and when the return-inflow has fully occurred, only then is there rest and stillness. When all things in a person become entirely one in God, then there is complete peace; there, all shouting, restlessness, works, and will fall silent. All things seek this by nature, and to achieve this, they consume their essence and life, and all things, and yet they can never come to true rest, except in the One, that is in God. Oh, how anxious and insecure a person stands outside of this union! How dare he remain outside for even a moment, and know, love, and find himself apart from God!

What now is the best way to enter in and become one with God? Truly no other than to die to oneself and leave oneself behind—that is, to abandon all self-interest <term>Eigensucht: literally "self-seeking" or egoism; the attachment to one's own will</term> and multiplicity. If you wish to become whiter, you must wash away the black; the less black, the more white; the less manifold, the more simple <term>einfältig: "single-fold" or unified; the opposite of being distracted by many things</term>. God does not properly work within you in multiplicity; it must be One. The more the powers of the soul are detached and unified from the outside, and the more they are expanded and spread from within, the more powerful, divine, and perfect the work of God becomes.

Dying to oneself. The sooner, more truly, and more perfectly one dies, the sooner, more truly, and more perfectly one confesses and attains this life within. Christ had to do this first, physically, so that we might confess and follow it spiritually. If he were to rise in immortality, he had to die in mortality <note>original: "in der Tödlichkeit"</note> (in that which is subject to death). If we wish to find ourselves in unity, it must cost us all multiplicity <term>Mannigfaltigkeit: the state of being many or divided; in mystical thought, this is the opposite of divine oneness</term>; we must die to mortality, to every characteristic of distinction, for the One has no distinction; it loses and is stripped of all multiplicity, yet it also unites all multiplicity. We read of Christ: that he died and rose again, and will die no more; death will no longer have dominion over him. From death comes this life which no longer dies; for there is no true, immutable life in us except that which comes from death. If water is to become hot, the cold must die; if wood is to become fire, it must die to its own nature. Life truly cannot be in us, nor become ours, nor can we ever become it, unless we first un-become <term>entwerden: a central mystical term meaning to strip away the ego, self-will, and "created" identity to make room for God</term> it and attain it through a dying.

In truth, there is essentially nothing more than one death and one life. However many deaths it may seem to be, there is no more than one, and they all serve a single death: that a person should be dead entirely and all at once to his own will, to all self-possession, to all distinction and created things, as far as it is possible for creatures. Thus, there is no more than one single life, a divine, super-essential <term>überwesentliches: life that exists beyond or above ordinary being or essence, a term used to describe God's transcendent nature</term>, super-cognitive, uncreated, essential life. And toward this life all lives hasten, hunt, and surge, so that they might obtain this life; and the closer they come to this life and become more like it, the more truly they live, for in and from this life all lives live and nothing else. There is no death that is not immediately answered by a blissful life. This must necessarily be so; God cannot refuse this to death, nor resist it. Just as death is stronger, more powerful, and more fundamental, so too the life that responds to death becomes stronger, more powerful, and more fundamental; the more personal the death, the more personal the life. Every life brings strength to a person and fortifies them for an even more powerful dying.

If a person were to "die" to a shameful word <note>This refers to remaining silent or patient when insulted, rather than reacting with the ego.</note> by suffering it for God's sake, or if they were to die to an inner inclination <term>Jnneigung: a natural tendency, habitual desire, or inner leaning toward something</term>—whether internal or external, whether to do something or to leave it undone—against their own will, regarding themselves or another, whatever it may be; whether in love or in sorrow, in words, in deeds, in walking, in standing, or in giving up a pleasure of taste or sight; or in not making excuses for oneself when wronged, or anything else where one is not yet "dead" <note>In the mystical sense, "undead" means still being driven by selfish desires or the need for recognition.</note>—this at first causes pain to an unaccustomed and "undying" person, more so than to one who has already died to themselves, and more than it will later feel to that same person once they have grown accustomed to it. No matter how small a death of this kind one dies with earnestness, such a life responds to it and strengthens the person to immediately die a greater death. This continues as long and as often as necessary, until it eventually becomes much more blissful, delightful, and joyful to die than to live; for one finds life within death, and the light shines in the darkness.

Thus, a person continues to die to outward things until they are completely dead to them and no longer need to die to external things, whatever they may be. Then they have fought a good fight; but then they still have much to die to internally. To a person who has died in this way, all things are their own, and they can use them quite properly and blissfully. No one can ever truly enjoy creatures <term>Creatures: a term for all created things, including people, animals, and objects, as distinct from the Creator</term>—neither internally nor externally—unless they have first completely gone out from them for the love of God, and the things have died to them and they to the things. Only then can you turn your attention to them without worry. Never did a person gain the true love and friendship of a father, mother, sister, brother, or other friends in God, unless they first went out from them for the love of God and died to them completely; otherwise, these relationships would be hostile to them, not friendly. Therefore our Lord spoke: "I have come to set the child against the father, the daughter against the mother..." <note>A reference to Matthew 10:35. The author interprets this not as literal family strife, but as the necessity of prioritizing divine union over human attachments.</note>

This is a hard death, when all the lights of the soul are extinguished; then, wonderfully, many celestial lights shine into the powers of the pure soul. Yet, because these are all still experienced through the soul's own lights and are delightful, perceptible gifts, the soul must die to them all—for they are not yet God alone. They are still a "part" and not the "One." For when one dies to everything that lives and shines within us, only then does one truly find the soul, and never before. How has a person "lost their soul" if they still retain some freedom or ownership in their soul, such that they may choose to do or not do as they please? If his soul still stands in its own powers, will, and works—choosing and rejecting—then he has not done what Christ, our model, did. In His highest hour of need, He said:

> Father, not as I will, but as You will! <note>Luke 22:42.</note>

It was as if He wanted to say: I have no will; but You, Father, shall have my will, for I am divested and dead to my own will, and formed and born into Your will.

One asks why our Lord did not answer Pilate when he asked, "What is truth?" <note>Referring to John 18:38.</note> To this, one commonly answers: He went out, therefore he was not worthy of the answer. If you wish to take all goodness, truth, and essence, then take them in the simple One, in their origin, in the essence without mode <term>Wesen ohne Weise: the existence of God that is not limited by any specific "way" or "manner" of being</term>. Leave aside the angel, the person, and the heaven, and take the essential good, truth, and essence purely in itself. For whatever you add to it, that displaces and covers the unity, and points toward an end, a lock, and a prison. The "One" does not look outward; it knows nothing foreign, neither far nor near; it has neither breadth nor length. This One, which is God, has all good within itself; nothing is outside Him. He gives goodness and essence to the creatures, but they do not give it to Him; thus it is also with everything that is divine, whether it be a person, a work, or a mode. ...is not outside Him; in Him is all goodness, without width, without length, simply, essentially, and truly; nothing is foreign to Him, nor far away.

A divine person <note>original: "göttlicher Menſch"; refers to a person whose soul is united with God.</note> who has thus died to all selfishness through love, and is one in God and God in them, so that nothing is added or taken away—whatever this person does or leaves undone in and through God, that is always the very best work, for they do it in the best and most perfect way. In this, they fail in nothing, for their works are done in God according to His most beloved will, whether in action or inaction. They find as much in the smallest work as in the greatest, for the work does not take its goodness from the outside; it possesses it essentially from within, and is not made better by length or breadth. An *Ave Maria* <note>original: "Ave Maria"; the "Hail Mary" prayer.</note> spoken with equal goodness has as much good in it as a whole Psalter <note>The 150 Psalms of the Bible; here used to represent a much longer, more arduous prayer practice.</note>, and a single step taken has as much as a journey across the sea; but a greater external effort corresponds to a greater accidental reward <term>zufallender Lohn: a theological term for secondary or "fringe" rewards in heaven, as opposed to the "essential" reward which is God Himself.</term>. The outward work takes <insert>receives</insert> its goodness according to the magnitude of love in the essence, and not from the outside, like other temporal things. A grain of gold has as much of the nature of gold as a thousand marks <note>A traditional unit of weight or currency.</note>; but if one does not seek the essence alone in the gold, then one also desires quantity. It is not so in divine matters, which take their goodness from within, not from without; therefore, there is as much in the least as in the most, in one as in all, if the foundation <term>Grund: the "ground" of the soul, the deepest point of being where the soul and God meet.</term> is the same.

The outward is nothing but a sign of the inward. A hung sign indicates that there is wine in the cellar; but there may well be wine where no sign hangs; the wine is therefore no less valuable to the master. So it is also in the truth; if I have a good, whole, divine will to do good and all the good works and all goodness—yes, even what all the saints and people have done and could do—to suffer all pain, to give all alms, and what I would gladly do through God, but I simply lack the power, then I have done this entirely before God. Not a hair's breadth is missing, as long as the will is not lacking. What happened a thousand years ago is just as present in God as what happens now in every divine will of a good person; what they thus will has full existence <note>original: "Weſen"; being or essence.</note> before God. Turn into yourself, and there you find God alone; as you turn into yourself, so you turn into God, for he is in you and you in him, a single One.

All things were in him—a life—says St. John <note>A reference to the opening of the Gospel of John, specifically John 1:3-4.</note>, and:
> He came into his own, and all who received him, to them he gave power to become sons of God.

God’s Son is one with the Father in nature; thus a divine person <note>original: "göttlicher Menſch"; a person who has attained mystical union.</note> is also one with God through grace, in that wherein they are divine; but if anything else lives, or if there is anything else in them, then it is otherwise with them. For in that wherein they are divine, they are truly God’s son, and one with God, like his only-begotten son, so that God does nothing apart from them, and the person does nothing apart from God. In truth, just as little as God could separate himself from his Son and from himself, so little could he separate himself from this person—unless that person first separates themselves from God. And if God were to leave this person, he would have to leave himself; and where he takes himself, there he takes this person, for they are One in the One. A Master <note>Likely a reference to Meister Eckhart, whose teachings emphasize this radical unity between the soul and God.</note> spoke:
> I do not begrudge the only-begotten Son all the good that his Father has given him, for I can become that same son through grace—the one from whom, through whom, and in whom all things are.

There one becomes so unified that there are no longer any parts.

It is commonly said that God acts and takes nothing outside himself; thus the person is good and divine whom nothing moves except God, so that God is the cause of all their works, whom they purely intend therein. But I say more: a divine person never "takes" God, nor thinks of God, as being outside of themselves; for where they take God, they also take themselves, since God and they have become One. They find God within themselves; they do not look outward, they know nothing foreign nor distant outside of God—for if they bring forth anything outside of God, those are idols <note>original: "Abgötter"; in this mystical context, an idol is any mental image or desire that is not God himself.</note>.

When God takes himself in the person, and stirs and works all his deeds through them, and takes the person as himself (for they are One in the One), then he also takes and stirs the person, and works through them; and consequently, it is not the person acting, as Jesus spoke:
> The Father, who dwells in me, does the works. <note>John 14:10.</note>

### 46.

# For Easter Monday.

## The First Sermon.

On the spiritual union <term>Vereinigung</term> <note>The process of the human soul becoming one with God.</note> and the entry of the uncreated Spirit into our created spirit. Although both their lives are separate and distinct in a fleshly manner and in the realm of the intellect, one person is so united with the other in the mind (though without any eternal bliss) that they become one in feeling and perception, as well as in understanding, just as if they were one person and had nothing divided between them.

This usually happens most often among guileless, open-hearted people who are of one will, or of one essence, or who stand upon one practice. <meta>This page continues the sermon for Easter Monday, expanding on the relationship between the human spirit and God. It moves from the concept of human intimacy to the superior, "uncreated" union between the Creator and the created spirit, drawing heavily on the mystical theology of Richard of Saint Victor and Saint Augustine.</meta>

how much more then can the spiritual union and entrance of the uncreated Spirit into our created spirit occur; for He is closer and more real in us, and we have more likeness with Him, than any human can ever have with another in fleshly matters, or can ever have in an intellectual manner. Therefore He has sent us His Holy Spirit, that He should draw and unite our spirit with and toward Himself.

Before this can happen, something wonderful must happen to the soul and the body, and thereafter something else wonderful must happen with our spirit and God’s Spirit before this can take place, as Richardus <note>Richard of Saint Victor (d. 1173), a prominent mystical theologian whose works on contemplation deeply influenced late medieval German thought.</note> says. St. Paul says: The Word of God is living and powerful, and sharper than any two-edged sword, and pierces until it divides soul and spirit, also marrow and bone <note>A reference to Hebrews 4:12.</note>. Augustine and Richardus say: In created things nothing wonderful is found, except that which is essentially one, undivided and indivisible in itself, is yet in some way divided. The one essence is spirit, and the soul is the other essence, but both are one essence and one simple nature. Each has its own name according to its power and its works: according to the lowest powers, where the soul gives life to the body, its name is "Soul"; but where it clings to God with the highest powers and gazes upon God, there it is called "Spirit." In this division the soul and everything that is essential remains in the lowest part, and the spirit and everything that is spiritual ascends upward, and is thus separated from the soul and joined to God. St. Paul says: He who clings to God becomes one spirit with Him <note>1 Corinthians 6:17.</note>. This is a wonderful separation, whereby everything that is bodily and coarse remains down here, and everything that is subtle and spiritual is raised to the contemplation of divine glory and is transformed into that image, from clarity to clarity <note>original: "von Klarheit zu der Klarheit." Referring to 2 Corinthians 3:18, where "clarity" or "brightness" is used synonymously with "glory."</note>, just as by the Spirit of God, as St. Paul says. The lowest part comes to great peace and stillness, as the highest part is drawn to the glory and to the divine joy. These are the words of Augustine and Richardus. From this we can notice that the more our spirit is separated from temporal things, and from the soul in this manner, the more easily and perfectly it enters [into union].

<meta>This page continues the sermon for Easter Monday, moving from the distinction between the "soul" (the life-giving force of the body) and the "spirit" (the part that clings to God) to the experience of mystical union. Into this entrance entered Saint John in the Book of Revelation <note>original: "Apokalypse"</note> when he said: "I was in the Spirit on the Lord's Day." <note>Revelation 1:10</note>. Regarding this, Richardus <note>Richard of Saint Victor (d. 1173), a highly influential mystical theologian.</note> says: He was with his spirit in the Spirit of God, and this happens when people so completely forget their outward affairs, just as if they were entirely ignorant of all external things that are performed in and through the body, and only those things belonging to the spirit were present to them—that is, those things practiced through thoughts and the intellect, performed out of love and an ascent toward God. Or, to be "spirit in spirit" means when a person has completely gathered and united themselves inwardly and strives to forget everything that happens externally.

Haymo <note>Likely Haymo of Auxerre, a 9th-century Benedictine scholar whose biblical commentaries were widely read in the Middle Ages.</note> says: Saint John's spirit was thus in the Spirit of God, not that he had left the body with all its powers, but his mind <term>Gemüth: a term for the seat of the soul's emotions, will, and intellect</term> was in God, and hung in the Spirit of Eternity, who revealed, taught, and showed his spirit wonderful things.

To this entrance Saint Peter had come when he was released from his bonds <note>A reference to Peter’s miraculous escape from prison in Acts 12.</note>.

Hugo <note>Hugh of Saint Victor (d. 1141), a philosopher and mystic who taught that love is a form of knowledge.</note> says: This is the nature and quality of love: that the spirit leaves itself, and in the presence of its Beloved, it scorns itself. Then it happens in a wondrous way that it is raised up by the drawing of love into Him who is above it, and is forced by the power of love to go out of itself and away from itself, so that it must forget itself and think of God alone.

Into this entrance the Queen of Sheba had come when she saw Solomon’s wisdom and "had no more spirit" <note>A biblical idiom from 1 Kings 10:5, meaning she was breathless with awe or overwhelmed.</note>.

Richardus says: Then the spirit does not possess itself, when it begins to pass away <note>literally "to become as nothing"</note> from itself and to deviate from its essence and human state. With a wondrous transformation <term>Ueberformigkeit: a mystical term meaning to be reshaped into a higher or divine form</term>, the human spirit seems to pass away in time when, by clinging to God, it becomes one spirit with God, and no longer belongs to itself, but to God.

Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a foundational 5th-century author for Christian mysticism.</note> says: It is much better for us to be God's than our own. And the Prophet spoke of this: "My soul has passed away into your Holy Spirit." Dionysius says: He who is thus united in truth with the Spirit of God knows better what he experiences and feels, and it happens that other people (who have not entered within) sometimes want to rebuke him for...

### 47.

# For Easter Monday.

## The Second Sermon.

Concerning the five degrees of true divine love, which are named: active reality, perseverance, fervor <note>German: *Hizigkeit*, literally "heat" or "hot-headedness," here referring to spiritual intensity.</note>, sharpness, and overflowing love.
*Did our heart not burn within us regarding Jesus, etc. Luke 24:32.* <note>Original Latin: *Nonne cor nostrum ardens erat in nobis de Jesu etc. Lucae XXIV. v. 32.*</note>
Did our heart not burn within us while he talked with us on the road and opened the Scriptures to us?

Dear children, you have heard in the Gospel how, when Christ our Lord had risen from the dead, he revealed himself to two of his disciples on the road in the form of a pilgrim <note>German: *Pilgrims-Gestalt*. This refers to the resurrected Jesus appearing as a traveler or stranger to the disciples on the road to Emmaus.</note>; one of whom was named Cleopas, and the other (as some believe) was named Luke. These two were speaking earnestly of Christ out of the great love and devotion they had for him, although their inward eyes were restrained so that they did not recognize him. Therefore, Gregory <note>Pope Gregory the Great (c. 540–604).</note> says: In the same manner that they doubted and loved within themselves, so did our dear Lord reveal himself to them outwardly in the form of a pilgrim and was present with them. But he did not reveal to them that it was he; and because they spoke of him, he gave them his presence, but because they doubted, he did not make himself known. He spoke with them, he rebuked the hardness of their hearts and their lack of understanding. He explained to them the secrets of the Scripture that had been written concerning him. Because

Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th–6th century theologian whose writings on the "Celestial Hierarchy" and mystical union deeply influenced medieval thought.</note> says: Love has five degrees. The first is a **moving reality** [active working], which possesses less of God than the others because it is only beginning to turn, and starts to love its God in various active cares; it is always diligent to perform all kinds of good exercises with earnestness, so that it does not grow cold on the path, but seeks and always follows its Beloved. As the loving bride says: *In my bed at night I sought him whom my soul loves.* <note>A reference to Song of Solomon 3:1.</note> But when this active love is too short and narrow for the Bridegroom to lie upon this "bed of activity," he cannot have his beloved according to his will, nor find her; and yet the soul does not cease, for she desires to seek and find him always with anxious love. This "little Zacchaeus" is every lover of God when they are first converted to the truth of God’s love. He is a prince of "open sinners" because he now recognizes himself to be a manifest, great sinner, and is not ashamed to prove himself through confession, revealing all that he has sinned. As St. Paul openly confesses when he spoke: *Jesus Christ came for the sake of sinners, of whom I am the very first and greatest.* <note>1 Timothy 1:15.</note> These sinners become rich through grace, for where sins have become many, grace shall also be superfluous <note>Meaning "abundant" or "overflowing"; a reference to Romans 5:20.</note>. Therefore, no one should despair because of their sins, however great they may have been or are, but should instead strive with Zacchaeus to practice this first degree of love—activity—for as St. Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD).</note> says: God does not only forgive his lovers their sin, but he wants to give great gifts in addition. These two disciples possessed this active love as they wandered from one city to another and expressed the love of their hearts outwardly with their mouths. The second degree of love is **perseverance**, which is to endure through love and suffering until the end with a "dark working"; and what it begins, it remains with, and does not cease until the end. ### 48.

## For Thursday in the Easter Holidays.

How one should love God, and how Christ is a Master of the eternal good, for which reason one should love him above all things; a Master of the supreme truth, for which reason one should contemplate him; and a Master of the supreme perfection, for which reason one should follow him without any hindrance.

->Turning, she said to him: Rabboni, which means Master. John 20:16. <note>original: "Conversa illa dixit ei: Rabboni, quod dicitur Magister."</note><-

When our Lord had risen from death, Mary Magdalene desired to see our dear Lord with all earnestness; then our Lord revealed himself to her in the form of a gardener, and Mary did not recognize him. Then our Lord said to her: "Mary," and in that word she recognized him and said: "Rabboni," which is to say, "Master."

Now take note: as long as Mary stood by the grave and looked at the angels, Christ stood behind her, hiding himself from her. For God the Lord hides himself from people who are preoccupied with creatures <term>Creaturen</term> <note>In mystical theology, "creatures" refers to anything created (people, objects, worldly status) as opposed to the Creator.</note> and who grieve over the loss of earthly things and creatures; but if a person turns away from the creatures to find God, then God reveals himself to the person. ...addressed: Mary; this signifies as much as a Star of the Sea, a Lady [Queen] of the world, and one who is enlightened by the Holy Spirit. <note>The author provides a traditional medieval etymology for the name Mary, specifically the Latin *stella maris* (star of the sea) and *illuminatrix* (enlightener).</note>

When she heard the word that Christ spoke to her: "Mary," she then recognized our Lord and said: "Rabboni," <note>A Hebrew/Aramaic term meaning "my teacher" or "my master."</note> which is as much as to say, "Master," for she and his other disciples and his followers usually spoke this word to him, as he says: "You call me Master and Lord, and you say rightly, for I am he"; <note>Refers to John 13:13.</note> for he is truly a Master of the highest good, and for this reason, one should love him above all things. He is (as I said first) a Master of the highest good, and therefore one should love him above all things. Now you might say: "God is unmeasured, a supreme good without end, and the soul is measured, as are all creatures; how then can the soul love and know God?" Ah, listen: God is unmeasured and without end, and the soul’s desire is an abyss that cannot be filled except with a good that is unmeasured; and the more the soul desires God, the more it wants to desire him, and the more the soul loves God, the more it wants to love him, for God is a good without any defect, and is a well of living water without bottom, and the soul is formed in the image of God, and for this reason, the soul is created to know and love God. Since Christ is then a Master of the highest good, the soul should love him above all things, for he is Love, and from him love flows into us, as from a well of life. The well of life is love, and whoever is not in love is dead. St. John says in his epistle: <note>Refers to 1 John 3:14: "He who does not love remains in death."</note> Since Christ is now a well and a Master of the highest good, the soul should love him without any resistance. For it is the soul's nature that it should love what God is, and therefore it should love that which is the highest good, without measure, without companion, and without silence. <note>In this context, "without silence" likely refers to the soul's constant, active expression of love or prayer.</note>

The soul shall love God without measure; of this, St. Bernard speaks thus: The reason why the soul should love God is God [Himself], but the measure of this love is to be without measure, <note>original: "Die Ursache, warum die Seele Gott lieb haben soll, ist Gott, aber das Maaß dieser Liebe ist ohne Maaß." Therefore Paul spoke: I pray to God that your love may always grow and be increased. And St. Bernard says: In the love of God, no other way or distinction is to be kept than that we love God as He has loved us. He has loved us unto the end, so that we should love Him without end. Therefore, here in this time, our desire should constantly increase inwardly; and although the inward work of our love for God should grow in every way, yet the outward work of love should be measured with proper discretion, <note>The German *Bescheidenheit* here refers to the medieval virtue of *discretio*—the ability to moderate physical penance and outward works so as not to destroy the body’s health.</note> so that one performs outward exercises in such a way that they do not destroy nature but subject it to the spirit.

Secondly, the soul should love God without companions; <note>original: "ohne Gesellen." In this mystical context, it means loving God exclusively, without allowing any other created thing to compete for the soul's primary affection.</note> that is, in the degree of love in which the soul loves God, no creature shall stand, and everything the soul loves, it shall love toward God and in God; furthermore, it shall love creatures for God's sake, toward God, and in God. <term>Creatures</term> <note>In theological terms, "creatures" refers to anything created by God—including people, animals, and material objects—rather than the Creator Himself.</note> The soul loves creatures for God’s sake when it loves them for the sake of the cause, which is God; it loves creatures toward God when it loves them toward the good which is God; it loves creatures in God when it loves them in such a way that it seeks no other pleasure nor any other goal in them but God, and thus it loves creatures in God and God in creatures. Therefore Christ says: You shall love God your Lord with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your thoughts. St. Augustine interprets these words and says: Our Lord says "you shall love God with all your heart, with all your soul, etc." so that man keeps no kind of power within himself in the soul that is vain or empty of the love of God, that is, without the love of God. And everything that comes into the soul's mind to love, let it love all that for God's sake and use it in divine love; for the Lord loves the soul, and so the soul should also love God without companions.

## 49.
# For the First Sunday after Easter.

->How we should ascend through three stages by the abandonment of ourselves and all things<-
->to true peace and purity of our hearts.<-
->Peace be with you. John 20:19–31. <note>original Latin: "Pax vobis."</note><-

"Peace be with you!" spoke our beloved Lord to His disciples after His resurrection. All people naturally desire rest and peace, and they pursue it with all their manifold actions, exercises, and labors; and yet they never come to true peace throughout eternity unless they seek it where it is to be found: in God alone. What then are the manners and ways to true peace, and to the purest, highest, and most perfect truth? Now note what I will tell you in a parable <note>The author uses "parable" (Gleichniß) here to mean a spiritual allegory or illustrative comparison.</note>: how our dear Lord drew Saint John in three ways; even so He still draws all people who are meant to come to the most direct truth.

First, our Lord Jesus Christ drew Saint John when He called him from the world and made him an apostle. Secondly, when He let him rest upon His lovely breast <note>This refers to the scene at the Last Supper where John, the "beloved disciple," reclined next to Jesus (John 13:23), a common image in medieval and early modern devotion representing intimate contemplation.</note>. Thirdly—which was the most perfect—on the holy day of Pentecost, when the Holy Spirit was given to him and a door was opened through which he was taken up.

Thus, the person is also, along with Saint John, first [drawn] from the <note>The text cuts off here, continuing the first stage of the spiritual journey on the following page.</note>

<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion on spiritual stages, specifically moving from the external imitation of Christ to the internal transformation of the soul. Following the description of the "spiritual flash" of the Holy Spirit, the author now focuses on the ultimate goal of this journey: the cultivation of a "pure heart."</meta>

A heart is worth more to God than anything else on Earth. A pure heart is a noble, well-adorned place, a dwelling of the Holy Spirit, a golden temple of the Godhead, a holy house of prayer for the only-begotten Son in which he worships his heavenly Father, and an altar of the high divine sacrifice upon which the Son is daily offered to the heavenly Father. 

A pure heart is a throne of the supreme judge, a place of rest and a chamber of the Holy Trinity, a lamp of the eternal light, a secret council chamber of the divine Persons <note>The "divine Persons" refers to the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit acting in council within the soul.</note>, a treasury of all divine riches, a storehouse of divine sweetness, a shield of eternal wisdom, and a cell of divine mystery. It is a requital <note>original: "Wiedervergeltung" – in this context, it suggests the heart is the place where Christ’s earthly suffering finally finds its reward and fulfillment.</note> for all the life and suffering of Christ, a tent for the heavenly Father, a bride of Christ, and a friend of the Holy Spirit. 

It is a delightful feast for the eyes of all the saints, a sister to the angels, a longing expectation of the heavenly host, a brother to all good people, and an abomination to enemies. It is a victory <note>original: "Victoria"</note> and an overcoming of all temptations, a weapon against every attack, a collection of all divine goodness, a treasure of all virtue, an example for all people, and a restoration of everything that was ever lost. 

What then is a pure heart? It is that which—as has been written before—is entirely and purely satisfied with God; that which finds no taste nor desire for anything but God; that which has placed its thoughts and mind entirely in God at all times. To such a heart, everything is foreign and distant that is not God, or for which God is not the cause. It is a heart that keeps itself free from foreign images <term>images: "Bilden" refers to the sensory or mental distractions that pull the soul away from direct, imageless union with the divine.</term>, from worldly love and sorrow, and from all external anxieties and cares as much as it is able, turning all things toward the best. For to the pure, all things are pure, and to the gentle, nothing is bitter. Amen.

## On Quasimodogeniti Sunday.
<note>The name for the first Sunday after Easter, taken from the Latin opening of the day's liturgy: "Quasi modo geniti infantes," meaning "as newborn babes."</note>

->Concerning the right, inward, and fruitful prayer, which is called: true union with God; which is above all words and the practice of external prayer. Concerning three ways through which one enters into the lowest <note>In this mystical context, "lowest" (unterste) refers to the most fundamental or deepest foundation of truth.</note> truth.<-

->Father, glorify me. John 17:1—5. *) Father, glorify me.<-
<note>original: "Clarifica me Pater." In mystical theology, "clarification" or "glorification" refers to the soul being made radiant and transparent by the light of God.</note>

The Son of God, as he lifted up his eyes to heaven, spoke: Father, glorify your Son.

This work teaches us that we should lift up our senses, hands, powers, and minds on high, and pray in him, with him, and through him. This is the most highly worthy prayer and work that God’s Son performed here, as he worshipped his Father. This is beyond the reason of all men, and no one can reach it or understand it unless it be by the Holy Spirit. Of this prayer, Anselm <note>St. Anselm of Canterbury (1033–1109), a Benedictine monk and philosopher.</note> and St. Augustine say that it is an ascent of the mind into God.

The wealthy come to you poor, weary, sick children, and give you four or six <term>Heller</term> <note>A small German copper coin of very little value.</note>, and command you to perform many prayers, or to say a hundred <term>Our Fathers</term> <note>original: "Pater noster."</note>. Of this transaction, and other such ways, God in his eternity holds as much as he wills; but I tell you one thing: turn yourself in truth away from yourself and from all created things, and direct your mind entirely toward God, above every creature, into the deep abyss. For all oral prayer is just like chaff and straw compared to noble wheat. Christ spoke: The true worshippers pray in spirit and in truth. In this, all exercises are fulfilled—all words, works, and manners that have existed from the time of Adam and will yet be until the final day; the inward worshippers accomplish all of that in a single moment through this true, essential inward turning. 

You see this church and the manifold things belonging to it, such as the foundation, the walls, the stones used for it, and those who carried it all here—all of this was done for the sake of prayer. And in this inward prayer, everything is essentially brought to true fruit and into God, for which purpose it all came to be; yes, in a single moment it is carried back into the "Ground" <note>The "Grund" refers to the deepest, most essential part of the soul where it meets the divine.</note> from which it flowed out and where it has been eternally present. 

Of this our dear Lord spoke: I have done all things well that you gave me to do <note>original: "Ich habe alle Dinge wohl gethan..."—A reference to John 17:4.</note>. Had he meant this according to human time, it would not have been so, for much was still undone; he was still to suffer and rise again. But he meant it according to the manner of eternity, where all things are as they have been eternally and shall be eternally; thus they are now in this "Now" <note>original: "Nu." A central concept in German mysticism referring to the "Eternal Now" (nunc stans) where time does not exist.</note>.

There they pray and work in the Spirit, where the Father brings forth his Son; there they are "in-born" <note>A mystical term for the soul being birthed back into God.</note> again. The spirit is carried back into the Ground, above all image and form, and—

Reason cannot grasp this union, and that is no wonder; for if a person cannot grasp how the soul is united with the body—how it acts and moves in the hand, the feet, and the other limbs—how then should a person understand divine union? This is closer than prayer—yes, much closer. Those who have grown up only in their natural reason, and are drawn into their own folly and have lived according to their own senses, cannot reach this state at all.

...belong to the truth? Our Lord Jesus drew Saint John in three ways; He still draws all people in this same manner who are meant to come to the closest truth. Now, our Lord drew Saint John first when He called him from the world and made him an apostle. For the second time, our Lord let him rest upon His loving heart <note>A reference to John reclining against Jesus at the Last Supper (John 13:23).</note>. For the third time—which is the most perfect—this was on the day of Pentecost, when the Holy Spirit was given to him, and he was thus completely taken up into God.

Now, regarding the first stage: a person is called from the world just as Saint John was. This means that the person governs and orders all their lower faculties through supreme discernment <note>original: "Bescheidenheit." In this context, it refers to the medieval virtue of *discretio* (discernment or spiritual judgment), rather than modern modesty.</note>, so that you learn to know yourself and remain centered within yourself. You must learn to take heed of your words, and do nothing to anyone else that you would not want done to you. You must watch your impulses, seeing whether they come from God and return to God; and guard your thoughts, so that you do not willfully possess any evil or useless thought. (Whatever thoughts might occur to you involuntarily are nothing more than a preparation and a purification for the improvement of your works.) In all your words and works, you should intend nothing but the honor of God, and your own salvation and peace, as well as that of all people. In this way, our dear Lord takes you from the world and makes you an apostle of God; and thus, you learn to transform the outer person into an inner person. This is still the stage of a beginner.

For the second stage, if you wish to rest upon the heart of our Lord Jesus Christ, you must maintain a diligent gaze upon Him. Look upon His gentleness and humility, and His gentle, enkindling love which He has for both His friends and His enemies. Look at the great, obedient yieldedness <term>Gelassenheit: A central concept in German mysticism meaning a state of letting go, detachment from self-will, and utter surrender to God.</term> which He maintained in every way and in every place where the Father called Him. Now, take note of His deep gentleness which He shows to all people, and His blessed poverty. The kingdom of heaven and the kingdom of earth were His, yet He never possessed them with self-interest <note>original: "Eigenschaft." This refers to the spiritual ego’s claim of ownership or attachment to things.</note>. Everything He spoke and everything He performed was intended for His Father's honor and the salvation of all people. Now, look into this lovely image of our Lord Jesus Christ much more closely and deeply than I can teach you. Look diligently at yourself and see how unlike this image you are; look at your own injustice and your smallness, and there our Lord allows you to rest well. For this purpose, nothing in this temporal life is better for you, nor...

...more useful than the Sacrament of the tender Body of Christ <note>original: "Frohnleichnam," referring to the Eucharist</note> our Lord Jesus Christ; for in this food you find all wealth and sweetness and power, through which you truly renounce all the comfort and sweetness of this world.

These two ways often exist in many people who think themselves to be in a very good state, yet they act with self-will <note>original: "Eigenſchaft," a technical term in German mysticism for the state of being attached to one's own ego or possessions</note> and a hasty spirit, and thus they distance themselves from the most direct path. Likewise, however holy you may be in these two ways, see to it that when you are attacked, you do not let your cloak fall; by this I mean your self-will and the hastiness of your spirit. That you practice yourself in these two ways is good and holy, and you should let no creature take the practice of these ways from you, unless God Himself draws you closer.

The third way: if Christ then draws you without form, without image, and without activity, then be His instrument; that is much more praiseworthy to Him and more useful to you—that you remain in this state for the duration of one *Our Father* <note>original: "Pater noſter"</note>—than if you practiced the other two ways for a hundred years. Now some people say: "Have you not gone beyond that?" I say: No! Now look with diligence and perceive the order of God from within, and take your ways one after the other. Here the door is unlatched and opened, to some with a single pull, to others with a state of releasement <term>Gelaſſenheit: a central concept in German mysticism meaning a spirit of surrender, letting go, and being at rest in God</term>. Here Saint Paul’s <note>original: "St. Pauli"</note> word is fulfilled: *What no eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man, that is what God reveals here.* <note>1 Corinthians 2:9</note> A person should never expect to become perfect (so far as it is possible here), unless the outer man is brought into the inner man; there the person is taken up. There such a wonder, such a wealth is revealed, that he who wished to gaze long upon it would often have to lie in bed, for nature could not bear it. Now know, before that which we have spoken of here can be fulfilled, many deaths must fall upon nature, outwardly and inwardly; to this same death, eternal life answers. And this does not happen in one day—

## On the second Sunday after Easter.

->The first sermon.<-

Concerning a good shepherd: how he should faithfully guard and pasture his sheep for the glory of God, and conduct himself well therein.
I am the good shepherd; the good shepherd gives his life <note>original: "Seele," literally "soul," but in this biblical context referring to one's life</note> for his sheep. <note>original: "Ego sum pastor bonus, bonus pastor animam suam dat pro ovibus suis." John 10:14 (modern verse 11).</note> I am a good shepherd; a good shepherd gives his soul for his sheep.

What our Lord says here with words, he later proved with his works. He gave his soul unto death for his sheep; he feeds or pastures his sheep with physical necessities, and spiritually with his grace and love, with the holy sacraments, with the holy scripture, and with many other benefits, and later with that same blessedness which he possesses and is. His sheepfold is the holy Christian Church. Whoever separates himself from it, through mortal sins or through unbelief, will find his pasture in the eternal fire with the devil. Now, this good shepherd or pastor has given us an image in himself of how we should follow him, especially those who are called by God or their superiors to care for souls. I am not speaking of those who force themselves into this burdensome <note>original: "sorglichen," meaning full of care, anxiety, or responsibility</note> office, or are called to it but intend or seek something else in it other than pure...

the glory of God and the salvation of souls, for they are all hirelings <note>original: "Heuerlinge [Miethlinge]," referring to the "hireling" in the Parable of the Good Shepherd (John 10:12–13) who abandons the sheep in danger.</note> together, and they stand in a thousand dangers.
