For whoever resists what he must do out of obedience makes a heavy life for himself, because a small thing done unwillingly is worse than many things done with a will. 

It is also very good that one comes to an office without one’s own will, and that one has much to suffer therein; and where one ought to have help and counsel, that one has instead sorrow and trouble; and where one ought to have obedience, that one has instead malice and opposition. To hold mastery and offices at this time, and then to do right, does not mean tending to one's own comfort; it is a martyr's life and a heavy cross. But man should take this cross upon his back (for the sake of Him who took the miserable cross upon Himself for him, and was obedient unto death), settle his mind, and give himself captive to God with whole, humble serenity <note>original: "Gelassenheit," the mystical practice of letting go of self-will to be filled by God.</note>, as long as it is desired of him. 

He should not complain of his incapacity and unskillfulness; if he does the best that he understands, he is free of guilt, even if it is not the very best. In all things he should look more to God than to physical gain; he should not permit (if he might prevent it) any of his little sheep to be harmed in their soul. He should be common and lovely toward friends and enemies; that gives birth to peace. He should keep the young people especially under mastery, for ill-bred youth is the destruction of the community. He should have a sweet earnestness, and command more with love than with fear. What is too powerful for him, he should lay before his superiors; where he cannot bite, he should at least bark. If he cannot fully accomplish a godly life, he should be diligent so that it at least does not decline, nor that grave crimes happen under him. # 52.

## On the Wednesday before Palm Sunday.

Concerning the internal temple and its dedication. Concerning the spiritual winter, of which two kinds are described, and what passive detachment <term>Gelassenheit: a core concept in German mysticism meaning a state of let-go-ness, surrender to God's will, and internal peace.</term> may bring; what the evil, envious, or the pious Jews signify for us spiritually. Why the friends of Christ are called his little sheep, and also concerning the different ways and practices of the Gentiles and Jews.

John 10:16. *) and especially on the words of Christ: *My sheep hear my voice, etc.* <note>original: "Oves meae vocem meam audiunt etc."</note>

At one time there was a Feast of Dedication <term>Kirchweihe: the anniversary of the consecration of a church; here referring to the Hanukkah festival in Jerusalem.</term> in Jerusalem, and it was winter, and the Lord Jesus walked in Solomon’s house of prayer <note>original: "Bethaus," likely referring to Solomon's Porch, a colonnade in the Temple complex.</note>, and the Jews went around him and said: How long will you keep our souls in suspense? If you are the Christ, tell us plainly. And among many words (which our Lord spoke), he also said: My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me, and I give them eternal life, and no one shall snatch them out of my hand. And this happened in Solomon’s house of prayer, for David says: He has made his city in peace. Solomon means as much as peaceful <note>original: "pacificus"</note>. This is the eternal Solomon <note>A common medieval trope identifying King Solomon as a "type" or precursor to Christ, the true King of Peace.</note>, whose city may be nowhere else but in peace, in inward peace.

Jesus went into the temple, and it was the Feast of Dedication. This temple, where Jesus enters, is the pure soul with its pure inwardness, upon which God has bestowed more diligence than upon all other creatures, and has worked more within it. In this temple was a Feast of Dedication, that is: a renewal. Now, how does this renewal happen in this temple, where God so gladly dwells—indeed, much more essentially than in all temples that were ever built or consecrated? That is called "new" which is near to its origin or beginning. When a person turns inward with all their powers and with their soul, and enters into this temple where they [encounter] God in eternity...

This occurred in the winter. Now, when is it winter? There is a true winter when the heart has grown cold and hard, so that neither grace, nor God, nor divine things are in the heart; for the cold snow and frost, these are the troublesome, withered, and corrupt creatures <note>In mystical writing, "creatures" refers to any created things—people, objects, or worldly desires—that distract the soul from the Creator.</note> which have possessed the heart with love and with pleasure. These especially extinguish the fire of the love of the Holy Spirit and create a strange coldness toward all grace, all comfort, and all intimacy, which they extinguish entirely. There is also another winter, where a good, godly person, who loves and intends God and diligently guards against sin, is nevertheless forsaken by God in an experiential way, and becomes dry, and dark, and cold, deprived of all divine comfort and sweetness.

In this winter was our Lord, who was thus entirely forsaken by his heavenly Father in his hour of need, and by the Godhead (with which he was nevertheless naturally united), so that not a single drop of his Godhead ever came to the aid of his sick, suffering humanity <note>original: "Menschheit"</note> for a single moment in all his distress and in his unspeakable suffering. He was, before all men, the most suffering and the most forsaken of all, without any help. In this way, his chosen...

For you are giving to the creature that which belongs by nature to God alone.

## 53.<sup>b</sup>

### On the third Sunday after Easter (Jubilate).

->The second part.<-

*How we cannot see God if the light of creatures shines in us (however small it may be). How the eternal Word is itself the medium and the image—which is without medium and without image—so that the soul may comprehend and recognize within the eternal Word, without medium and without image. "A little while," or "a small thing," <note>original: "Ueber ein wenig, oder Kleines"</note> and you will not see me. You should know this: if the soul saw God from afar—as if through a medium, or in a cloud, even for a single moment—she would never turn away from God for the sake of this whole world. What then do you imagine it is like when one sees God clearly within oneself as He is, without any medium, in His naked essence? All <term>creatures: all things that have been created, including people, animals, and objects</term> that God ever made, or could still make if He willed, are all just "a little" or "a small thing" compared to God. The heavens are so large and so vast; if I told you the scale, you would not believe it. Yet, if someone took a needle and touched the sky with its point, the proportion of that needle-point to the heavens and this whole world would be far greater than the proportion of this whole world to God. Therefore, it is very well said:
> A little while, or a small thing, and you will not see me.

As long as any "something" <note>original: "icht," meaning any trace of creaturely attachment</note> of created things shines within you, you do not see God; however small that thing may be, it must be removed. Therefore, the soul spoke in the <term>Book of Love: the Song of Solomon</term>:
> I went about and sought him whom my soul loves, and I found him not.

She found angels and many things, but she did not find the one her soul loved. She said:
> Afterward, when I had gone a little further, I found him whom my soul loves;

It is as if she were saying: "When I leaped over all creatures (which are the 'little' and the 'small thing'), then I found the one I was seeking."

Now know that God loves the soul so powerfully that, if one could take away God’s love for the soul, one would take away His life and His essence—or one would "kill" God, if such a thing could be said. For that same love with which God loves the soul is the very love in which the Holy Spirit blossoms forth, and that same love *is* the Holy Spirit. Since God loves the soul so powerfully, the soul must be a great thing indeed. One <term>Master: likely referring to a philosopher like Aristotle or a scholastic scholar</term> writes in the *Book of the Soul*:
> If there were no medium, the eye would see an ant or a gnat in the heavens,

and he speaks truly, meaning the fire and air and many things that exist between the heavens and the eyes. Another Master says:
> If there were no medium, an eye would see nothing;

they are both right.

The first says: "If there were no medium, my eye would see an ant..."

Boethius, a master, says: <note>original: "Boethius, ein Meister." Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius (c. 477–524 AD) was a philosopher whose works, especially *The Consolation of Philosophy*, were central to medieval education.</note>

Note this by looking at a mirror: if you have it before you, your image appears in the mirror, yet you are not in the mirror yourself. The eye and the soul are such a mirror in which everything appears that is held before them; therefore I do not see the hand or the stone, but rather I see an image of the stone. But that same image I do not see through another image, or through a medium; rather, I see it without a medium and without an image, for the image itself is the medium and not another medium. Thus also is the "image without an image," for it is not seen in another image. Therefore, the eternal Word <note>The "Eternal Word" refers to Christ (the Logos), who is seen here as the perfect bridge between the human and the Divine.</note> is the medium and the image itself; it is without medium and without image, so that the soul may grasp and recognize in the eternal Word, without medium and without image.

A power is in the soul: <term>Reason: the higher intellect or the faculty of spiritual understanding</term>. As she becomes aware of God or tastes Him, she gains five properties. The first is that she separates from "here and now"; the second, that she is not like anything else; the third, that she is unmixed; the fourth, that she is active or seeking within herself; the fifth, that she is an image.

...to ensure that the dear disciples of God and His dear friends might not receive the Holy Spirit, unless Jesus Christ first departed from them. What then is His departing from us? Any person who could maintain themselves essentially and remained detached within this state would find all multiplicity turned into unity; they would have joy in suffering, be patient in contempt, and possess constant peace amidst discord; all bitterness would become true sweetness to them.

### 56.

# For the Fifth Sunday after Easter.

->On three kinds of attachment, <term>Attachment (Ungelassenheit)</term> <note>The original German "Ungelassenheit" refers to a state of being "un-let-go," or clinging to one's self-will and worldly desires. It is the opposite of "Gelassenheit" (detachment/releasement).</note> and how we should let go of ourselves again and again, and always begin anew, until we are completely transformed into Christ, and concerning true poverty of spirit.<-
->“Again, I leave the world and go to the Father.” John 16:28. <note>Original Latin: "Iterum relinquo mundum, et vado ad patrem."</note><-

The labor, diligence, teaching, and example of our lovely Lord Jesus Christ were all directed toward teaching his beloved friends and bringing them inward into the pure ground, into the light of truth. He saw that they were so focused on his outward humanity that they could not attain the true Good, and therefore he had to leave them. Children, away with all glosses and all cloaks! <note>Suso uses "glosses" (interpretations) and "cloaks" (coverings) as metaphors for the intellectual excuses or spiritual pretenses people use to avoid the raw demands of faith.</note> Just as the Son of the Heavenly Father, the Eternal Wisdom, was a hindrance to his disciples, so too there is no creature on earth that does not hinder you—regardless of what it is, what it is called, or how it appears to you—it must be fundamentally cast off and out if we are to receive the lovely Good which is God.

Now, one finds three kinds of people: some are "departing," others are "approaching," and the third are "entering." These are the beginning, the increasing, and the perfect people. <note>These correspond to the traditional three stages of the spiritual life: the Purgative (beginners), the Illuminative (proficients), and the Unitive (the perfect).</note> When a person begins, he should drive through bravely and search through every corner of his soul to see if he finds anything therein that he has possessed with worldly desire, or if any fleeting creatures dwell in some corner; let him hunt them all out. This must of necessity be the first of all things, just as children are first taught their A-B-C. If all this does not happen at once, do not be terrified; only do not stop. One reads a word to children over and over until they know it well; again and again. So, let go of yourself again, and again, and again. “Again I leave the world”; that means all things. In the morning, when you first open your eyes, say: “Alas, most beloved, highest Good, see, now I will begin again to let go of myself and all things for your sake.” And do this a thousand times a day.

Now, one finds people who, when they "let go" of themselves, promptly take themselves back again: some in a crafty way, others in an animalistic way, and the third in the manner of Lucifer. Now, understand the crafty way. Human nature is truly rogue-like and seeks its own interest very nimbly. "God bless me," one says, "I surely mean well." Many people are so "un-let-go" <note>Ungelassen: lacking detachment.</note> that if they are in a gathering, they behave like rabid dogs—barking and scolding—simply because of a book or some other small thing. A noble, spiritual person should be so detached that if they were struck on one cheek, they should offer the other; whatever was done to them, they should remain at peace. Of the lovely image of our Lord Jesus Christ, people said he was a misleader, a traitor, and was possessed by the devil. He remained silent, and endured and suffered it graciously.

Whether one eats, one sleeps, one speaks, one remains silent—whatever it may be on earth, or whatever one does—one should suppress one's animalistic inclination and act from reason and love, thus praying and thinking: "Dear Lord, for You and not for myself I eat, I sleep, I live, I suffer, and I let go of all things."

A spiritual man once desired a "great life" <note>In this context, a "great life" refers to a state of high spiritual perfection or enlightenment.</note>, and it seemed to him that he was led before a great school in which there were many students who were studying intensely and were very industrious. Then his brother spoke to them: "Dearest companions, this is a high school of which I have heard wonders; tell me, what study do you learn here?" One answered: "Nothing other than a thorough **letting go** of ourselves in all things." "Ah, here I truly wish to remain, even if I should die a thousand deaths for it, and I want to build a cell here." "No," said the other, "go on, gently and easily; the less you *do* and the more you *let go* of yourself, the more you have done." 

People are truly blinded and want to do much, and ask so many questions, as if they wanted to educate God, doing everything according to themselves, in their own will, full of self-opinion, in their own nature. No, it is not through your own fighting, but through **letting go**, through dying and perishing, and through renouncing; as long as a single drop of blood in you remains un-killed, un-died, and un-conquered, you are lacking. The dear Paul spoke: *I live, yet not I, but Christ lives in me!* <note>original: "Ich lebe, nicht ich, sondern Christus lebt in mir!" from Galatians 2:20.</note> Know this: as long as anything lives in you that is not God—whether it be yourself or whatever else it is—God never lives perfectly in you.

The third group turn themselves around in a Lucifer-like way. God created Lucifer delightfully and adorned him nobly; what did he do...

Our Lord teaches us therein that we should ask, and says:

> Whoever asks, to him it shall be given. Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives, and he who seeks finds, and to him who knocks, it will be opened.

Now, what distinction should one draw from these three words: ask, seek, knock? We wish to explain that first. **Asking** signifies a soul turned toward God with an inward desire, requesting something from Him. But **seeking** is a choosing of one thing over another; for he who seeks has turned his diligence especially toward that which he seeks above all other things. **Knocking**, however, signifies persistence and not giving up until one obtains or receives that which he intends and desires to have. And thus, these words have a clear distinction: ask, seek, knock.

Now let us take the interpretation of the teacher <term>Bede</term> <note>Bede the Venerable (c. 672–735), an English monk and scholar whose homilies and biblical commentaries were widely read in the Middle Ages.</note> in his homilies, where he says:

> This friend who has come from the country to his friend, that is the <term>mind</term> <note>original: "Gemüth." In this context, it refers to the seat of human thought, will, and emotion.</note> of man. The mind often and truly wanders from the person into a far, "foreign land of inequality" <note>original: "fremdes Land der Ungleichheit." This is a reference to the Augustinian concept of the *regio dissimilitudinis*, the "land of unlikeness," where the soul wanders when it forgets its divine origin.</note>, and often returns again hungry and thirsty for all that is good; and so, the person then has nothing to set before it. Thus, he goes to his friend, who is God, and knocks and asks at His door that He might give him three loaves of bread—that is, the understanding of the **Holy Trinity**. And He who is within excuses Himself and says: "Do not trouble me, for my doors are locked, and my children are with me in bed." This means: the teachers are with God in the "bed" of holy **contemplation**.

Now, this man persists for a long time, knocking until the other rises and gives him everything he desires. He gives him an answer through teaching or through Himself "without means" <note>Without intermediaries or physical tools; a direct spiritual experience.</note>. And therefore Christ said:

> Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you.

Here we should note the inexpressible <term>gentleness</term> <note>original: "Mildigkeit." This carries the sense of both mercy and bountiful generosity.</note> of God, that He so gladly gives if we would only ask Him—He who so diligently admonishes, draws, and teaches us that we should ask Him. But the gifts are not given to the idle, nor to the sluggish and negligent, nor to those empty of grace, but to those who ask and persist in prayer.

Children, if you knew how perilously these people—with such a [false] foundation—receive the highly venerable, precious Blood (which God shed for us), and do not perceive their own false foundation, you might perish from anxiety. For this reason, it is the custom in some monasteries that one must go to the **Sacrament** every three weeks; and they provide so much time so that one may always prepare oneself well for the **great banquet** <note>A traditional metaphor for the Eucharist, framing it as a spiritual feast for the soul.</note>, so that the holy, worthy Sacrament may achieve its work within the person. You should stir up your desire for it and conduct yourselves so that you may frequently receive the holy Sacrament. Pray to our Lord that he may prepare you himself, and live willingly and inwardly, and be gentle, humble, and <term>detached</term> <note>original: "abgeschieden." A master of scripture was asked how it pleased him that some people desired to receive our Lord so often, outside of their usual community and custom? Then this master spoke: "O Lord God, how we should inwardly rejoice that there might be someone who hungers for God and desires Him; and those monasteries that do this, the others serve them and help them toward it with great diligence." Let no one among those who go to our Lord think that people are more wicked who do not do so; for they refrain out of great humility and a sense of worthiness, because it is such a great thing. If it happens that someone throws stones of judgment against you and strikes you with words, remember that it has, without doubt and without intermediary, come from God.

There are also other stones: when a person is abandoned from within—one who desires God with all their heart—and finds themselves hard and dry, cold and sluggish. ...you, remain steadfast and reprove yourself even more harshly; and if that judgment should stand for an entire year, that would be very good; stone yourself with it before God, within your own self. You should do this as soon as you have fallen into any kind of **disorder** <note>original: "Unordnung." In this context, it refers to a state where the soul's priorities or passions are out of alignment with God's will.</note> in any way; confess to God immediately, without any delay. If your failings then slip your mind, so that you do not know how to speak of them when you come to the **confessor**, then believe that your sin is more forgiven than if you had confessed it to the priest himself. For the Holy Church has ordained **confession** <note>original: "Beichte."</note> for **mortal sin** <note>original: "Todsünde." A grave sin committed with full knowledge and consent that separates the soul from God's grace.</note>; and if you are in doubt whether something is a mortal sin, make it brief. And do you think that outward works hinder you—such as going to the choir or performing dutiful works of obedience? No, these cannot lead you astray or hinder you; rather, your own lack of order in these works hinders you, because you have not set God purely before you in your love, in your intention, and in your **inner disposition** <note>original: "Gemüth." A central term in German mysticism referring to the deepest seat of the soul’s powers.</note>. Thus, you are distracted and **deformed** <note>original: "verbildet." Literally "mis-imaged"; the soul is distracted from God's image by filling itself with worldly images.</note> <insert>[clinging to the images of multiplicity]</insert>, and in this way, you hinder yourself.

Furthermore, our Lord says: He is the door through which one must pass.

At this door, the petitioning person should knock in three places, so that they may be let in through the Truth. Firstly, one should knock with devotion before the opened heart and the pierced side of our Lord Jesus Christ, with an inward drawing-in, with all devotion and acknowledgment of one's bottomless poverty and one's nothingness—just as the poor **Lazarus** <note>A reference to the beggar in the Gospel of Luke who waited for crumbs at the rich man's gate.</note> did at the rich man’s door—and beg for the **crumbs** <note>original: "Brosämlein."</note> of His grace. Grace grants you a divine, supernatural being.

Knock a second time at the door of the holy, opened wounds of His sacred hands, and pray for true divine knowledge, that it may enlighten you and lift you up to Him. After that, knock at the door of His holy feet and pray for true, divine love, which may unite you with Him, and sink and enclose you within Him. That we may all thus pray, seek, and knock, so that we may be let in—may God help us in this. Amen.

## 58.
# On Ascension Day.
### The First Sermon.

How God the Lord punishes certain people, especially the clergy, because of their unbelief and the hardness of their hearts; where such hardness comes from, described under the parable of an old, foul cistern that is dug into these people. Concerning defilement through foreign images; also regarding the living water and the four degrees of divine love.

*As the eleven disciples were reclining, Jesus appeared and rebuked their unbelief and the hardness of their hearts. Mark 16:14.* <note>original Latin: "Recumbentibus undecim discipulis apparuit Jesus, et exprobravit incredulitatem illorum et duritiam cordis."</note>

When the disciples of our Lord sat together, the Lord Jesus appeared to them and rebuked them for their unbelief and the hardness of their hearts.

Our Lord still carries out this rebuke every day and at all times, because of the unbelief and hardness of heart found in all people from all places in the world. He especially rebukes all "spiritual people" <note>original: "geistliche Menschen." In this medieval context, this refers to anyone who has taken religious vows or dedicated their life to the Church, including monks, nuns, and friars.</note>, whether they are from established religious orders or are "assumed" spiritual people, such as <term>Beguines</term> <note>Beguines were laywomen in the Middle Ages who lived in religious communities but did not take formal, permanent vows like nuns.</note>, sisters, brothers, and the like. Our Lord rebukes them through teachers, or through Himself in their <term>Interiority</term> <note>original: "Inwendigkeit." A central concept in German mysticism referring to the deep, inward space of the soul where man meets God.</note>, to see if they will take heed of the rebuke. These spiritual people are rightly to be rebuked for being so hard of heart and for not believing; for it is a great thing that God chooses a person and calls them to the high nobility of a spiritual life. For this, we owe God great love and, above all things, gratitude.

Our Lord rebukes these people because they are unbelieving and hard of heart; but they are reluctant to be rebuked for it. Yet it would be good if they acknowledged the hardness of their hearts and their unbelief, so that they might still receive good counsel. <term>St. James</term> <note>original: "St. Jacobus." Refers to James 2:17: "Faith by itself, if it is not accompanied by action, is dead."</note> says: Faith without works is dead; but they only say,

as it is written:

We profess the faith with our mouths. St. Paul, on the other hand, says:

when these people have fallen away from the true, living faith, and especially those who have a "spiritual" name <note>Referring to those who hold religious titles or have taken vows.</note>, and those who have perhaps been touched by God, whether sleeping or waking, and called into the depths, but have fallen away from it.

Our Lord also punishes them for the hardness of their hearts, and it is a great and grizzly thing that God has called them to Himself, yet they are so hard that divine things do not "taste" good to them—whether it be their prayer or other good exercises—and that other things are so easy and joyful to them, while toward God their hearts are entirely stones! > I will take from you your stony hearts, and give you again a fleshy heart. <note>Ezekiel 36:26. A "fleshy heart" here refers to a heart that is soft, receptive, and alive, rather than literal flesh.</note>

Of this, our Lord spoke through Jeremiah the Prophet:

While literally "unlock yourselves," in this scriptural context (Jeremiah 2:12) it implies being shocked into desolation or shuddering.</note> with dread over my people, for they have committed two evils: They have forsaken me, the living water, and have dug for themselves hewn-out wells <note>The "hewn-out wells" refer to man-made cisterns, which collect stagnant rainwater rather than being fed by a fresh spring.</note> that contain no water.
Whatever enters there comes from the outside or from above—the rain or other water—which rots and stinks; and in the ground, they have nothing. God laments this great evil to heaven and earth, and to all creatures.

Who are the people over whom God laments? These are the "spiritual people," who have so completely forsaken the living waters that their own depths have as little light and life as outward things; and they remain in their sensual ways, in their formal ordinances...

brought in from the outside, through the senses in a pictorial way; but from within, in the Ground <term>Ground: "Grund," a central concept in German mysticism referring to the innermost essence of the soul where the human meets the Divine</term> where it ought to leap forth and well up, there is nothing at all. They do not turn inward to the Ground; therein they have no welling up, nor thirsting, and they seek nothing further. Once they have performed their tasks according to their own ways—which were brought to them from the outside through the senses—this satisfies them well enough. They cling to their "cisterns" <note>A reference to Jeremiah 2:13: "They have forsaken me, the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water."</note> which they have made for themselves, and God does not "taste" good to them, nor do they drink from the living water. They lie down and sleep, and in the morning they take up their old ways again; they are well satisfied with this and remain in it. Of such people, our Lord speaks in another chapter:

> You have practiced much unchastity <note>original: "Unkeuschheit." In this context, it refers to spiritual infidelity or being "cluttered" with worldly images rather than literal physical unchastity.</note> and have defiled yourself; that is, you have left me, the living fountain, and have dug yourself a cistern.

In the cistern, whatever is placed and carried into it becomes stinking and foul. That is to say: along with these sensory rules, there remains in the Ground pride <term>Hoffart: spiritual arrogance or vanity</term>, self-will, stubbornness, and harsh judgments; harsh words and the rebuking of one's neighbor—not out of love and gentleness, but where it has neither the right place nor time. Many a man imagines he wants to extinguish another’s house fire, while he burns down his own. Indeed, even if he had three houses, with his hard, hasty words and gestures, he would destroy them. If a poor child <note>Likely referring to a "child of God" or a simple, humble believer.</note> comes to them, they say: "That is a lowly or foolish person." If another person comes to them, they say: "That is a Beguine <note>A member of a lay religious community. In this period, the term was sometimes used pejoratively by critics of mystical or informal spirituality.</note>." 

Be gone, you true "cisterns"! If the living wellspring were in your parched Ground, there would never be such distinctions of persons within you; everything would become equal. If divine love were welling up from the Ground, there would be no belittling, no harsh judgments, nor any "bringing to nothing" <term>Vernichtigung: here used in the sense of disdainfully dismissing others, though in other contexts it refers to the mystical annihilation of the self before God</term>. This foulness all grows within the cisterns.

Furthermore, these cisterns are the "rationalists" <term>Vernünftigen: those who rely solely on natural reason or intellectual understanding in spiritual matters</term> with their lofty words and high understanding. One is satisfied with his good-seeming works; the other with his lofty words and understanding. How do you imagine it will go for them when the great storm-winds come rushing, throwing all things into confusion and causing them to fall—and such plagues that are so grisly and so full of anguish...

Then it will come to pass that such misery will be seen—which is unbelievable—in those who previously appeared quite beautiful in words and deeds with a seeming holiness, but in whom there is no true, living Ground <term>Ground: "Grund," the innermost essence of the soul where the human meets the Divine</term>. This is the greatest pain of the damned: that they acknowledge this within themselves, yet they shall never enter it.

Note and see the great, inexpressible, bottomless mercy of God—how gladly He would help us if we were willing, and how gladly He would speak kindly with us if we would turn to Him. Beware that He does not say there, that you [are far] from His...

[brought], concerning this I must contend with you at the judgment. If you would turn to me, I would pour living water and true love into you.

Regarding this living water, Richard <note>Likely Richard of St. Victor (d. 1173), a prominent mystical theologian famous for his treatise on the "Four Degrees of Violent Love."</note>, a great master of Holy Scripture, said that love has four degrees. The first degree is called a **wounded love**; when the soul is wounded by the beam of God's love so that the living water of true love is granted to her, she in turn wounds God with her love. Of this love, our Lord spoke in the Book of Love <note>The Song of Solomon (Song of Songs), which was interpreted by medieval mystics as an allegory for the love between God and the soul.</note>:
> My sister, you have wounded my heart with your eye, and with the hair of your neck.

The eye is the diligent gaze of acknowledgment and of the spirit <term>Gemüth: the seat of the soul's inner disposition, intellect, and will</term> that turns purely toward God, and the hair is pure, unmixed love; by these, God is wounded by the soul. By the second degree of true love, this master means **captive love**. It is written:
> I will draw you by the rope of Adam <note>Hosea 11:4. In the Latin Vulgate, "in funiculis Adam" refers to the "cords of a man," interpreted here as the bonds of love pulling the soul toward God.</note>.

The third is a **languishing love** <note>original: "quälende Liebe" (tormenting or agonizing love), reflecting the physical and emotional distress of longing for the Divine.</note>, of which the bride spoke in the Book of Love:
> You daughters of Jerusalem, if you find my beloved, tell him that I lie sick and ill from love.

The fourth love is the **consuming love**, of which the prophet spoke in the Psalter:
> Lord, my soul is consumed and has wasted away for your salvation.

Regarding wounded love, one may use a parable: whoever is wounded by love acts like a merchant who wishes to steer a ship for profit; his heart is as if sore with longing to gather much. He scrapes all sorts of things together and collects here and there so that his ship may become full. Thus does the wounded person: he gathers and pulls together all images, thoughts, and practices, and whatever he is able to do for the sake of the one he loves. 

Now when the ship is fully laden, he pushes off from the shore. He is still very much in control of the ship, to guide it against the storm. So it is with wounded love: it throws its ship into the storm of the Godhead <term>Gottheit: the essence of God beyond personal attributes, often described as a vast, trackless sea in mysticism</term>, and sails forth gloriously and plays therein according to its desire and will, and throws its oar into the sea, which is bottomless. And the more it draws divine influences into itself, the wider it becomes; He completely fills its receptivity, and this fulfillment creates new receptivity and new vastness, and new wounds of love. After this, the Lord cuts the ship's rope in two, and lets the ship

For it happens to him like a knight who is very badly wounded in a battle and yet mightily escapes; but if he is captured, he is no longer master of himself. So it is with one imprisoned by love: he is master of neither his thoughts nor his works; he must leave himself entirely to the Beloved under the power of love. So that we may leave all cisterns <note>Referring to the "broken cisterns" of Jeremiah 2:13 mentioned on the previous page.</note> and that the water of true love be poured into us—may true love help us to this. ### 59.

## On Ascension Day.

### The Second Sermon.

Concerning five kinds of imprisonment by which people are held captive and only with great difficulty set free; that is, the imprisonment of love for <term>creatures: all created things, people, and worldly objects as opposed to God the Creator</term>, self-love, love of reason, and love for the sweetness of the spirit and one's own will. Thereafter follows a very useful instruction on how one should prepare oneself for the reception of the Holy Spirit.

> <note>original: "Ascendens Christus in altum, captivam duxit captivitatem."</note> Christ, ascending on high, led captivity captive. Ephesians 4:8. *)
> Our Lord ascended to heaven and led the imprisonment captive with Him.

One finds five kinds of imprisonment with which people are heavily captive here in this time, which Christ carries up and takes away when He spiritually ascends within us.

The first is that man is made captive by the love of **creatures**, whether they be living or dead—anything that is not God—and especially human love, which is so close to our nature because of the similarity between people. The harm that comes from this cannot be fully expressed, and it manifests in two ways. Some acknowledge themselves...

The fifth prison is that of **self-will**, where a person wants to have their own way, even in all divine things and with God Himself. But when I reflect on whether I should have that will and desire, I would say: "No, Lord, not my grace, or gift, or will; but Lord, as You will, so I take it; or if it were not Your will, I want to go without and suffer want within Your will." It is infinitely more useful for them to have a willing, humble lack of the same, and to forgo all possession in true releasement and in the passing away of their own will. And therefore, I would rather have a truly released person with fewer works and less outward appearance, than a very high-minded person in works and appearance, with many grand images, but less releasement.

# On Ascension Day.

## The Third Sermon.

Tells how it is necessary for those who wish to ascend with Christ that they first follow him in his life; how one should recognize those who have been rightly touched by Christ; and what the cause is that some are not touched by God. Concerning Mount Olivet, upon which Christ ascended, and what that signifies to us spiritually; concerning the valley of tears, and concerning true inward devotion.
->Indeed, the Lord Jesus, after he had spoken to them, was taken up into heaven. Mark 16, verse 19. <note>original: "Dominus quidem Jesus postquam locutus est eis, assumptus est in coelum."</note> *)<-

And just as it happened to Jesus Christ, who was killed by the Jews—and they believed they were honoring God thereby—the same shall happen to you. For all the people who despise and condemn, torment or martyr you, believe in their own minds that they are doing God a great service, and intend to do so. Oh, dear children, how heartily blessed that person would be who then lived entirely in Jerusalem, in the city, and had a total peace within themselves amidst this unrest; then the true peace of God would be essentially and purely born in that person from the ground of God in truth.

Children, on this mountain grows the olive tree, by which we understand true divine devotion <term>devotion: "Andacht"; more than just a prayer, it implies a state of being "collected" or focused entirely on the divine</term>. Oh, God, what a sweet devotion that is for a person who always has a fervent, longing attachment to the pure God, with a ready and whole mind always to love and to intend all that belongs to God, so that one is always inwardly bound to God in will, in intention, and in all things. This is a joyful <note>original: "lustiger"; in this older context, it means delightful, pleasant, or flourishing.</note> olive tree, which always smells sweet before the heavenly Father and before all His chosen ones. If you have this within your ground, then you are in truth a devout person. This devotion should often be refreshed and renewed with the fire of divine love, and always with a diligent looking-upon and looking-into the ground...

Yet, alas! One finds it often, among both clergy and laypeople, that a person does not intend God purely in all things, and nothing else. He intends more for himself, in spirit and in nature. ### 61.

## On the Festival of the Ascension.

### The Fourth Sermon.

Teaches us how we can become God's witnesses, that is, to seek peace in unrest, joy in sadness, and comfort in bitterness, and thus to give witness to the Lord Jesus through life and following, and to confess Him, not only in pleasure and in comfort, but also in adversity and in suffering.

> You shall be my witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all the land of Judea and Samaria. <note>original: "Eritis mihi testes in Hierusalem, et in omni Judaea et Samaria." Acts 1, verse 8.</note>

Dear children, since our Head—which is Jesus Christ—has ascended into heaven, it is fitting and possible that the members follow their Head into heaven <note>A reference to the Pauline metaphor of the Church as the "Body of Christ," where Christ is the head and the faithful are the limbs or members.</note>, and seek nor desire no comfort, nor joy, nor residence in this time of instability, but only follow Him, and always [belong] to Him alone

Therefore, all people who ever wish to arrive there must become one with Him, and arrive there in Him, and with Him, and through Him.

Whichever person turns to this with diligence and earnestness, and gives leave to all creatures in love and in suffering, that same person would not err in his conscience, nor would he gain a dull, sick head; he would not always be turning about, asking one thing here and another there, thereby losing time and gaining a wandering mind.

## 63.

# On the Sunday after the Ascension.

*Concerning the right and orderly preparation for receiving the Holy Spirit, and how a person should conduct themselves in the midst of the sensible sweetness and consolation of divine grace, so that mischievous nature does not intervene. How we should watch in prayer, and concerning the true truth and the benefit of internal prayer.*

> Be prudent and watch in your prayers. <note>original: "Estote prudentes et vigilate in orationibus."</note> 1 Pet. IV. v. 8. *)

St. Peter says in the Epistle: Be wise and watch in your prayer.

We now have the Feast of the Holy Spirit <note>Pentecost</note> before us, for which every person should prepare themselves with all their might to receive Him, by purely intending God, and so that the person, with the light of their integrity, may bravely look through everything—their actions and omissions, and their life—to see if anything lives or dwells therein that is not God. This preparation lies in four pieces: <term>detachment</term> <note>German: *Abgeschiedenheit*; the state of being un-tethered from worldly concerns</note>, <term>emptiness</term> <note>German: *Ledigkeit*; a spiritual freedom or being "unoccupied" by created things</note>, <term>inwardness</term> <note>German: *Innigkeit*</note>, and <term>union</term> <note>German: *Einigkeit*</note>. Also, how the outward person should be set and exercised with natural virtues, and the lower powers with moral virtues; and how the Holy Spirit adorns the highest powers with divine virtues, and how this should be directed and ordered with <term>discretion</term> <note>German: *Bescheidenheit*; here meaning the spiritual discernment to judge one's own progress</note>. This applies to a person in all their doing and in all their life, whether it be right, and whether it all goes toward God or not; if he finds anything in his doing that does not purely intend God, he should correct it. He should do just like the <term>farmer</term> <note>German: *Ackermann*; literally "acre-man"</note>, who has work to do in March: when he sees that the sun begins to approach, he prunes and clips his trees, and digs out his ground, and turns over his soil, and digs it with great diligence. In the same way, a person should dig through themselves with great diligence, and look into their <term>ground</term> <note>German: *Grund*; the "spark" or deepest essence of the soul where God dwells</note>, and with their works at once turn over their ground, and prune their trees—which are their outer senses—

But when nature is uncertain of any help, it works, strives, and helps itself. See, children, how nimbly this poisoning of nature—this turning back upon oneself—strikes into all things, seeking its own rest and comfort. 

This is a thousand times more true for <term>spiritual people</term> <note>German: *geistlichen Menschen*</note>; when a person thinks they find this special, unusual good within themselves, they rely on it and think themselves all the more secure. They do not work as diligently or as faithfully, and they immediately become so delicate that they think they can no longer suffer or act as they did before, believing they must keep themselves in total peace. Now, when the enemy sees that the person is lying idle, he comes and pours false sweetness into them, so that the person remains there and is kept in this false rest.

How should we act then? Should we run away from this <term>bliss</term> <note>German: *Seligkeit*</note> and rest, or drive it away? No, by no means. We should receive it with great gratitude and offer it back to God with <term>humility</term> <note>German: *Demuth*</note>, thanking and praising God for it, and acknowledging ourselves as entirely unworthy of it. We should act like a vigorous young man who has little, is hungry and thirsty, and has a journey to make. If he could only run four miles, but then received a good meal, he would become so joyful, strong, and willing that he would surely run ten miles. This is how the person should act whom God feeds and strengthens with His divine comfort and presence. He should do much more than he...

Augustine says: The soul has within itself a hidden **abyss** <note>German: *Abgrund*. In mystical theology, this refers to the "bottomless" depth of the soul where it is most like God.</note>, which has nothing to do with time nor with the whole world, and is raised far above that part which gives life and movement to the body. In this noblest and most blissful abyss, in the kingdom of heaven—where that "sweetness" <note>Referring to the spiritual consolations mentioned on the previous page.</note> we spoke of is immersed—there is its eternal dwelling place. There, a person becomes so still, so **essential** <note>German: *wesentlich*. To be "essential" is to exist in one's true being or essence, rather than in outward appearances.</note>, and so composed; and more detached, more inward-drawn, and more upright; more pure and free, and more **released** <term>Gelassen</term> <note>German: *gelassen*. For God himself is present there, and works there, and dwells there, and reigns there. And this state cannot be compared to the first <note>The "first" likely refers to the lower levels of spiritual experience or sensory "sweetness" discussed previously.</note>, for there the person gains an entirely divine life; there the spirit melts completely and shines through itself in all things, and is drawn into the hot fire of love, which is God himself, essentially and naturally.

From this state, these people then go out again into all the distress of holy Christendom, and they go with holy prayers and desire into all that for which God wishes to be petitioned, and for all their friends. They even enter into sin and into purgatory <note>The author suggests the mystic's spiritual reach extends to those in need, whether they are living in sin or suffering in the afterlife.</note>, and they go thus to provide counsel in all love for every person's need in holy Christendom. Yet it is not that they pray for this one or that one specifically, but in a **simple manner**, just as I see you sitting here before me with a single countenance; in this way, they draw everything with them into that same abyss, into divine love, in a **contemplative way** <note>German: *anschauliche Weise*. A way of seeing or knowing through direct spiritual intuition rather than discursive thought.</note>. Then they look again into that same abyss, into the fire of divine love, and rest there, and look back down upon all those who are in distress in holy Christendom. 

Thus they go out and in, and yet remain always within, in the still, lovely **ground** <note>German: *Grunde*. The deepest interior part of the soul.</note>; there is their life and being, and in it is all their working and their moving. One finds nothing in them, however they are found, but a divine life; their "letting go," their "doing," and their manner are altogether divine. These are noble people, and they are useful to holy Christendom; they bring improvement to all people, they are praiseworthy to God, and they are comforting to all people. They dwell in God, and God in them, wherever they are. To such a manner and devotion may God help us always. Amen.

## 64.

# On the Holy Day of Pentecost.

### The First Sermon.

Teaches us to have prudence <note>German: *Vorsichtigkeit*. In this context, it implies a careful discernment or spiritual "cautiousness" in one's conduct.</note> in all our actions and omissions, with a clear distinction as to whether it is God or a creature <note>In mystical theology, "creature" or "created thing" refers to anything that is not God—including worldly objects, other people, or selfish desires.</note> with whom we are dealing. What true detachment <term>Abgeschiedenheit</term> <note>German: *Abgeschiedenheit*. A central pillar of Rhenish mysticism, referring to a state of being "cut off" from worldly distractions to remain open to the Divine.</note> is, and how the receptivity for the Holy Spirit differs among people.

> Be prudent. 1 Peter 4:8. <note>original: "Estote prudentes."</note> *) Be prudent.

The holy Church celebrates today the venerable and noble mission of the Holy Spirit to the dear disciples, and that was necessary so that they would also be at the beginning of all perfection, that they might be fervently enlightened and ignited in the superlative love of God, above all other people living at that time. It was fitting that they should be comforted, for they stood entirely without comfort and were abandoned, both outwardly and inwardly. Therefore, because they lived here in this time, they increased continually in this reception of the Holy Spirit; likewise, every Friend of God <note>The "Friends of God" (*Gottesfreunde*) were a 14th-century mystical movement of both clergy and laity who sought a closer, interior life with God.</note> should celebrate this lovely feast every day and every hour in his soul, so that he may receive the Holy Spirit in every hour; for according to his preparation and his receptivity, so is the Holy Spirit sent to him. For just as the Holy Spirit was sent to the disciples on the holy day of Pentecost, so it still happens spiritually every day to all people who fundamentally and earnestly prepare themselves for it; to them the Holy Spirit comes with new and special graces and gifts.

Now comes the dear, heavenly prince St. Peter, and points us specifically to what the preparation is, and says: *Be prudent* <note>original: "Estote prudentes."</note>. This signifies not only wisdom, but it also means experience—that is, if a person has tried a thing often and well, he knows it all the better. Thus this word means, the

St. Peter teaches us here and says that we should have experience and prudence in all our actions and omissions, with a clear distinction in what we deal with—whether it is truly God or the creatures <note>In mystical theology, "creature" or "created thing" refers to anything that is not God—including worldly objects, other people, or selfish desires.</note>.

Those people who could truly grasp the closest, purest preparation for this receptivity of the Holy Spirit in a noble, high way—that is true, pure detachment <term>Abgeschiedenheit</term> <note>A central pillar of Rhenish mysticism, referring to a state of being "cut off" from worldly distractions to remain open to the Divine.</note>, freedom <note>German: *Ledigkeit*. Implies being "empty" or "unencumbered" by worldly ties.</note>, inwardness, and unity—they have the closest and the truest preparation; and whoever possesses this is most receptive to the Holy Spirit.

What then is true, pure detachment? It is that a person turns away and separates themselves from everything that is not purely God, and with the light of their discretion <note>German: *Bescheidenheit*. Here used in its older sense of "discernment" or "distinguishing power."</note> looks through all their words, works, and thoughts with an understanding mind to see if there is anything in the ground <note>German: *Grund*. The "ground of the soul" is the deepest part of the human spirit where man meets God.</note> of the soul that is not purely God, or whether they do not mean God alone in all things, in their actions and omissions. If one finds something there that is intended more than God alone, let that be separated and excluded. And this belongs not only to an inward person <note>The "inward person" refers to one who focuses on contemplative life and the internal movement of the soul.</note>, but also to every good person.

Many good people are found in great, good exercises who nevertheless know nothing at all of inwardness; yet they are all bound to perceive what might hinder them from God, so that they may immediately leave it for God’s sake and separate themselves from these hindrances. One must necessarily have this detachment if one is to receive the Holy Spirit and His gentle gifts. That same person should mean God purely and separate themselves from everything that is not God. 

This detachment and the waiting for the Holy Spirit is unequal among people. Some receive Him in a sensory and perceptible way through the senses; others receive Him much more nobly, in the highest powers <note>Refers to the intellectual or "superior" faculties of the soul, such as reason and will, which were thought to be above the physical senses.</note>, in a rational way, far above all senses; the third group receives Him not only in the aforementioned ways, but also in the hidden abyss, in the secret kingdom, in the delightful ground where the noble image of the holy Trinity lies within—which is the most noble part of the soul. There the Holy Spirit finds His own place, and there His gifts are most nobly

...received in a divine manner. And as often as a person truly turns toward God in this, just as often there occurs a union and a new in-breathing <note>German: *Eingeistung*. A mystical term for the Holy Spirit entering and permeating the human spirit.</note> of God, the Holy Spirit; and in every single moment, he receives new gifts and graces when he turns toward this with earnestness and desire, with this knowledge [expertise] and true detachment <term>Abgeschiedenheit</term> <note>A state of spiritual stillness and being "cut off" from worldly distractions to be open to God.</note>.

Then the person, with true earnestness, overlooks and looks through all his doing and leaving <note>A common mystical idiom referring to all one's actions and omissions.</note>, and all his ways and manners and words, to see if anything is there that is not God, and whether his intention is directed toward God alone; and wherever he finds something else that is truly not God, discretion <note>German: *Bescheidenheit*. Here used in its older sense of "discernment" or "the power to distinguish."</note> judges and governs it. This light should correct natural virtue with its light—that is, humility, gentleness, mildness, stillness, and mercy. A person should contemplate these virtues to see whether they are born of God or not. This light should also shine into the moral virtues—that is, wisdom, justice, strength, and temperance. This is called the "ordering of man"; the light of discernment should look through, report, and order all of this with a true, pure intention, putting all things into a right divine order, so that everything may be done purely in a divine intention, in God and through God.

When the Holy Spirit thus finds that the person has done his part, He then comes with His light and outshines the natural light, pouring into it supernatural virtue—that is, faith, hope, and divine love—and His grace. Thus, the person becomes knowing, and a virtuous, divine person in this detachment. 

And this must be very well scrutinized with the light of truth, for much often intervenes of which one imagines that God is intended, but when one reaches the true ground <note>The "ground of the soul" (*Seelengrund*) is the deepest, most essential part of a person where they meet the Divine.</note>, one often finds something else; yet one should guard against this with diligence. For in the person who purely intends God, there also comes at times a distress <note>German: *Gedränge*. A state of spiritual pressure, feeling "crowded" or overwhelmed by internal conflict.</note> and a sadness, fearing that he has not purely intended God and that everything he has done of good is lost; this then terrifies the person's peace within himself, so that he becomes troubled by it. This distress comes at times from natural melancholy <note>German: *Schwermuth*. Now, corrupt nature is so grasping and so very inclined toward itself that it always creeps in and takes for itself what does not belong to it, thereby spoiling and staining the pure gifts of God and hindering the eternal God in His noble work. Now, this poisoning is rooted so deeply in the ground of man...

# 65.

## On the Holy Day of Pentecost.

### The second sermon.

Concerning the two-fold effect of the Holy Spirit—that is, unburdening and refilling—and how a person should conduct and hold themselves with <term>releasement</term> <note>German: *Gelassenheit*. In this context, it refers to a state of surrendered stillness and letting go of self-will to be receptive to God.</note> in this process. Concerning the signs of the Holy Spirit that he works in the believing person, of which Christ spoke. And whether external good works also hinder the indwelling of the Holy Spirit.

<note>original: "Repleti sunt omnes spiritu sancto, et coeperunt loqui magnalia Dei. Actuum II. v. 4."</note> They were all filled with the Holy Spirit, and began to speak of the great things of God. (Acts 2:4).

Dear children, today is the day on which the noble, precious treasure was restored, which was so harmfully lost in Paradise through sin—and most especially through disobedience—so that the entire human race had fallen into eternal death. This treasure was the Holy Spirit, who is a Comforter, together with all his gifts and consolation; for all people had fallen into the eternal wrath of God and into the bonds of eternal death. Jesus Christ broke these bonds on <term>Good Friday</term> <note>German: *Charfreytag*.</note>, when he allowed himself to be captured and bound, and died on the cross; there he made a complete peace and <term>atonement</term> <note>German: *Sühne*.</note> between man and the heavenly Father. But today, on this day, the atonement is confirmed, and the noble, precious treasure is restored, which had been entirely lost—that is, the Holy Spirit. To the richness and love and fullness that is within him, no senses, hearts, or understandings could ever reach. This Holy Spirit came into the disciples, and into all who were receptive to him, with

What, then, is his work by which he prepares the person to receive him? The Holy Spirit has two works within a person: the first is that he makes one <term>empty</term> <note>German: *ledig*. This emptiness is the first and the greatest preparation for receiving the Holy Spirit, for the more a person is emptied, the more receptive they become. If a barrel is to be filled, what is already inside must first come out; if wine is to go in, the water must first come out, for two material things cannot exist in their full and perfect essence in one place. In this context, it refers to all created things, worldly attachments, or the "self" which occupies the space intended for God.</note> must go out. For there is so much straying and clinging—now here, now there—that it has completely taken the upper hand. It is all our own self-acceptance, our own activity, our own rules, and our own self-conceit; no one wants to leave themselves to the Holy Spirit anymore, and everyone works for their own ends. This is the behavior of all people in these troubled times. St. Bernard <note>St. Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153), a Cistercian abbot and influential mystic.</note> says: "I curse and reject much outward speaking; but with God, there can never be too much of it." You should praise and thank God greatly with your tongues; for even if you had nothing else to thank God for but that he suffers you, tolerates you, bears with you, spares you, and waits for you, and remains so greatly silent regarding all your disorder—even though he can find nowhere for his divine work within you—still, you would have much to thank him for with "new tongues." 

That is to say: when you come together, you should speak of God and of a virtuous life, and not dispute about the Godhead, nor in any other way about **reason** <term>Vernunft: In this context, the author is warning against intellectualizing or rationalizing faith through clever debate rather than experiencing it through virtue.</term>, for that does not concern you; nor should you use clever or subtle words, especially those not rooted in virtue. You might conduct yourselves thus, speaking in a rationalizing way, but you condemn yourselves with it, and also those to whom you bring such talk.

Also, you should guard yourself against "subtle" people—these are the "serpents" we spoke of before—for once they have been driven out in an outward sense, you must ensure you do not let them back in spiritually. For the Enemy <note>The Devil.</note> constantly besets you, seeking to sneak in with clever ways, according to whatever he finds you inclined toward. In the same way, the work of the Holy Spirit directs and adapts itself according to how it finds your nature prepared. For God wishes to "increase" <note>Using the imagery of the Parable of the Talents, where a master expects his servants to invest and grow the gifts given to them.</note> his gifts, and wants to draw spirit and nature to himself; according to how he finds a good, compliant nature, so he directs his work. 

For just as a **downpour** <term>Schlagregen: A heavy, driving rain. The author uses this image to describe how God's grace pours down and must produce fruit rather than returning to Him "empty."</term> falls and does not return empty, so he does not want his gifts to return to him unfruitful; they bring nature and spirit back into their potential, and from potential to acting in the right order. This is how the Holy Spirit works, when he finds you in true **poverty of spirit** <note>A reference to the first Beatitude; here meaning a state of being empty of self-will and worldly attachments.</note>. And everything that might occupy this place, in all ways and possessions that you have drawn or might draw into yourself—all hardness, suspicion, and judgment, and all things that the Holy Spirit has not worked within you—these must be cast out, and you...

<summary>The author interprets "speaking in new tongues" as the spiritual discipline of guarding one's speech, avoiding intellectual speculation, and maintaining an inner silence that allows the Holy Spirit to work. He emphasizes that God's grace, like a heavy rain, is intended to transform a person's nature and produce the "fruit" of virtue.</summary>

<keywords>silence, speech, St. Bernard, Holy Spirit, virtue, reason, grace, humility, poverty of spirit</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the sermon for Pentecost. The previous page (136) ended mid-sentence, warning the listeners against intellectualizing their faith or using "clever words" to discuss the Godhead. It transitions here to the necessity of internal emptiness to receive the Spirit.</meta>

...you must be empty and void of all those things. But here you should note: all the thoughts that flash into your mind against your will cannot harm you.

Also, you should not think that you must wait for the **Holy Spirit** <term>heiliger Geist: In this mystical context, the Holy Spirit is seen as an active, indwelling presence that requires a prepared, quiet inner state to be felt.</term> in such a way that your outward good works hinder you—such as acts of obedience, singing, reading, and serving the sisters, or other works of charity. No, it is not the case that one must abandon all things and simply wait for Him. A person who gladly loves and serves God should do all things out of love, to the praise of God, in right order. You should perform the tasks that fall to you as God ordains, doing so in love and gentle kindness, and in peaceful **serenity** <term>Gelassenheit: A key concept in German mysticism meaning "releasement" or "lettingness"—a state of being detached from selfish desires and resting entirely in God's will.</term>, so that you remain at peace with yourself and your neighbor.

These works do not hinder you; rather, it is the disorder in your works that hinders you. Cast that disorder aside, and intend God purely in all your works. Secondly, observe yourself often and guard your mind; let no disorder enter it—whether through joy or sorrow—and guard your words and your outward conduct. If you do this, you will remain in peace in all your works. And the **Holy Spirit** will come to you, and fill you, and dwell within you, and work wonders in you, provided you keep His teaching. May God help us all to achieve this. Amen.

It emphasizes that internal peace and the guarding of one's mind against emotional disorder are the true prerequisites for the Spirit's indwelling.</summary>

### 66.

# For the Holy Day of Pentecost.

## The Third Sermon.

Concerning three qualities that a person must possess within themselves (if they wish to receive the **Holy Spirit** <term>Holy Spirit: In the context of German mysticism, the Holy Spirit is not just a theological concept but an active, indwelling presence that transforms the soul through its "sevenfold gifts."</term>): namely, they must be enclosed, gathered within themselves, and sitting still, just as the disciples of Christ did. Following this, concerning the sevenfold gifts of the Holy Spirit, with which He works seven types of wondrous works within a person.
They were all filled with the Holy Spirit, etc. Acts 2:4. <note>original: "Repleti sunt omnes spiritu sancto etc. Actuum II. v. 4."</note> *) They were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak of the great things of God.

This is the day when the Holy Spirit was sent to the holy disciples, and to all those who were united with them in the love of God, so that the lovely treasure was restored—the treasure that had been lost in Paradise through the counsel of the evil spirit and because of human weakness. It has been restored today, on this day, through the mercy of God. The outward manner of this was wondrous, yet that which was hidden and enclosed within was far beyond the grasp of all reason, all senses, and all created things. The Holy Spirit is such an incomprehensible, great, blissful, and immeasurable Good, that all the greatness and immensity that reason can conceive of in symbols is, by comparison, absolute nothingness. The kingdoms of Heaven and Earth, and everything one might imagine within them—indeed, all creatures together—are at once as nothing as the tiniest point is against the whole world. Even a thousand times more so are all creatures lesser than the smallest thing one can conceive of regarding the Holy Spirit. **) Therefore, where the Holy Spirit is to be received, He Himself must prepare the place and create the **receptivity** <term>Empfänglichkeit: Often translated as "susceptibility" or "receptivity," this refers to the soul's capacity to be acted upon by God once it has been emptied of worldly distractions.</term> within Himself. For the unutterable **abyss** <term>Abgrund: A central term in Tauler’s mysticism referring to the "groundless ground" or the deepest, most unknowable part of God and the human soul where the two become one.</term> of God must be its own place and its own receptivity, and not that of the creature. This house was—

...completely filled, in which the disciples of God sat. Now know, wherever God comes, he fills all things of the soul that is receptive to him.

The disciples of God were all filled with the **Holy Spirit**. Here it is for us to know what the condition was that the disciples of God possessed, who were thus filled with the Holy Spirit, and which every person must have who wishes to receive the Holy Spirit: they were enclosed and gathered, and sat still, when the Holy Spirit was sent to them. This Holy Spirit is given to every person as often and as much as the person turns with all their strength away from all creatures <note>In this mystical context, "creatures" refers to any created thing—people, worldly possessions, or selfish desires—that is not God.</note> and turns toward God. In that same moment when a person does this, the Holy Spirit comes with all his household goods <note>original: "Hausrath"; this refers to the spiritual "furnishings" or gifts and virtues the Spirit brings to the soul.</note> and fills every desire of the person and the entire ground <term>ground: "Grund" refers to the deepest, most essential part of the soul where the mystical union with God occurs.</term> and essence of the soul. And so, conversely, in that same moment when the person turns away from God toward creatures with a deliberate will—whether it be toward themselves or whatever kind of creature it may be, outside of and without God—so that they seek themselves in all things, as soon as that happens, the Holy Spirit flees and departs with all his wealth. 

This house was completely filled, in which the disciples sat. By this "house," one means the **Holy Church**, which is a house of God. And in another sense, every person is meant, who is intended to be a **temple** and a dwelling place of God, in which the Holy Spirit desires to dwell at all times, in every person’s heart. And just as there are many dwellings and chambers in every house, so there are many senses, powers, and workings in a person. Into all these chambers the Holy Spirit comes with his graces, and when he comes, he draws the person toward **virtues** and illuminates them inwardly in their soul. 

Not all people become aware of this entering and working, even though he is indeed in all good people. But whoever wishes to feel his working especially, and become aware of him with a sweet taste, must gather themselves within themselves and close themselves off from all outward things, and give themselves to the Holy Spirit with rest in a silent stillness; for then the person becomes aware of his working in their whole soul, and the Holy Spirit reveals himself in them all the more, the more the person turns toward him from hour to hour.

### Tauler's Sermons, Vol. II, 10.

...[the] person acknowledges and turns back to God. It is a noble and good thing to acknowledge the fall from God and then turn back to Him. In this and in all things, one must let go of oneself <note>Original: "sich lassen," referring to the act of self-abandonment or surrendering one's ego.</note>, follow God’s counsel, leave and transcend all things, and return to the Origin, to the Ground <note>Original: "Grund," the deep, essential core of the soul where it meets God.</note>, and into the Will of God.

With the first three gifts, one is indeed a good person, but one becomes much more heavenly and divine in these last ones; for in this deep **Detachment** <term>Gelassenheit: A central concept in German mysticism, meaning a state of "letting-be" or surrender, where the soul is free from self-will and worldly attachments.</term> the person truly sets their foot into eternal life. After this pain <note>Referring to the "mystical death" or the painful process of ego-loss described on the previous page.</note>, they will never again enter any pain, nor any hell, nor suffering. It is impossible for the eternal God ever to leave this person—just as little as God can leave Himself—for they have surrendered themselves to Him. ## 67. ª

# For Tuesday in the Pentecost Holidays.

*A very subtle and profound interpretation of today’s Gospel concerning the sheepfold and the shepherd, of the sheep, thieves, and murderers. All directed toward the idea that we should purely intend <term>Purely intend: In German "lauter meinen," a central mystical concept of having a "pure intention"—seeking God only for Himself, without any self-interest, spiritual pride, or desire for personal reward.</term> God in all things, without any seeking of personal pleasure or presumptuous judgment of our neighbor.*

> Amen, amen I say to you, he who does not enter by the door into the sheepfold, but climbs in another way, the same is a thief and a robber. John 10:1. <note>Original Latin: "Amen, amen dico vobis, qui non intrat per ostium in ovile ovium, fur est et latro."</note> *)

Our Lord spoke to His disciples: Truly, truly I say to you, whoever does not enter into the sheepfold <note>Original: "Schafhaus," literally "sheep-house."</note> through the right door, but comes in by other means, he is a thief and a murderer.

Our Lord said: He is the door of the sheepfold. What then is the sheepfold? That is the Fatherly heart; in that and from that, Christ is a lovely door, who has rightly unlocked and opened for us that lovely heart which was previously closed to all people. In this sheepfold is a gathering of all the saints.

**Fourth**, they resolved that their dear Master had so completely emptied Himself in all things, that He never sought His own in all His life, and that He had said: "Whoever wants to follow Me, let him deny himself"; and with this they went into themselves and recognized clearly that they were still far from true **detachment** <term>Gelassenheit: a central concept in German mysticism referring to a state of perfect letting-go and surrender to God's will</term>, and that they had taken the example of Christ in a merely natural way. ...with their whole heart, for otherwise I do not believe they would have ever received the Holy Spirit.

**Sixth**, they placed themselves in a **humble trust** that their dear Master had promised to grant them help and comfort, and that He would surely keep such a promise to them. Therefore, although they saw themselves unprovided for in their basic needs, and felt that the whole world wished to set itself against them, they nevertheless maintained that great trust which they had in their merciful Lord and sweet Master, believing they would not be abandoned by Him. This remained true even though the confession of their own failings kept them somewhat in fear that they might perhaps pay a price for their **lack of detachment** <term>Ungelassenheit: The state of being still attached to one's own will, ego, or worldly concerns; the opposite of the mystical ideal of "Gelassenheit" or let-go-ness.</term>.

Now one might ask: if the whole world was now dead within them, and they desired that all **naturalness** <note>original: "Natürlichkeit"; referring here to the unrefined, creaturely state of human nature or the "natural man" as opposed to the "spiritual man."</note> should be taken from them by the divine light, why was the Holy Spirit withheld from them and not given immediately after the **Ascension** <note>original: "Auffahrt"</note>? 

**Answer:** It is not to be believed that the Holy Spirit was withheld from the disciples until the **Day of Pentecost** <note>original: "Pfingsttag"</note>; for they received Him before the Ascension, and even more so afterward. For the more they acknowledged and annihilated themselves, the more the Spirit of God penetrated into them. But because they were not yet completely **free of themselves** <note>original: "ihrer selbst ledig"</note>, the Holy Spirit did not give Himself to them as truly in spirit or in His gifts as He did on the Day of Pentecost. At that time, a perfect **emptying** <term>Entledigung: The process of divesting oneself of ego and worldly attachments to make room for the indwelling of God.</term> of themselves occurred. It was not that they were entirely abandoned before they received the Spirit of God, for the divine power was already increasing within them without resistance; through its total penetration, it emptied them of their own nature and brought them to peace within themselves, as is explained again in the following sermon. Of these disciples and those like them, **St. Gregory** <note>Pope Gregory the Great (c. 540–604), a central figure in medieval theology whose writings emphasized the soul's internal growth toward God.</note> says: "As much as the divine power grows, so much does our own spirit decrease within itself; and then we increase entirely in God as we completely depart from ourselves."

May the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit grant us this. Amen.
