67. c

# On the Holy Day of Pentecost or during the Feast Days.

## The Sixth Sermon.

->How God drew His disciples with six drawings out of six obstacles, out of<-
->and above themselves into divine union, just as He still draws His friends.<-

> "No one comes to me, unless the Father, who sent me, has drawn him." <note>original: "Nemo venit ad me, nisi pater, qui misit me, traxerit eum." John 6:65. In modern biblical numbering, this verse is usually found at John 6:44.</note>

So spoke the dear Jesus: "No one comes to me, unless the Father who sent me draws him." The oppressed, miserable disciples of Jesus—who were held captive by their own bonds as if with iron chains, and who in their own estimation lay in the deep dungeons of their failings—since they fully acknowledged their own lack of power, they called out with inward prayer to the eternal Father (as St. Luke writes, that they were persevering with one accord in their prayer) and desired of the heavenly Father that they might be drawn from their hard bonds and out of the deep dungeons. Therefore their Father, to whom they had faithfully entrusted their desire, heard them and set them free from all bonds, and drew them out of the deep dungeons with **six drawings** <term>Züge: Mystical "pulls" or attractions of grace that move the soul toward God.</term> into the **high school of the Holy Spirit** <note>original: "hohe Schule des heil. Geistes"; a metaphor for the profound spiritual education and enlightenment provided by the Spirit, far surpassing human academic learning.</note>, in which they were filled with all truth.

First, He turned His merciful eyes toward them and sent them, not to a common drawing—such as He commonly uses to draw people over—but He sought to draw them into Himself in a special way above other people; for one finds three other ways in which God draws people to Himself. The first is through **creatures** <term>Creaturen: In this historical context, "creatures" refers to all "created things" in the universe—nature, animals, and objects—which were seen as mirrors reflecting the Creator's power.</term>, in which He shows Himself very clearly to humanity in the created light of their soul. As **St. Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential philosopher and theologian whose work shaped late medieval thought.</note> says, some pagans held that because of the inwardness and presence of God in all creatures, He was a Creator and Lord of the world, and that one should offer Him honor in every part of the world. This drawing through creatures is a beckoning and offering from God.

<meta>This page continues the "Sixth Sermon" for Pentecost. Having established the "first drawing" on the previous page, the author now details the second and third mystical "drawings" or movements by which God pulls the soul toward divine union, referencing Church Fathers and the nature of the human will.</meta>

The second way is through an inward speaking within the soul, in which the eternal Truth presents itself in a hidden manner, as St. Augustine says: "That the pagans spoke of some truth, they took that from the eternal rules of God, and not from their own nature." This is present in all people, whatever truth they speak; as St. Ambrose says: "Everything that is true, by whomsoever it is spoken, comes from the Holy Spirit." <note>original: "Omne verum, a quocumque dicatur, a Spiritu Sancto est." This was a widely cited medieval maxim attributed to Ambrose, emphasizing that all truth has a divine source.</note> Therefore, when the soul is now gathered into its **inwardness** <term>Inwendigkeit: A state of interior focus or "recollection" where the soul turns away from external distractions to find God within.</term>, it often happens that the eternal Truth reveals itself quite perceptibly, and we also find this at times in sleep toward the breaking of day. This drawing is called an endearment or an admonition.

The third way is when the human will has completely surrendered itself, and stands above itself in expectation of the most beloved will of God, in true **emptiness** <term>Ledigkeit: A spiritual state of being "unburdened" or "free" from selfish desires and worldly attachments.</term> of itself and all things. At this time, the eternal Father draws the created will without any resistance, so that the soul clings to Him with a singular delight. This drawing is called a union and an embrace. Man receives this drawing from the Supreme Good, who created heaven and earth and all creatures for the sake of man, and who also humbled Himself even unto death. Because man is more pleasing to Him than all the adornments of the kingdom of heaven and earth, He seeks him and admonishes him in all things and in no other way. To bring this drawing to the dear disciples, He turned His eyes full of grace toward them and, with love and with sorrow, turned their will so that He might make them ready for this drawing. Because the disciples let Him work as He willed, they finally arrived perfectly at this drawing, as one may well recognize in the drawings that follow. Now one might ask: why did God send the disciples to this drawing, and not me or other people before me, to whom He does not act in such a special way? Answer: There are two causes for this special drawing. The first is the free will of God, who chooses certain people above others to possess His **intimacy** <gloss>Heimlichkeit</gloss> and sweetness, just as a king, out of his free will, chooses knights for his secret council to wear his livery. The other cause is that a person clings more to the divine inward speaking, and perceives God’s drawing more diligently, which God [expects] of him...

It explains that God chooses certain individuals for deeper intimacy based on His free will and their own responsiveness to His call.</summary>

God does not make a person **justified** <note>In the sense of "righteousness" or being made right before God (Rechtfertigung).</note> without his free will, just as our eyes cannot see unless they are brightened and illuminated by the light of the sun or by another light. Even though the light is with us, nevertheless the person must open his eyes; otherwise, he would never see the light. If he had a coarse cloth or a board hanging before his eyes, he would have to remove it, for however brightly the sun poured out its radiance, he still could not see. Since the eternal Father now approached the disciples with His divine light, they opened their eyes and cast off the boards of all means as much as they were able. Therefore, God also did His part and pulled them into this special "drawing." This was done by the delightful, divine Son, who is the admonisher of all hearts, and drives out all hindrances, and dispels all boards of darkness from before the inward eyes of the soul.

Secondly, the Heavenly Father drew them out of the bonds of all physical creatures, so that they came to the aforementioned drawing in true **detachment** <term>Gelassenheit: A core concept in German mysticism, referring to a state of total surrender and releasement from self-will and worldly attachment.</term>, in order that they might stand free of these bonds and never fall back into them again. First, that it is situated far beyond all time—not only beyond the third physical heaven, but beyond all movement of the heavens and beyond everything that is subject to time.

Secondly, whatever it finds of its own property within itself, it cannot suffer to have any place or room within it. <note>This suggests that in the divine "school," there is no room for the "self" or individual ego-driven qualities.</note>

Fourthly, that it is light, clear, and pure; for the shine of the sun or the moon, which at times pass away and leave the earth dark, do not shine there. He is the **Eternal Sun**, constantly shining in His clarity. Because all physical, created things are lowly, narrow, restless, and impure, it was therefore necessary that they be drawn above the bonds of all physicality, as St. Jerome says: "Just as it is impossible for a stone to have **angelic wisdom** <note>Original: "englische Weisheit." In Middle High German and early modern German, "englisch" often meant "angelic" (derived from Engel) rather than "English."</note>, so it is impossible for God to ever give Himself into time or into temporal things."

Upon this a question arises: since the Eternal Father draws some people with love and some with suffering out of all physical things, were the disciples then drawn more with love or with suffering? 

**Answer:** Whoever considers their life will find that they were drawn much more through great hardship than through sweetness; for while they dwelt with Christ, they were always in contempt and in the suppression of themselves, and after the noble death of Christ (before this drawing happened to them), they were indeed beaten and suffered much before they were released from their bonds. And the Heavenly Father did this out of special love. The drawing through suffering is safer in itself than the drawing through love, as St. Gregory... <note>The text breaks off here, referring to St. Gregory the Great, who frequently wrote on the redemptive value of suffering.</note>

<meta>This page continues the sermon's explanation of how the Holy Spirit prepares the soul. It transitions from discussing the disciples' internal state to the specific gifts they received on Pentecost, addressing why some received more than others despite all being "emptied" of self.</meta>

One might ask: if the disciples were all drawn out of themselves and surrendered to God, did God then draw them all equally into Himself, and give Himself back to them in equal measure? Answer: Although the disciples were all free of themselves, one nevertheless turned to God more lovingly than the others, and with greater desire. This is just as it was with the angels who remained faithful <note>Referring to the traditional belief in the "Fall of the Angels," where some chose to stay with God while others followed Lucifer.</note>; they all surrendered themselves to God, yet one turned to God with greater love than another, and accordingly, God gave more of Himself to one than to the other, even though they were all in one "turning" <term>Kehre: The soul's orientation or "turn" toward the divine, which determines its capacity to receive grace.</term>. So it was also with the disciples, for their turning was unequal; therefore, God revealed Himself to them unequally within their own being and in His gifts. Because the beloved John <note>John the Evangelist, often called "the beloved disciple," traditionally considered the most mystical of the apostles.</note>, out of great and deep love, looked back into God, he was more highly gifted; yet it is also true that the free will of God was very much at work here, distributing His gifts as He wills.

It should be noted here that God did not give Himself to His disciples personally only on the day of Pentecost; for, as Richard <note>Richard of Saint Victor (died 1173), a prominent mystical theologian whose works on the degrees of love and the Trinity were highly influential.</note> and other teachers say, as often as "love-making" grace is given to a human being, so often is the person of the Holy Spirit also given. Therefore, the disciples had often received the person of the Holy Spirit before, but they had never before fully surrendered <term>gelassen: The state of "Gelassenheit" or releasement, where one lets go of the ego to be filled by God.</term> themselves, nor had they fully reached out toward His gifts. For this reason, He was first given to them in this sense on the day of Pentecost.

Sixthly, the Eternal Father led them into the High School of the Holy Spirit, in which they immediately recognized the hidden depths of Holy Scripture and the shining, naked truth, which is incomprehensible to all worldly masters in their schools. First, in this school, the greatness of God was set before them, and with it, the gift of **child-like fear** <note>Also called "filial fear," this is an awe of God based on love rather than a fear of punishment.</note> of God descended into them, which they kept until their end. Secondly, they were taught to be capable of all things and to have a constant gaze upon God, and with that came the gift of **fortitude**. Thirdly, He taught them to keep not only the commandments, but also the "counsel of Christ" <note>The "Evangelical Counsels" (poverty, chastity, and obedience), which go beyond the basic requirements of the Law.</note>, and with that they received the gift of **counsel**. Fourthly, He taught them to experience the sweet intimacy of God and gave them the gift of **kindness** <note>Usually identified as the gift of Piety.</note>. Fifthly, He taught them caution among created things and to know the difference between the light of God and the promptings of nature, and gave them the gift of **knowledge** <term>Kunst: Literally "art," but used here for the gift of Scientia or Knowledge in the spiritual sense.</term> or wisdom as well. Sixthly, he taught them to acknowledge every state <note>Here "state" (Stand) refers to one's spiritual condition or rank in life.</note> in which they now stood, and in which they had been before, and he gave them the gift of understanding for this purpose. Seventhly, he taught them a God-like transformation through a loving union with God, and he gave them the gift of wisdom for this. These seven points, in which the seven gifts are contained, the Holy Spirit teaches his disciples in his school. For just as the natural school teaches the seven arts <note>The "seven natural arts" refer to the classical Liberal Arts: Grammar, Logic, Rhetoric, Arithmetic, Geometry, Music, and Astronomy.</note>, and the school of faith teaches the seven sacraments, so the school of the Holy Spirit teaches these seven points with his seven gifts. 

Now a question arises here: Did the disciples, in the school of the Supreme Spirit, receive wisdom regarding all the arts that are taught in the natural school? 

Answer: Yes, every art—whether it be concerning the movement of the stars or whatever it may be—insofar as God’s honor may be fulfilled through it and whatever pertains to human salvation <term>Seligkeit: A state of spiritual blessedness or the ultimate salvation of the soul.</term>, all of that was given to them to know. But whatever exists in those arts in which no "fruit" for the soul can be found, that was not given to them to know; and for that reason, they were no less blessed or perfect. 

St. Augustine says:

> He is an unhappy man who knows all things and does not know God; and he is blessed who acknowledges God, even if he does not know all other things. But whoever acknowledges God and all other things is not more blessed because of those other things, for he is blessed by God alone. <note>Original Latin sentiment from Augustine's *Confessions*: "Infelix enim homo, qui scit illa omnia, te autem nescit; beatus autem, qui te scit, etiamsi illa nesciat."</note>

May God help us so that we also may be drawn into this, and be enlightened within our inwardness <term>Inwendigkeit: The deep, interior spiritual life or the "inner ground" of the soul.</term> with this same truth. Amen.

### 67. d

# On the Holy Day of Pentecost.

Of the two-fold in-pouring <note>original: "Eingießung." This refers to the theological concept of "infusion," where God’s grace or essence flows into the human soul.</note> of God, one of which occurs in God's own way, the other in an intentional way; likewise, wherein the Lordship of God is actually felt; and that our salvation <term>Seligkeit: A state of spiritual blessedness or the ultimate salvation of the soul.</term> depends most highly on the fact that God is a Spirit who unites us with Himself. For the more of God's likeness is in us, the more spiritual we are, and the more blessed, as our spirit unites with God's Spirit; likewise, how the soul may suffer <note>In this context, "suffer" (leiden) means to "undergo" or "receive" an impression, like wax receiving the mark of a seal.</note> the impression of God within itself so that it does not die or pass away.

> The Spirit of the Lord has filled the compass of the earth. Wisdom of Solomon 1:7. <note>original Latin: "Spiritus domini replevit orbem terrarum. Sapient. I. v. 7."</note> *)

The Spirit of the Lord has filled the circumference of the earth. A Master <note>Likely referring to a great scholastic teacher or Meister Eckhart himself.</note> says: All creatures bear within themselves a testimony <note>original: "Urkunde," meaning a record or legal document; here used to mean a physical mark or proof of origin.</note> of divine nature, from which they pour forth <gloss>originate</gloss>, such that they would gladly act according to the divine nature by which they were created.

Now, there are two ways in which creatures pour themselves forth. The first way of pouring forth is at their roots, just as the roots pour themselves forth into the tree. The other way is an intentional way <note>original: "meinende Weise." This refers to acting with a specific purpose or "meaning" rather than just by natural necessity.</note>. Behold, thus the pouring forth of divine nature happens in two ways. One out-pouring is of the Son from the Father, which happens in the manner of a birth. The other out-pouring is from the love of the Father and the Son; that is the Holy Spirit, because they both love one another in Him. Behold, all creatures prove this—that they have flowed out from the divine nature—and of this they bear a testimony in their works. Regarding this, a Greek master <note>Possibly a reference to Aristotle or a Greek Church Father like Dionysius the Areopagite.</note> says: That God guides all creatures, as if by a bridle, to act according to His likeness. Therefore, nature always works toward the very highest. The other out-pouring is in the intentional way of the Holy Spirit, who may direct them to act. Nature would not only want to produce the Son, and if she could, she would perform the Father's work; and therefore nature would always produce sons <note>In medieval biology and philosophy, "sons" or the male sex were often viewed as the "intended" perfect result of nature, while "daughters" or defects were seen as nature being hindered by matter.</note> if she did not have accidental <gloss>incidental</gloss> defects. Therefore, when nature, in time and in place—

Why is He called Lord? Because He fills us and makes us altogether rich; and He is called Spirit because He unites us with Himself. Lordship is measured by three weights or pounds: first, that He be rich. He is rich in that He possesses all things without a single defect. Therefore (to speak truly), no one is rich except God alone, who has simply enclosed all things within Himself. Therefore, He can give all at once, and that is the second weight or pound of richness. A Master says: That God offers Himself <note>original: "feil trage." I have also said this more often: that God has eternally conducted Himself just as if He were striving to make Himself pleasing to the soul. The third pound of richness is that one gives without any return; for whoever gives something for nothing is perfectly rich. Therefore, the richness of God is proven in this: that He gives all His gifts for free. Of this the Prophet speaks: 

> *I have spoken to the Lord: You are my God, for You have no need of my goods.* <note>Psalm 16:2. This emphasizes that God's giving is purely altruistic since He lacks nothing.</note>

This one alone is Lord, and is a Spirit. I say that He is Spirit; in this lies our blessedness <term>Seligkeit: A state of supreme spiritual happiness or salvation.</term>, that He unites us with Himself. The noblest thing that God works in all creatures is essence <term>Wesen: The fundamental nature or "being" of a thing that comes directly from God.</term>. My father may well give me my nature, but he does not give me my essence; that is worked by God alone. Therefore, all things that exist have a rational delight in their essence. The soul is created in a place between time and eternity, touching them both. With her highest powers she touches eternity, but with her lowest powers she touches time. See, thus she performs works in time according to the eternity which she has in common with the angels. The spirit leads life into all the limbs through the great <term>union (Vereinigung)</term> that the soul has with the body; and although the spirit is rational and performs the work all at once, one should not say: "My soul does this or that," for they both together are one human being. See, I may well say this, and it is true: through the great unification <note>original: "Einigung."</note> that the soul has with the body, the soul is as perfect in the smallest limb as in the whole body.

Regarding this **St. Augustine** <note>Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a foundational theologian whose works on the soul and its relation to God heavily influenced medieval mysticism.</note> says: If the unification between body and soul is so great, then the unification is much greater when spirit unites with spirit. See, He is Lord and Spirit for this reason: that He may make us blessed in His union. Now there is a question, and it is difficult to explain: how can the soul <term>endure (leiden)</term> <note>In this context, "leiden" (to suffer) means to "undergo" or "passively receive" the divine presence without being destroyed by its intensity.</note> so that she does not die or pass away when God presses Himself into her? For what is His is hers, because He has brought her out of what is hers; thus what is His must be hers, and what is hers is actually His. In this way, she is able to endure in the union of God. This is the Spirit of the Lord, who fills the compass of the earth. Amen.

### 68.

# For the Feast of the Holy Trinity.

## The First Sermon.

->How one may come to the high <term>knowledge (Bekenntniß)</term> of God in no other way than through the testimony of Christ in likeness and unlikeness; that a person finds themselves prepared in the "like" against the "unlike," and can maintain themselves as equal in the "unlike"—that is: they accept love in suffering, and suffering in joy, in shame honor, in comfort lack of comfort, <term>etc. (2c.)</term> <note>The abbreviation "2c." was commonly used in older German texts for "et cetera."</note>. ->What we know, we speak; and what we have seen, we testify. <note>original Latin: "Quod scimus loquimur, et quod vidimus testamur."</note> John 3:11.<-

Dear children, this is the lovely, wedding-like day on which we celebrate the holy feast and <term>wedding (Hochzeit)</term> <note>In this mystical context, "wedding" refers to the highest state of spiritual celebration and the union between the soul and the Divine.</note> of the Holy Trinity. All the feasts that have taken place so far this year are to be valued, according to their greatness, against this holy high wedding just as flowers are to be valued against the noble fruits of the tree. For this holy wedding is the reward and a perfect end to all labor; and therefore I cannot think of which words we should use to express it, for it is beyond all words and ways and thoughts of man. Just as the understanding of the highest <term>Seraphim</term> <note>The Seraphim are traditionally considered the highest order of angels, characterized by their proximity to God and their "burning" love.</note> surpasses the understanding of an animal, so this holy wedding surpasses all human and angelic reason and understanding a thousand times more. Therefore <term>St. Dionysius</term> <note>Referring to Dionysius the Areopagite, a theologian famous for "apophatic theology," which suggests that God is best described by what He is not, as He exceeds all human language.</note> said: Everything that one may speak of this has no truth in it, but is rather like a lie; for how and what the Holy Trinity may be, that cannot be thoroughly understood. And since it cannot be understood, it cannot be expressed; and when one speaks of it, it is more like a lie than the truth, on account of our ignorance.

Now ignorant people come and act as if they have seen right through it, and they speak of it presumptuously, though in truth no creature can express it. Therefore un-

Do not presume to speak of this high wisdom, nor to talk much about it, as St. Paul says: And let the great teachers study and debate it. These two witnesses are exactly like two sisters, and they run together within a person without ceasing; it is not that one goes one way and the other follows after, but they should be together. This means that one finds oneself prepared in "likeness" against "unlikeness," and that one can maintain oneself as equal in "unlikeness"—which is to say, that a person accepts love in suffering, and suffering in joy, and honor in shame, and lack of comfort in comfort. 

This equality cannot exist in the outer man, nor in our poor nature; but a person can certainly become essential through grace, making likeness out of unlikeness. However, many a bitter death must fall upon nature, through which it must painfully die to itself, both outwardly and inwardly, if it is to stand essentially equal in love and in suffering. Oh, how many deaths we owe to God, to which a noble, divine life answers for each one, if only we would truly perceive it within ourselves. Children, this life, and this death, and everything we lack for a true, perfect life, we could well obtain through true, inward, devout prayer of the spirit. And if the transfigured spirit then stood equal in love and in suffering, it would truly take the "unlike" into the "like," and "unlikeness" would become for it a pure "likeness." Thus, one would stand so equal in love and in suffering that a person would be neither troubled nor moved whether they were hated or loved; to that person, the one would be just like the other.

# 69.

## On the Feast of the Holy Trinity.

->The Second Sermon.<-

That one should not **dispute** <note>original: "disputiren" — to engage in intellectual or academic debate or argument.</note> much about the **Holy Trinity** <term>Trinity (Dreyfaltigkeit): the Christian doctrine that God is one essence existing in three persons: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.</term>, but rather observe how we are truly formed in its image, and where one might find such perfection, and the inner **spiritual birth** <note>original: "geistliche Geburt" — a central theme in medieval mysticism referring to the birth of God or the Word within the human soul.</note>, etc. Where the true testimony offers itself in the foundation of the soul, and how one may attain it, with brief points and excellent teaching.

> We speak of what we know, and testify to what we have seen. <note>original Latin: "Quod scimus loquimur, et quod vidimus testamur."</note> John 3:11. *)

Our Lord spoke: **What we know, that we speak, and what we see, that we testify to**, and you have not received our testimony. And if I tell you of **earthly things** and you do not believe me, how would you believe if I told you of **heavenly things**?

These words are read today in the **Gospel** <term>Gospel (Evangelio): the accounts of the life and teachings of Jesus.</term> regarding this worthy wedding of the high, transcendent Trinity; and all the "weddings" [feasts] that have taken place throughout the entire year have all taken their goal and their end from this one. The journey of all **creatures** <note>original: "Creaturen" — any created being, whether human, animal, or angelic.</note>, and especially of rational creatures, has the Holy Trinity as its goal and end, for it is truly a **beginning and an end**. Regarding this highly worthy Holy Trinity, we can find no proper word that we can speak, and yet there must be words about this **super-essential** <note>original: "überwesentlichen" — existing beyond the standard categories of "being" or "substance."</note>, **unknowable** Trinity. If we are now to speak of this, it is as impossible to reach it as it is to touch the heavens with one's head. For everything that one may speak or think of it is a thousand times less than a needle's point is compared to heaven and earth—yes, a hundred thousand times less, beyond all number and measure. ## 70.

# On the Day of Our Lord’s Corpus Christi.
<note>original: "Frohnleichnam" — literally "the Lord’s living body," this feast celebrates the Real Presence of Christ in the Eucharist.</note>

### The First Sermon.

Concerning three degrees or steps of divine praise; the many useful effects of worthily receiving the most venerable Sacrament; and how often and with what preparation every person, according to their life and condition, should receive it.

->My flesh is truly food, etc. John 6:55–58. <note>original: "Caro mea vere est cibus"</note><-

to offer honor with renewed devotion, just as one celebrates other high festivals <note>original: "Hochzeiten" — though this means "weddings" in modern German, it traditionally refers to any "high time" or great religious feast.</note>, and with this the Holy Church has satisfied us. Therefore, people perform outward works and decorations to demonstrate the worthiness that they hold for the venerable Sacrament in many ways. The Holy Sacrament is carried from one church to another, and the people have given silver and gold there; the bells are rung, the singing is high, and the organs sound beautifully, and there are many such things. All of this serves the inward praise that one should offer God from within, for nothing is so small that it does not serve this purpose; however, all these outward works and methods are the least praise that one may offer to God. Yet, one should rightly do whatever can and may be devised out of reverence, for there is no little worm so small that—if it had reason—it should not rightly lift its head in His honor and, in return, bow down.

Now there is yet a higher degree of praising God, which is that a person, with all their reason and their power, should praise God greatly with love and with intention from the bottom of their heart; and this is far above everything that one may do externally.

After this, there is a much higher degree than all of these, which is that a person recognizes God as so great, and themselves as so small in their own ground, that they cannot praise God enough. This praise surpasses speaking, singing, memory, and understanding. There was a Master who praised God with words, then another Master spoke: "Be silent, you are blaspheming God," and they both spoke the truth. This is a wondrous thing: that the unspeakable goodness is so great that no one can nor may fully praise it with words. This praising is countless times beyond the first two degrees, so that the greatness of the incomprehensible majesty of God, in a pure confession—that is, in itself—falls away from all words and manners into a sinking and a drowning of oneself, melting into God. There, God must praise and thank Himself, and if someone were truly sunken into this, it would be impossible to understand that God would ever let him fall away. *)

Now our Lord said:
> My flesh is true food, and my blood is true drink, and he who eats me remains in me, and I in him. <note>original: "Mein Fleisch ist eine wahre Speise..." — a reference to John 6:55-56.</note>

Here we should carefully note the profound humility of our Lord, in that He remains silent about the greatest things and speaks of the least. The greatest is His most venerable divinity, yet He speaks of the flesh and the blood, although the divinity and His holy soul are just as truly present there as the flesh and the blood. The excellent, super-essential, and unspeakable love shines so wonderfully in this, that it was not enough for Him to have become our brother and to have taken on our miserable, sickly nature. For He became human so that humanity might become God <note>This refers to the doctrine of "divinization" or *theosis*, a central theme in early Christian theology where God shares His divine life with humanity.</note>, and even that was not enough for Him; He also wished to become our food. Regarding this, Saint Augustine says:
> There is no race so great as the Christian race, to whom its God comes as near as He does to us.

We eat and enjoy our God. What wonderful, unspeakable love is in Him, that He found this way! This love is beyond all senses, and it should rightly wound the hearts of all people that His love toward us is so great. There is no physical thing that comes so close and so deep within a person as eating and drinking what a person takes into the mouth. And because He wanted to unite Himself to us in the closest and most inward way, He found this wonderful method.

Now we must speak of physical food, though it sounds coarse, it nonetheless makes the matter understandable. Saint Bernard says:
> When we eat this food, we are eaten. <note>original: "So wir diese Speise essen, so werden wir gegessen." St. Bernard of Clairvaux used this paradox to suggest that while we consume the host, the divine life of Christ actually "consumes" and transforms us into Himself.</note>

Physical food, which we take into the mouth, is first chewed, and it then passes gently through the throat into the stomach; there it is consumed by the heat of the liver, and the stomach cooks the food and separates the coarse and the bad from the good. And if a person were to eat as much as a pound, not even the smallest weight of it enters into the <term>nature</term> <note>In medieval science, "nature" (*natura*) often referred to the actual substance of the body's tissues.</note>; the stomach casts all the rest out through various ends. And when it comes into the stomach, it still has three stages to pass through before it reaches the nature. And once the stomach has thus cooked and digested it with natural heat, a superior power of the soul (which God has ordained for this purpose) comes and distributes it all to the head, the heart, and every limb, and it then becomes flesh and blood,

and then passes through all the veins. So it is also truly with our Lord’s **Body** <note>original: "Leichnam" — while this often means "corpse" in modern German, in this medieval context it refers to the living, sacramental Body of Christ.</note>. Just as physical food is transformed into us, so whoever eats this food worthily is transformed into the food. As our Lord spoke to Saint Augustine:

but God eats us when He punishes our failings within us, opens our internal eyes, and allows us to recognize our faults; for His "eating" punishes the conscience. The biting and the chewing occur as one tosses the food back and forth in the mouth; in the same way, a person is tossed back and forth by God’s punishment, in anxiety, in fear, and in sadness.

In this chewing, biting, and punishing, you should suffer gladly; let yourself be well-eaten and chewed, and do not try to escape it. Instead, speak with an inward sighing from the bottom of your heart: "Oh, Lord, have mercy on me, a poor sinner, and remain within Your own self." This is much more useful to you than if you were to read a great many things, or pray, or do whatever else you might do to escape this process. Guard yourself, so that the enemy does not sneak up on you with "disordered sadness." He very much likes to bring a bitter, sour **mustard** <note>In medieval allegories, mustard represented the "bite" of repentance or suffering. The author warns against the "sour" mustard of despair brought by the devil, vs. the "sweet" mustard of Godly sorrow.</note> to such people; but our Lord’s mustard is sweet and good. After His punishment comes a sweet soothing of the soul, a loving confidence, and a divine trust with holy hope; and thus, God swallows you. 

For just as food that is well-cooked and chewed enters gently and sinks down into the stomach, so when you are well-chewed in your conscience—yet with a divine confidence—and you then surrender yourself to our Lord, you enter into Him gently. If we have "examined ourselves," according to **Saint Paul’s** words <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 11:28: "But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread..."</note>, regarding this divine food so that we enjoy it worthily, then He eats us, and we are swallowed up and digested by Him. ## 71.

# On the Feast of the Body of Our Lord <note>original: *Frohnleichnams-Tag* — popularly known as Corpus Christi.</note>

### The second sermon.

Concerning three degrees or stages of the worthy reception of the Holy Sacrament. The first is to suffer with composure during the internal punishments of God. The second is a pure terror and an un-becoming <term>un-becoming</term> <note>original: *Entwerden* — a mystical concept describing the process of letting go of one’s individual ego or "selfhood" to be filled by God.</note> of all selfhood <term>selfhood</term> <note>original: *Eigenheit* — the attachment to one's own will, identity, or possessions as separate from God.</note>. The third is the internal pressure that is born from such terror.

> He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood, etc. John 6:56. <note>original: "Qui manducat meam carnem et bibit meum sanguinem etc."</note> He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him.

Dear children, regarding the Holy Sacrament and its sublime dignity, no heart or tongue can speak perfectly, nor express its fullness, nor praise it enough; and yet, all our spiritual practice is directed toward it. For within this, all our salvation and all our blessedness lie enclosed and hidden. Now, however, let us take up the holy words of Saint Bernard, who speaks of a physical eating; with these words, he intends to speak of this holy, high food as if it were a matter of chewing, swallowing, cooking <note>In this context, "cooking" refers to the internal process of spiritual "digestion" or assimilation.</note>, and digesting. And although this sounds somewhat coarse, nevertheless, subtle and noble people should guard themselves against hostile, proud spirits; for a humble human spirit always loves small, humble, and lowly things. Of such people our Lord speaks: I thank you, heavenly Father, that you have hidden these high things from the great and wise of this world and have revealed them to the little ones and the humble.

We should look upon this high, noble work of God with a rational countenance and with great love. That our Lord is so fundamentally and inexpressibly humble that he gave himself so willingly and joyfully, under the humble, coarse appearance of wine and bread, so that we might all receive him into our mouths like a physical food—this signifies nothing other than that he [gives] himself...

...to press and sink Himself so near and inwardly into us with all His goodness, and here intends to unite us entirely with Himself, just as one can perceive and grasp with the senses. Therefore, God could well have provided a much higher, more agile way, had He wished to do it with great show and clarity (as Saint Hildegard <note>Hildegard of Bingen (1098–1179), a famous German Benedictine abbess, mystic, and visionary.</note> describes, and as still happens every day). It happened to a sister of our order that she saw, with her physical eyes, an incomprehensible clarity that surrounded the priest and the altar, and a great miracle of angels and many beautiful internal things. 

And therefore, in this time of grace, no practice is more useful, nor better, nor more fruitful, than alone to receive the worthy Sacrament worthily and humbly; just as, on the other hand, no thing is more worrisome or terrifying than to receive the Holy Sacrament unworthily and unprepared. And therefore the beloved Saint Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian theologian and philosopher whose writings were foundational to medieval mysticism.</note> says:

> That a person should have four qualities within them who wishes to go to the Holy Sacrament. The first is that the person should be innocent of all sins. The second: he should be clothed with the virtues of our dear Lord Jesus Christ. The third: that the person be displaced <term>displaced</term> <note>original: *entsetzt* — in this mystical context, it means to be "removed" or "un-seated" from one's own ego or self-will.</note> from himself, and placed <note>original: *gesetzt*</note> into God. The fourth: that the person become a temple of God.

We should well interpret and explain these teachings, such as how a person should be without sin. When a person acknowledges their sin from within, and then confesses that same sin, and receives penance for it, and what belongs thereto, as the Holy Church has ordained, and sighs inwardly from a profound acknowledgment of their failings—this purifies the person much more than reading or praying. In this way, one becomes free and clear of all sin, with a whole will to sin no more, and henceforth to more diligently flee all causes of sin. 

The second point is that a person be clothed with the virtues of our Lord Jesus Christ; these should be humility and gentleness, obedience, purity, patience, mercy, being gladly silent, and for God's sake loving all people, whether bad or good, friends or enemies. 

The third point is that, once the person has been thus clothed with virtues, the person is then displaced from himself in an internal, true divine peace, and then the person finds the Wor— <note>The text cuts off mid-word; likely *Wortes* (Word).</note>

...words that our Lord spoke: "Whoever eats me remains in me, and I in him." <note>A reference to the Gospel of John 6:56, emphasizing the mystical union between Christ and the believer through the Eucharist.</note> A person should guard and keep this peace with all diligence and earnestness, so that it is not destroyed, neither in words nor in works. By this peace, one does not mean natural peace; one means an inward, internal peace of the spirit, in God alone, and in all things—that is, in love and in suffering, in spirit and in nature. For as much as one is truly in God, so much is one surely in peace; and as much as one is outside of God, so much is one in unrest. And when a person truly and essentially enters into this peace, he becomes truly and actually a temple of God, for God’s dwelling place is in peace. The person also becomes a temple of the Holy Spirit—which is the fourth point—for then God performs all of the person's works in him and through him, and the person does nothing of himself, because he is a tool through which God performs His work.

Now let us take for ourselves the words of Saint Bernard <note>Saint Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153), a highly influential Cistercian abbot and mystic.</note>: "Just as we have eaten Him, so shall we in turn be eaten by Him." This "eating" is nothing other than a punishing and a biting of our conscience; and God does not want to punish us alone, He also wants the person to be punished by all creatures. For in the same way, the devout person is hunted like a wild animal that one intends to give to the Emperor; that same animal is hunted, torn and bitten by the dogs, and this is much more pleasing to the Emperor than if it had been captured gently. The eternal God is this venerable Emperor who wishes to eat this hunted prey. He has His dogs for this purpose: that is the evil spirit, who hunts the person with various impure temptations <term>temptations</term> <note>original: *Anfechtungen* — a specific term in German mysticism for spiritual trials, inner turmoil, or demonic attacks that test the soul.</note>. Stand firm in this; it does you no harm at all, for you must without doubt be hunted if things are to go right for you. In addition to this, the world and other people come with their heavy, blustering words and their judgments, and they hunt and persecute you. After that come your own failings and the inclinations <term>inclinations</term> <note>original: *Neiglichkeit* — the natural tendency or "leaning" toward sin.</note> of your nature. ...remain in complete peace, and fall simply upon your own nothingness, then you should not doubt that He will become yours spiritually, and perhaps even more fruitfully than if He had come to you in the Sacrament. There you shall eat and enjoy Him in the Holy Spirit, just as He said: 

> He who eats me remains in me, and I remain in him. 

Thus you truly remain in Him; this is one degree of the Holy Sacrament.

Now there are two further degrees that are much higher, nobler, and more worthy than the one we spoke of before. One of these is with recognition and with a certain finding; the other is with finding but without recognition. The first consists in a pure "setting aside" <note>German: *Entsetzen*; in this mystical context, it refers to being displaced from one's own ego or being "startled" out of the self.</note> and an **un-becoming** <note>German: *Entwerden*; a central mystical concept describing the process where the soul lets go of its individual identity to be filled by God.</note> of all selfhood. The other degree is the inward pressure that is born from this displacement. The more selfhood a person has possessed, and the more they have held onto those things they have "taken on" as their own, the more bitter and heavy this pressure must be. 

Now we take for ourselves the words of Saint Bernard: <term>I am consumed while I am deprived</term> <note>original Latin: *Coquor dum destituor*. St. Bernard of Clairvaux used this to describe the painful but necessary transformation of the soul.</note>. That is to say: just as the stomach "cooks" or digests food, so that the food must pass away from its own form, so must you truly and purely pass away in yourself to be united in God. You must pass away from all selfhood, self-love, activity, and everything you have taken on—in every way that you have "possessed" yourself. 

Know for a truth: it cannot be otherwise, for two distinct beings and two forms cannot in any way exist in the same place. If warmth is to enter, then cold must of necessity depart. That is to say: if God is to be truly and purely within, then all "creatureliness" <note>The state of being a created thing, or being attached to created things rather than the Creator.</note> and all possession must of necessity depart. If God is to work specifically in you, then you must be in a state of pure **passivity** <note>German: *Leidenheit*; the state of being "acted upon" by God rather than acting through one's own will.</note>. All your powers must be so completely displaced from their own activity and attachments, and must truly stand in a pure denial of themselves; they must be emptied of themselves and stand upon their bare, pure nothingness. 

The more bottomless this nothingness is, the more essential, true, and fundamental the union with God becomes. If this nothingness were as essentially and as clearly revealed in a person’s soul as it was in the pure, noble, and worthy soul of our dear Lord Jesus Christ—if someone could achieve that (though it is not possible)—the union would be as great as it was in Him. For if God is to truly speak into your soul, then in truth all the powers of your soul must be silent. For here, there should not be a "doing," but an **un-doing**...

<meta>This page continues the sermon on the spiritual degrees of the Sacrament. The previous page used the metaphor of digestion—how food must lose its own form to nourish the body—to explain how the soul must "un-become" or lose its self-centered identity to be transformed by God.</meta>

...be, for if physical food is to be transformed into a person’s nature, it must above all things be brought to nothing in itself, and become entirely unlike itself, as if it had never been food. If this happens in nature, it must happen a thousand times more in the soul and the spirit. But you should know that the greatest harm happens here: that human **reason** <note>German: *Vernunft*; in mystical thought, the intellect often tries to grasp or control spiritual experiences that can only be reached through surrender.</note> wants to interfere too much, wanting to participate and know what it is, refusing to **un-become** <note>German: *entwerden*; a central term in German mysticism referring to the process of letting go of one's ego and individual identity to return to a state of oneness with God.</note> as it rightly should. Guard yourselves against this, for God's sake and for your eternal **blessedness** <note>German: *Seligkeit*; refers to the state of ultimate spiritual joy and salvation.</note>. But if the Holy Sacrament were a help and an advancement to you in this, then you might well receive the Holy Sacrament two or three times a week, running to it with a hungry desire, especially if you find that it advances you toward your spiritual level.

Those people who stand here, in this degree, experience an unbearable, painful woe born from this **un-becoming**. This happens when this whole wide world becomes too narrow for a person; nature is so bitterly constrained and pressed by this that the person cannot know what is happening to them or what they lack. But I will tell you what you lack. This **un-becoming** causes you this woe; you do not want to die, and yet you must truly die within yourself. In this dying, the words of **Saint Paul** become true when he says: *You shall proclaim His death until He Himself comes.* <note>Reference to 1 Corinthians 11:26. Proclaiming the Lord's death is interpreted here not as a ritual, but as the soul's participation in Christ's death.</note> This "proclaiming" is not done with words or with thoughts—for whatever that is, it is a very small thing. It is solely dying and **un-becoming** in the power of His death. 

In this degree, three things hinder you which you must do without: the precious **Body of Christ** <note>German: *Frohnleichnam*; here meaning the physical reception of the Host.</note>, the Word of God, and your own spiritual practices. For all such assistance is a hindrance to you here. If you could suffer through this "squeeze" <note>German: *Gedränge*; the internal pressure and spiritual distress felt during the final stages of self-surrender.</note> kindly and willingly, without running away or breaking out, it would be much more useful to you than all the works you could ever perform. And many people do not want to remain in this state, running from one teacher to another, seeking comfort and help wherever they can; and thus they remain unhelped by the Eternal Truth. But if you truly remained in this **Ground** <note>German: *Grund*; the "spark" or deepest essence of the soul where the distinction between the self and God disappears.</note>, the true essence would be born in truth.

<meta>This page continues the sermon's exploration of the "un-becoming" of the soul. This manifold "remaining" <note>German: *Verbleiben*; refers to the act of staying or dwelling in a state of spiritual stillness and suffering without seeking a premature exit.</note> that happens here within a person, no one can fully express, given the troublesome searching of our restless nature, which would always gladly be free and rid of distress and suffering if it could do or wish otherwise. For now your **reason** <note>German: *Vernunft*; the intellectual faculty that seeks to understand and control experiences.</note> comes and wants to raise an objection; then your own **integrity** <note>German: *Redlichkeit*; here used to describe a sense of moral duty or "religious busyness" that feels virtuous but actually distracts from the internal work of God.</note> comes and whispers to you: "Oh, what are you doing? Shouldn't you have a plan? You are neglecting yourself in all things at once." So you think to yourself that you should pray, but then the evil spirit comes and says to you: "Why are you sitting here? You should go and practice your devotions," and says within you: "Go away, you are wasting your time here; go out and do this or that good work." To this are added coarse people, who are possessed by their own ways, and say to you: "Dear person, why are you sitting here instead of hearing the Word of God?" Know this: such people are all hunting dogs, and you yourself become a hunting dog along with them, and you then bark at yourself, saying in your heart: "What are you doing? You should help yourself; you should go to the Holy Sacrament."

In this conflict, one should not seek a remedy, nor expect to receive [relief] from the **Sacrament**. I tell you, if you came to me in this distress and suffering, and I knew that you had come to me for that reason—seeking to receive the Holy Sacrament from me because of it—I would test you. I would speak to you and ask who sent you to me: whether it was God, or if **nature** <note>In mystical theology, "nature" (Natur) often refers to the human ego's instinctive drive for comfort and self-preservation, which opposes the "supernatural" work of God.</note> had done it for its own relief, or your own good habit. If I found the latter two in you, I would not give you the Holy Sacrament, unless your nature were so exceedingly sick that you could not well endure this distress and suffering. If that were the case, you might well go to the Holy Sacrament once or twice a week—not for a release from the pain, but so that you might be better able to endure it to the end.

You should know that the true **divine birth** <note>German: *göttliche Geburt*; a central theme in the Rhenish mystical tradition, referring to the birth of the Word or God within the essence of the soul.</note> never happens in you unless this distress and suffering necessarily precedes it; only then does the birth occur. Whatever thing releases you from this distress and suffering births *itself* into you instead, and robs you of the birth that truly should have been born in you, if only you had endured it through to the end. Know also for a truth: nature would venture...

Oh, how a noble end truly meets this ground at last, for these "way-less" <note>German: *weislose*; describing people who have abandoned their own "ways" or methods for God's way.</note> people are over-formed, and united, and shaped into God. > We are transformed from glory to glory, into the same image, by the Spirit of God. <note>Original Latin: *Transformamur a claritate in claritatem, in eandem imaginem a spiritu Dei.* (2 Corinthians 3:18)</note>

# On the Feast of Corpus Christi.
<note>The German *Frohnleichnams-Tag* literally means "The Day of the Lord’s Holy Body."</note>

->The Third Sermon.<-

Regarding the wonderful effect and union that this most venerable Sacrament works in a pure, devout, and composed <term>composed: translating *gelassenen*, a central term in German mysticism referring to a state of detachment and total surrender to God's will.</term> person; and with what great benefit and abundant gifts Christ gives himself here.

> My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink, etc. John 6:55. <note>original Latin: *Caro mea vere est cibus, et sanguis meus vere est potus.*</note>
> My flesh is truly a food, and my blood truly a drink, and whoever drinks and eats of this shall live eternally.

The more gifts a person receives, the more they are indebted, and the more gratitude they should have, proving their praise, honor, and service to God. Now, all spiritual exercises and grace are a path and a preparation toward God, so that through them a person may come to God and into God. But grace is the end and the reward; it is God himself without mediation, without any distinction or comparison, altogether simple and pure. Therefore, this is a loving and super-essential <term>super-essential: translating *überwesentliche*, meaning something that exists beyond the nature of physical substance or ordinary being.</term> gift and wedding feast that surpasses all things.

Now, on Maundy Thursday <note>original: *grünen Donnerstage*, literally "Green Thursday."</note>, one cannot do enough justice to this, for the Easter wedding <note>The intense period of the Passion and Resurrection.</note> comes too close to it, so that because of our weakness and His greatness, we cannot do enough for Him. Therefore, the Holy Church has improved this <note>Referring to the establishment of Corpus Christi as a separate feast day in the 13th century to focus specifically on the Eucharist.</note> and has called out once more, so that we are summoned with all our might to behold this wonderful work—with all our capacity and senses, and with thankful praise and love, and far beyond what one is capable of.

My flesh is truly a food, and my blood is truly a drink. Those who look upon this only outwardly, as the food and drink of bread and wine, neither taste nor know anything of this noble fruit, nor of the unspeakable sweetness that lies hidden within. Other physical food that a person enjoys is

Alas! one finds many people with a spiritual appearance who all their lives, from childhood to old age, rely upon themselves in a sensory way. They move from one activity to another, now here, now there, yet they can know nothing of this richness, nor can they taste and perceive the noble, precious treasure; for they cannot do otherwise, since they receive only in a sensory manner. Dear child, do not despair of Him—the very best, purest Good—as if He were something that could not be attained; for if you are diligent, you can indeed reach God and that noble, pure Good in all the ways and modes of being in which you exist. But you must maintain a faithful, diligent awareness of yourself, and keep a watchful eye and insight toward your present God in all diversity, in ways and works, among all people, in doing and in leaving aside, and in outward exercise. In this way, the greatest part of you should be turned inward, hunting after God and maintaining insight. Yet when one is free and idle from outward exercise, then one should be gathered and united inwardly with all parts, powers, and senses, and sunken into the Ground. <note>In German mysticism, the 'Ground' (*Grund*) refers to the deepest, most essential part of the soul where the human spirit meets the Divine essence.</note>

How then could a small reason grasp this super-essential <note>original: *überwesentlichen*. This is a union greater than any human understanding might conceive in all things and beyond all transformation; far more than a small drop of water is lost and united within a large cask of wine, or the sun with its radiance in a glass, or the soul with the body, which together make one person and one being.

Now, here in this union, the spirit is drawn above all its sickness, naturalness, and inequality; it is purified, transfigured, and raised above all its own power, and above itself and all its works and being. It is permeated with God and directed and led into a divine manner. There, the Birth <note>A reference to the 'Birth of the Word in the Soul,' the mystical experience where God is said to be born within the believer.</note> is born in truth, and there the spirit loses all inequality and flows over into divine unity. By then, the food has become so unlike its original self that no eye is clear enough, nor any sense so subtle, that it could grasp or see that it was once food. Indeed, it becomes so small and subtle <note>In medieval thought, "subtle" describes matter that has become so refined and "thin" that it approaches the nature of spirit.</note> that no reason can find where or how that subtleness lies and works; one may believe it, but cannot grasp it with the senses.

Much less can one grasp how the spirit <term>passes away</term> into divine oneness, losing itself there so completely that no reason can reach it. This reaches into a divine abyss, where no created thing can ever go. Now, no creature is so sharp-sighted as to grasp the wondrous ways of natural food, or the nobility of nature; yet you wish to pursue that hidden abyss, where this noble food works inwardly in the purified spirit that has been transfigured? Now, when some people gather three or four times a day, and have noble thoughts, and say their prayers, and things go well for them, and they find comfort and sweetness, they think everything has been done correctly and they are in a good state. No, children, it is still immeasurably far off. We are created, called, and invited to immense, great things, and God takes it very poorly of us that we allow ourselves to be satisfied with such small things. For He is more generous and ready to give nothing so much as Himself—and that in the highest and most noble manner of His own being, abundantly and greatly. Therefore, in every gift, we should be pulled tight <note>original: *gespannt*. This refers to a spiritual "tension" or stretching, like a bowstring, toward God.</note> with all our senses and powers, heart and desires, and press toward God Himself. We should stretch and strain all the capacity of our body and soul so that nothing less satisfies us—not in a sensory or image-bound way, but in a supernatural way, everything toward the divine abyss. For one can never reach the bottom, no matter how high one goes; one could always come much higher and closer.

Oh, how much immense harm many people do to themselves when all of this remains only in their senses and lowest powers, and they take all of this in a manageable way and remain entirely there, so that nothing comes of it. Just as if physical food stayed in the stomach and did not pass further, failing to share itself with the heart, the head, and the limbs, then nature would have to perish and nothing would come of it. So do all those who take God only in their lowest powers, in their senses and thoughts, and no further. None of them ever reaches the pure Good to which God has called and invited us with this high, noble food, unless the <term>Gemüth</term> <note>A central term in German mysticism referring to the seat of the soul, combining mind, heart, and will.</note> with all its powers, both the highest and the lowest, is entirely joined to God and offered to Him with all its strength, far beyond all human capacity, with pure, simple faith that [lives] with good works and virtues...

## On the Feast of our Dear Lord's Corpus Christi.

Concerning the various distinctions and the proper ways in which this holy Sacrament is received. Concerning various failings—that is, daily sins, both those that remain and those that pass—and other hindrances to a worthy approach to this aforementioned Sacrament.

...innumerable graces that are given here [are of no use] to them if they remain only on the outward display and do not enter into the ground <note>original: *Grund*. In the tradition of Rhineland mysticism, the "ground of the soul" refers to the deepest, innermost essence of a person where the soul and God are united.</note>, and instead go about with many daily sins and lukewarmness, departing from there without grace, remaining desolate, idle, and cold because of great obstacles.

What, then, are the specific obstacles that do people such great harm, preventing them from obtaining this precious treasure (which fills heaven and earth with riches), so that they remain desolate and empty despite it, as you see every day in many people? This is exactly what you should take note of. They are daily failings <term>Gebrechen: minor moral weaknesses or "infirmities" that, while not necessarily breaking one's relationship with God, hinder spiritual progress</term> that cool the heat of love in its work, scatter the heart, drive away devotion, rob one of the Holy Spirit's comfort, and make God Himself feel uncanny and foreign to them; although they do not entirely kill grace within a person, they still cause this harm and provide great cause and inclination toward losing grace and falling into mortal sin, even though they are "daily" sins. Now, these daily obstacles are of two kinds, both of which hinder this outflow of the grace of the holy Sacrament. Understand the difference as follows:

The established failings hinder some quite severely; that is, when a person is willfully and knowingly possessed by creatures <note>original: *Creaturen*. In this context, "creatures" refers to any created thing—people, objects, or worldly status—as opposed to the Creator.</note> and clings to them with love, satisfaction, and desire, whatever they may be on earth, whether living or dead, for which God is not the true cause. Everything in which a person seeks sensory joy, desire, or satisfaction is all daily sin; and (as the teachers say) everything that is thought, spoken, or performed where the judgment of reason does not go before it, is all daily or venial sin <term>läßliche Sünde: "venial" or "pardonable" sin; in Catholic theology, a lesser sin that does not result in a complete separation from God</term>. Some are so great that one must perhaps burn for ten years or much longer in Purgatory because of them, if one enters it without having done penance. Now, these failings exist such that the person will not leave the creature and its satisfaction for God's sake, and then the creature occupies God's place within him, so that God may not dwell or work in him. Therefore, a person must notice what is within him. It can even be himself, in his own disordered focus on his joy or his possessions, or that his own ways please him. This failing is now, alas! so very common, as everyone now wants to gain, gather, and hold...

When you have two works or ways before you—that is, doing or refraining—and you do not know which is best, then first of all take notice of yourself. For the more you live for nature and its pleasures, the less you live for God and His will; and the less you live for nature and its pleasures, the more you live for God and His will. The more you wish to live for the Spirit, the more you must learn to die to nature.

Second, you should guard yourself against anger, so that you are not moved with an angry disposition toward anyone; for as often as you break your own will in anger, God will give you a special crown. You should be kind and intimate with those who may improve you, and who themselves strive after a godly life. Two times should be especially precious to you. After <term>Matins<note>original: *Mette* — the prayers traditionally held in the middle of the night or at the very break of dawn.</note></term> in the night, you should spend a good while with God in devout prayer and arrange how you wish to conduct yourself during the day in spiritual progress according to God’s most beloved will. After <term>Compline<note>original: *Complet* — the final church service of the day, held before retiring for sleep.</note></term>, examine yourself on how you have conducted yourself throughout the day; for the good, praise and thank God; and for what was neglected or for your faults, have a displeasure with a firm will to improve yourself. And if this does not always go well for you at all times, you should not despair. Do not cease; if you do not reach the very top of the mountain, you will still be found on the path of your eternal salvation.

## 74.

# On the Second Sunday after Holy Trinity.

Regarding three kinds of supper that God the Lord has prepared for His friends, and especially regarding the meal of the Holy Sacrament, and the usefulness of the Mass—how a person may make themselves partakers of it, and what obstacles may arise—with beautiful parables.

A man had made a great supper and sent out his servant, and bade those who were invited to come to his supper, for all things were ready. Each one made an excuse. One said: "He had bought a village <note>In this biblical context, it refers to a piece of land or a farm.</note>; I pray you, excuse me." The other said: "I have bought five yoke of oxen, and I pray you, excuse me." The third said: "He could not com—"

<meta>This page continues the sermon for the second Sunday after Trinity, interpreting the parable of the Great Supper from the Gospel of Luke. The previous page ended as the invited guests began to make excuses for why they could not attend.</meta>

— 215 —

...excuses, and none has an excuse. The Lord spoke: None of these shall ever taste my supper.

This supper, in one sense (says Saint Gregory <note>Pope Gregory I, known as Gregory the Great (c. 540–604), whose writings on the "inner life" were foundational for medieval spirituality.</note>), to which we are all invited and called, is the most inward, purest, and barest acknowledgment and awareness of the inward <term>ground<note>The "ground" (German: *Grund*) is a central concept in German mysticism, referring to the deepest, most essential part of the soul where the human spirit meets God directly.</note></term>, wherein the Kingdom of God resides. It is the tasting of how God dwells and works there, which one should experience through confession and love. In another sense, this supper is the Holy Sacrament <note>The Eucharist or Holy Communion.</note>. In the third sense, this supper is eternal life; that is the true supper. Every meal that all creatures ever obtain in this time, or ever obtain in spirit and in nature, is as much less than this supper as a tiny crumb is compared to everything that the entire world together could possibly provide.

Whosoever wishes to come to this noble supper must diligently attend to the first two suppers, for the holy teachers say: those who do not have some form of precursor or foretaste of it in some way will never partake of it. But since the precursor is quite varied, the supper will also be partaken of and exist in varied ways. And although this is true in one way, God nevertheless withholds the foretasting sensitivity of the ground from many a good, pure person, and keeps it from them all their life, so that they never receive a drop of the supper until their end, or perhaps until they arrive there <note>Meaning, until they reach the afterlife.</note>. Such a person may well be a thousand degrees above those who have felt much here. There is also many a person who has revelations here, yet they may use them in such a way—making them so useless to themselves—that the one who never felt anything can be a hundred degrees closer to God in this supper. For God measures the supper by the measure of love, and gives to each what is best for them; but whoever is to taste this ground must of necessity have turned their heart and their love away from everything that is not purely God.

The other supper is the holy, worthy Sacrament; this supper brings so much grace and blessedness that it cannot be told, and it is beyond all human understanding. For these great graces, a person should be all the more grateful, since we are able to have them every day.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "supper" mentioned in the previous page, specifically focusing on the second sense of the word: the Holy Sacrament of the Eucharist. It addresses why the Mass is celebrated daily and its effects on the living and the dead.</meta>

It is a question of whether it is necessary that one should commemorate the death of our Lord anew every day in the Holy Sacrament, given that our Lord did quite enough for all this world on holy Good Friday <note>The day commemorating the crucifixion of Jesus.</note>. Indeed, even if a thousand worlds had been sinful, he would have done enough for them all. Our Lord did this out of great love, and found for us this delightful way because we are in need every day due to human infirmity, so that the worthy sacrifice might be offered anew every day for the sin and infirmity of mankind. For according to the words of St. Thomas <note>Saint Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), a hugely influential philosopher and theologian who wrote extensively on the Eucharist.</note>: All the fruitfulness and benefit that God worked on the day he died—this same fruit is found every day in every single Mass, and this same grace is received by every good person who worthily receives the worthy body of our Lord.

This Holy Sacrament drives away and kills sin, and gives great new grace; it makes a person increase and grow in a virtuous life, and protects them from future accidents and from the enemy’s snares <note>The "enemy" refers to the devil.</note>, which he lays for a person without ceasing. A person would surely fall heavily, both spiritually and physically, were it not for this powerful help and protection. Furthermore, great grace comes from it to the souls in Purgatory. There are many thousands of souls who would lie in the boiling furnace until the Last Judgment <note>The final day of divine judgment at the end of the world.</note> were it not for the holy practice of the Mass, through which they are redeemed by the holy office—and especially by pure, holy priests, whose practice works great wonders in Purgatory and here in this time. With this sacrifice, every person should carry themselves with inward desire into all Masses, as far as the world reaches, and should desire the Holy Sacrament from all of them, and especially from those by whom this sacrifice is acceptable. They should draw into it everyone who shares their intention, whether living or dead. A person does not only participate in the Mass that they hear, but in all Masses that are read in all the world. And if there were an inward person <note>A common term in German mysticism for someone focused on the internal spiritual life rather than external distractions.</note> who could turn within, I would certainly advise them to hear one Mass a day inwardly by turning into themselves; for the more inwardly they turn to God, the more fruitfully they hear every Mass, and let that be enough for them.

What is the cause of such great grace lying in this Sacrament, and yet many a person takes this Holy Sacrament...

The fault lies in this: they do not diligently take notice of their daily <term>shortcomings<note>original: "Gebrechen"—referring to minor sins or human frailties.</note></term>, and do not view them as a serious matter; thus their failings stand in the way of their grace and its influence. Now, a person should look so closely into their life and conduct that they retain no persistent shortcomings; and above all things, one should guard against unguarded, useless words, for all words are useless where one does not consider their benefit. A person should guard their words with everything they are able.

The other obstacle that hinders a person from the actual influence of grace is that they lack constant devotion, and that they have no stillness, but run out too much toward other things. They do not wait for grace to give it a place to work within them with a focused, inward spirit; for the Holy Sacrament works for two or three days in those who take heed of it.

Whoever is to find this fruit must have departed from the **land of Egypt**; out of the land of darkness, the <term>Heavenly Bread<note>A reference to Manna, the food God provided to the Israelites in the desert after they left Egypt (Exodus 16).</note></term> shall be given to him, which tastes however one desires it. But this bread was not given to the chosen people until they no longer had the flour they brought out of the land of Egypt. And when they had entirely consumed that flour, then God gave them the Heavenly Bread, in which they found every taste that their heart might crave. Now, after a person has departed from the "land of Egypt"—from the world and from worldly conduct—and even when they have come out and intend to be spiritual, as long as that person still has the "flour" of nature or of the creaturely within them, as well as an inclination toward imagination, then this noble, divine food will never taste of its true nobility or according to the right delight of their <term>inner nature<note>original: "Inwendigkeit"—the internal spiritual life of a person.</note></term>. All who ever perceive anything from within should realize that this clings to them, and they should go to this worthy food, not because of their perfection, but because of their great sickness. Just as if a person were to fall into such a great illness that one despaired entirely of their life, yet they were well-off with external goods and could sustain their life with them: one would prepare for them a precious <term>electuary<note>original: "Latwerge"—a medicinal paste or syrup, often made with honey or sugar.</note></term> of gold and of pearls to sustain their life; one would give him the food not for pleasure, but for his dire need—

...of life. Thus, a person should not take this noble, precious food except for his illness, so that he does not fall into death—that is, into the love of all created things. If a person were to eat this noble, costly food and then drink water upon it, the coldness of the water would spoil the actual heat of the food and hinder its work. Just so it happens here, when a person has received the high, worthy food, the **Holy Sacrament**, and afterwards takes foreign images into himself, along with <term>worry<note>original: "Bekümmerniß"—anxious attachment or preoccupation with worldly matters.</note></term> and a multiplicity of outward things; thus he is hindered, so that he is not receptive to nobility, and the heat of love is extinguished and cooled, and the spirit and nature become unfit for the inward words of the Holy Sacrament and its working.

Now the **Enemy** <note>A common term for the Devil or spiritual temptation.</note> comes, when a person reaches the point where he wishes to separate himself from all <term>creatures<note>In this context, "creatures" refers to any created thing (people, objects, or worldly desires) that distracts from the Creator.</note></term>, and says: "It is a folly; you cannot endure." Thus the blind person acts just like the people of Israel when **Moses** led them out of **Egypt**, and they looked back and saw those of Egypt following them, with perhaps six hundred chariots; then they said: "Woe, if only you had left us in Egypt; we would have suffered whatever we had to, for that would be better than having to perish here now." Just so do these faint-hearted people of little faith when the Enemy approaches them, rushing over the stones with many chariots of <term>temptation<note>original: "Anfechtung"—refers to spiritual trials, doubts, or attacks intended to shake one's faith.</note></term>; they think, "It is a folly; I would be much better off staying in Egypt, in the world, in the worry of creatures and in their love, than to have lost them." Thus many a person remains behind because he does not trust God. Therefore, a person should cast himself upon our Lord **Jesus Christ**, and ask him to pray to his **Heavenly Father** for him, and cast himself upon him with full trust.

Of the third meal we shall find more when we arrive there. To that, may God help us. Amen.

## The First Sermon.

A useful and excellent interpretation of today's **Epistle** <note>The "Epistle" refers to the scheduled reading from the New Testament letters in the church calendar.</note>, in which mention is made of these three virtues: humility, divine love, and true modesty; wherein also true trust in God in all <term>temptation<note>original: "Anfechtung"—refers to intense spiritual trials, doubts, or crises of faith.</note></term>, and obedience, is praised and advised.
