The dear Prince of Heaven, **St. Peter**, describes these words to us, and they speak in English thus: "You most beloved brothers, humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God, so that He may exalt you on the day of visitation, and cast all your care upon Him, for He is the one who cares for you. For the person who suffers a little for his honor, his praise and honor shall remain forever without end."

Children, this is the Epistle that St. Peter writes to us as an instruction and teaching, in which a person finds a complete doctrine and life, to fulfill and follow everything that the Holy Church has observed throughout the entire year. Here everything is <term>harmonized<note>original: "concordirt"—brought into agreement or "concordance" with other scriptures.</note></term>, concluded, and followed, if we indeed keep this teaching.

For I tell you in truth, that here in this time there is no lovelier or more worthy sacrifice to almighty God than a truly humble, obedient heart. This humble **surrender** <note>original: *Gelaß*. Related to *Gelassenheit*, this refers to the "letting go" of one's own desires and ego to be fully open to God's will.</note> would be dearer and more joyful to God than if that same person, at that very moment, were to penetrate into eternal life with all the angels.

Here is a parable regarding this: there was a pure, clear virgin in a convent who loved God with a longing and heartfelt love. Once, she yearned so very heartily for her beloved spouse, Jesus Christ; then she began to speak from a full heart: "O, my only most beloved Son of God, my Redeemer, if only it were possible that I might see You for one moment in this time." Immediately, our dear Lord stood before her in the form of a child. 

Now it happened that a woman of the convent came to the cell of this holy, devout virgin and quickly called her to obedience, saying that she should come at once to help perform a work for the community of the convent. When this holy virgin heard the voice of obedience, she began to speak: "My most beloved Lord Jesus Christ, I will go to be obedient; I pray You (if You will) to wait for me until I may return to You." 

So this holy virgin went out of her cell and was humbly obedient with a willing, joyful face. When she had fulfilled her task of obedience, she returned to her cell with great haste. As she unlocked it, a clear, pure light met her eyes, so bright that she could hardly endure it, and she saw her most beloved Lord standing there perfectly, like a **stately young man** <note>original: *stolzen Jüngling*. In this context, "proud" or "stately" denotes nobility and splendor rather than the sin of pride.</note> of about 34 years. Then the holy virgin began to laugh inwardly with a joyful heart and spoke thus: "My most beloved Lord Jesus Christ, how are you [so changed]..."

In the same way, all humble, obedient people should act; they should be humbly obedient, outwardly and inwardly, in all divine things, without any murmuring or contradiction, so that God may work his high works of love in them, without ceasing and without hindrance. # 76.

## On the Third Sunday after the Holy Trinity.

### The Second Sermon.

*Of four kinds of sinners who draw near to the Lord, yet very differently: these are the worldly mortal sinners, the hypocrites <note>original: *Gleißner*. This term literally refers to those who "glisten" or shine on the outside while remaining dark within.</note>, the lukewarm and negligent (of whom much is specifically said here), and the good-hearted sinners who, like the little sheep, are sought and found by the Lord in various ways; what their dignity and rest may be, here and hereafter.*

->Now the tax collectors and sinners were all drawing near to hear Jesus, etc. Luke 15:1–10. <note>original: *Erant appropinquantes ad Jesum publicani et peccatores etc. Luc. XV. v. 1—10.*</note> *)<-

We read in the Gospel of this week that the sinners drew near to our Lord, and it is written in the Gospel that our Lord told a parable and said: "Who among you, having a hundred sheep and losing one, would not leave the ninety-nine in the wilderness and seek the one until he finds it? And when he has found it, he takes it upon his shoulders and invites all his friends and neighbors, saying to them: that they should rejoice with him, for he has found his lost sheep again." This sermon is based on these words.

Dear children, we are all sinners and sinful people, and whoever says he is without sin is a liar, and the truth is not in him, as St. John says <note>A reference to 1 John 1:8: "If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us."</note>.

Now I will speak of four kinds of sinners. The first are coarse, worldly people who live a reckless, wanton, proud life—a life forgetful of God, where the fear of God...

It would be a great necessity for them to have faithful confessors <term>confessors: priests who hear confessions and provide spiritual direction</term> who would forbid them our Lord's Body <note>The consecrated bread used in the Sacrament.</note> and tell them how precarious their state is. To have brave teachers and confessors now, rather than accomplices, would be a great necessity for these stony hearts.

The others are also great sinners, yet they exist in a good, holy appearance; they perform great spiritual exercises, good works, and present a very good image or example to people. And these are the hypocrites <term>hypocrites: the original German *Gleißner* literally means "those who glisten," referring to those who have a shiny outward appearance of piety.</term>; they have a Pharisaic <note>Pharisaic: characterized by an emphasis on outward ritual and self-righteousness, like the Pharisees of the New Testament.</note> way; they are full of self-will, and love themselves and what is theirs in all things, and are haughty, stubborn, and rebellious. These people are great mortal sinners, yet they do not consider themselves as such; they neither think of nor love God, for they are lovers of themselves. These are—

Were He to give it everything He ever created in heaven and on earth, it would not be satisfied, nor would it be sated; this is its very nature. 

This perverse person condemns this ground and this longing, and he gapes his mouth as wide as if he could be sated by the wind. They approach our Lord with an outward life and with their outward innocence, yet their heart, their ground <term>ground: 'Grund' in German mysticism refers to the deepest, most essential part of the soul where it meets God</term>, and their love remain foreign and distant from Him.

The fourth kind of sinners are blessed and lovely sinners. It may well be that they have fallen further than all these other people, into many heavy, great mortal sins (I do not care now how many or how great they are), but these approach our Lord from their inner ground. They have made a true, thorough turning away from everything that is not purely and simply God, or where He does not shine within; they have turned their heart and their favor toward God. In such a way, they love and intend Him above all things; in this, they surrender themselves to God, outwardly and inwardly, so that whatever He wills shall be everything. God will never demand an account of these people’s sins, nor does He want to know of their sins, for they have turned themselves completely away from them, and so God has also turned away from them. If they no longer wish to know of their sins, then God no longer wishes to know of them either. 

Now, what is the manner that belongs to this? It is when a person finds within themselves in truth, without any gloss <term>gloss: 'Glosse'—an interpretation or excuse used to justify one's behavior</term>, that from the ground of their heart they intend to love God alone and no one else, and intend and desire to love Him purely above all things and before all things, and intend Him in all their works. If this finds in him a good, well-prepared will to do or leave undone everything he knows God wants of him—whatever it might be—and he finds himself entirely ready for it, and intends to follow God on whatever path He wishes to pull or lead him, whether through means or without means <note>original: "durch Mittel oder ohne Mittel" — referring to whether God acts through external tools like sacraments and teachers, or directly upon the soul</note>, that he would follow Him gladly, simply and detached, just as God wills and in whatever way He wills.

The Gospel says: That he sought the lost sheep.

Now, how should one understand this "seeking"? God seeks and desires to have a humble, gentle, and poor person, a pure and a detached <term>detached: 'gelassen' in German, referring to Gelassenheit, a central concept in German mysticism meaning a state of utter surrender, letting go of self-will and worldly attachments</term> person; one who stands steady (this is not to be understood as merely sitting down and pulling a cloak over one's head <note>The author is likely criticizing those who perform the outward gestures of contemplation—like the hooded silence of a monk—without the inward transformation of the soul</note>). You must let yourself be sought by God, so that you are so greatly pressed and annihilated <note>original: 'vernichtet'; in this context, it refers to the mystical 'death of the self' where the ego is brought to nothing to make room for God</note> until you learn humility in all ways, from wherever it may come. When someone seeks a thing they have lost, they do not look for it in only one corner; they seek it in many corners, here and there, until they find it. In the same way, God must seek you in many different ways. Just let yourself be found in all the ways and circumstances that fall upon you, no matter where they come from, through whom He wills, or in what shame or lowliness; take it as nothing other than coming from God, who is seeking you. He wants to have a gentle person; therefore, let yourself be struck so often and so much that you are thoroughly trodden down in your suffering, so that you may learn gentleness therein. God wants to have a poor person; let yourself be found when they want to take your goods, or your friend, or the treasure to which you cling. See to it that you may hand over your ground, bare and poor, to God. God seeks you; let yourself be found there. He wants to have a pure person, whom He seeks with much adversity, until they are purified and transfigured. God seeks you in everything that falls and may fall upon you, from wherever it may come or flow, or through whomever it comes, be it enemy or friend, whether it be done to you by your mother or your sister. Do not take it from the people, but alone, purely and simply from God, and let yourself be sought by God there.

Dear children, if someone had a wound in which something rotten and evil grew, he would allow himself to be cut and treated horribly in perhaps many places so that he would not suffer even greater pain; for this reason, he would not spare himself, so that the evil would come out and he might thus recover. In the same way, you should rather suffer the afflictions in which God seeks you, so that your ground may altogether become healthy and whole eternally. When unforeseen suffering falls upon you, whether from within or from without, speak in your mind: "Be welcome, my dear faithful friend; I did not expect you here, nor did I wait for you." Bow yourself humbly before it. Thus, know that God seeks you in all things; He wants you to be a detached...

->77.<-

# On the Sunday Mentioned Above.

->The Third Sermon.<-

Regarding the parable of the lost coin <note>The German *Pfennig* (penny) here refers to the silver *drachma* mentioned in the Gospel of Luke</note>, which signifies the soul: how it should possess its proper weight, its right material, and its right image; how man seeks God and is in turn sought by Him, and must be transformed through various forms of detachment and trials; and herein is also described what true divine love is.

> "Or what woman, having ten silver coins, if she loses one coin, does not light a lamp and sweep the house and seek diligently until she finds it?" Luke 15:8. <note>original Latin: "Quae mulier habens drachmas decem, si perdiderit unam etc. Luc. XV. v. 8."</note> *)

On this day, I spoke of this Gospel—how the sinners approached our Lord, and how the lost sheep was sought and found.

Children, turn it however you will, and interpret it as you wish: you must be sheep in true meekness, in silence, and in a state of utterly yielded patience <term>yielded patience: 'gelassener Leidenlichkeit'—a key concept in German mysticism referring to a soul that has let go of its own will to endure whatever God permits</term>. You must have a submissive spirit—submitting to God and to all creatures in a patient manner, just as God seeks you or wishes to seek you; in whatever way He wills, through whomever He wills, whether through Himself, or through other people, or through the Enemy, or through all creatures in heaven or on earth. Even through ghastly, harsh words, you must remain yielded. Whatever storm comes against you, do not defend yourself, but remain silent. In this, you shall follow the example of our Lord Jesus Christ, who was the most meek little lamb, who did not open His mouth when He was led before the judges.

So speak the self-willed and the blind, hardened people who stand upon their own opinions and have stood there for forty years: "You have a stubborn head <note>literally "a deaf head" (*ein taubes Haupt*)</note> to say that one should suffer and submit under God and all creatures." But I say: Dear child, let them scold you or judge you with heavy, harsh words, or let them shear you—however it may be, however the Lord wishes to seek you—remain silent and let it be.

The Gospel tells of how a woman had lost a coin <note>original German: *Pfenning*. While Tauler says "penny," he is referring to the silver *drachma* from Luke 15:8</note>; she lit a lamp and searched for the coin. This woman is the Godhead, the lamp is the divinized humanity, and the coin is the soul. This coin must have three things, and if it lacks even one of them, it is not a proper coin. This divine coin must have its weight, which is beyond measure <note>original: *ungewichtlich*</note>, for it weighs more than the kingdom of heaven and the kingdom of earth and everything contained within them; for God is in this coin, therefore it weighs as much as God. Now, the material of this coin is the sunken-in Godhead, which, through the super-essentiality of His ineffable love, has immersed itself into this spirit, and has in turn swallowed up and immersed the spirit entirely and completely into itself. If this is to happen, you must walk a much closer and more agile path, which is far beyond what the external man may seek, and beyond all the practices of the external man—whether in a passive or active manner, or however one wishes to take it, whether in images or in forms. The woman lit a lantern and turned the house upside down. This lamp is lit by Eternal Wisdom, and that which is ignited, we understand to be true divine love; this shall be ignited in your soul and shall burn.

<meta>This page continues the interpretation of the Parable of the Lost Coin. The previous page established that the woman represents the Godhead, the lamp represents Christ’s divinized humanity, and the coin represents the soul. Here, the author defines the nature of true love and the process of searching for God within the "house" of the soul.</meta>

[People imagine] that love is when you have a great feeling of well-being, sweetness, and delight; they call that love. No, that is not love; that is not its essence. But this is love: that one has a burning desire in the midst of lack, in deprivation, and in a state of abandonment; that there stands a constant, unmovable springing [striving], and that one meanwhile persists in true detachment <term>detachment: 'Gelassenheit'—a central mystical concept referring to a state of being yielded to God's will, free from selfish desire or emotional attachment to spiritual "consolations"</term>. In that springing forth, there is a melting away, and a parching in the heat, or in the fire of this lack—all while remaining in the same detachment. Children, that is love. And that is the lighting of this lamp.

Now, she turns the house upside down and seeks the coin. How does this seeking happen, this thing that occurs within a person? One way is active in the person, the other is passive <note>original: 'leidentlich'. In mystical theology, this refers to a state of 'undergoing' God's action rather than performing an action oneself</note>. The active way is when the person seeks. In the other way, he is the one being sought. The seeking with which a person seeks is external; the other is internal. One is as high above the other as the heaven is above the earth, and they are altogether different. The external seeking, with which a person seeks God, consists of the outward practice of good works in many different ways, as he is exhorted and driven by God and directed by God’s friends. Most of all, it is the practice of virtue, such as humility, gentleness, silence, detachment, and all other virtues that one practices or can practice.

But the other seeking is far above this; it is that a person enters into his own ground, into the innermost part, and there seeks the Lord, as He Himself demonstrated when He said: "The Kingdom of God is within you" <note>Luke 17:21</note>. Whoever wishes to find the Kingdom (that is, God with all His riches and in His very own essence and nature) must seek it where it is: in the innermost ground (where God is closer and more internal to the soul than the soul is to itself). In that very place, this ground must be sought and found. A person must go into this house and abandon all the senses, and everything that is sensory, and everything that is brought in or impressed upon them by the senses—all images and forms, and everything that the imagination and the "image-maker" <note>original: 'Bildnerin'. Refers to the faculty of the mind that creates or processes mental images</note> and all sensory images have ever brought in. Yes, one must even go beyond rational images and the activity of reason in its rational mode and its effects. When a person comes into this house and seeks God there, then the house is turned upside down. Then God seeks him...

And those who succeed rightly in this become the most lovely of people, and everything becomes easy for them. Whenever they wish, they can turn inward at any moment and soar above all things.

<meta>This page concludes the reflection on the soul as a "lost coin" that must be sought by God. It follows the previous discussion on the necessity of self-renunciation and internal "overturning" to reach the soul's true depth.</meta>

This penny <note>original: 'Pfenning'—referring to the silver coin in the Parable of the Lost Coin (Luke 15), representing the divine spark in the human soul</note> must have its weight, and its minting or image. Its weight ensures that it falls back into the <term>Ground</term> <note>original: 'Grund'—the *Seelengrund*, or the innermost "ground of the soul" where the human and divine meet</note> and sinks in, just as it first issued forth in all purity and immaculateness—as bare and unburdened as it first flowed out. It also possesses nothing but its image. This image does not merely mean that the soul is formed in the likeness of God; rather, it is the very same image that God is himself, in his own pure, divine essence. And here in this image, God loves, God acknowledges, God makes use of himself, and works within the soul. In this state, the soul becomes entirely "God-colored" and divine. She becomes by grace everything that God is by nature. In union with God and in sinking into God, she becomes so God-colored that, were she to see herself, she would take herself to be God entirely; or whoever saw her would see her in the garment, the color, the manner, and the essence of God—by grace and not by nature. Such a person would be blessed by that sight, for God and the soul are one in this union, by grace and not by nature.

Conversely, if one were to see a soul in its <term>Ground</term> that had willingly colored its love and its foundation after <term>creatures</term> <note>original: 'Creaturen'—in mystical writing, this refers to all created things (people, objects, worldly desires) that are not God</note>, one would see (without a doubt) that she was created no differently than the devil, who is indeed created ghastly and unbearable. If a person saw him in his true image, flesh and bone would all scatter from the horror of it. In this horror, the soul that is found in the ground of created things must eternally look upon itself without end and without ceasing. 

But the pure, divine soul will be looked upon before God eternally as God, and she will receive her blessedness within herself and out of herself in this union. She will look at herself as God, for God and she are one in this unification. Oh, how blessed are those who let themselves be sought and found in this way, so that the Lord leads them in and unites them with himself in an inexpressible manner! This goes far beyond all senses and understanding, and beyond everything one might speak or think. Whoever wishes to arrive here must walk this path and this road in an orderly fashion; then he cannot err. If he does not do this, and remains stuck in the senses, in the creatures, and in created things, he must by necessity remain behind, both now and eternally. That we all may thus be found in the Lord's search, may God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit help us. Amen.

### 78.
## On the Fourth Sunday after Holy Trinity.

How we should be merciful, judge no one, and possess within us a good, leveled, pressed-down, and heaped-up measure—that is, a noble, pure, detached, and <term>composed</term> <note>original: 'gelassenes'—referring to *Gelassenheit*, the mystical state of letting go of self-will to be filled by God</note> soul, into which the Lord God pours himself with an overflowing measure; that is, in an overflowing manner that surpasses all desire.

-> Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful, etc. Luke 6:36–42.*) <note>original Latin: 'Estote misericordes sicut et Pater vester misericors est etc.'</note> <-

Saint Luke writes in the Gospel that our Lord said to his disciples: Be merciful, as your Father is merciful. Judge no one, so that you are not judged. Condemn no one, so that you are not condemned. Forgive, so that you may be forgiven. A good measure, a full, pressed-down, and overflowing measure will be given into your lap. With the same measure that you use to measure, it will be measured back to you again.

In this Gospel, we are taught two things: one our Lord bids us to do, and the other he bids us to refrain from doing. Here there is a "doing" and a "leaving." The "doing" presented to us here is that we should be merciful; the "leaving" is that we should judge no one. I have not yet spoken in this sense about how perilous and anxious a thing it is for one person to judge another, and how much a person must take care to guard themselves. For the Mouth of Truth (which never spoke a lie) says: With the measure you use for measuring out, it shall be measured back to you in every way. If you are greatly merciful, you shall find great mercy; but if you are little, you shall find little. If you are not merciful at all, then you will find no mercy. This mercy a person should find and practice within their own <term>soul</term> <note>original: 'Gemüth'—the inner disposition, heart, or seat of the will and emotions</note>.

### 79.

## On the Same Sunday.

### The Second Sermon.

An interpretation of several parts of today’s Gospel, namely concerning mercy, and the fourfold measure of God’s dear friends in this time; regarding the four degrees of a true Christian life toward the heights of the perfect love of God and of one's neighbor. The same text and:
With the same measure you use, it will be measured back to you. <note>original: "Eadem mensura qua mensi fueritis, remetietur vobis." — a reference to Luke 6:38.</note>

We read in the Gospel that our Lord Jesus Christ spoke: Be merciful, just as your heavenly Father is merciful; and forgive, so that you may also be forgiven; for with the same measure with which you measure out, it will be measured back to you. And a good measure will be given to you—one that is pressed down, shaken together, and running over will be poured into your lap.

I wish to say a little about the word that says: *Be merciful, just as your heavenly Father is merciful.* This noble virtue is now so foreign to the hearts of many people that it is a great pity. Every person should have this mercy toward their neighbor in every way that the neighbor requires it. Not only in **temporal gifts** <note>Meaning physical or financial charity.</note>, but also in the gentle bearing of a neighbor's failings with mercy. 1. The **good measure** is that a person stands here in this time in a blessed, holy life, through the help and grace of God, through which the person may come into eternal life. 
2. The second measure, the **given measure** <note>In the biblical source, this is often "shaken together" (*concussam*).</note>, is that the body of the blessed person shall be glorified along with the soul after the Day of Judgment. 
3. The **pressed down measure** is that the person shall share in fellowship with all the saints and angels of God in eternal life. 
4. The **overflowing measure** is that the person shall fully enjoy God in eternal life, according to all delight, bliss, and joy, and according to all their desire.

Dear children, now we want to lead and interpret this teaching in another way and ask: What is the measure with which one measures? Secondly, who is the measurer? The measure with which one measures is the **loving** *) power of the soul—that is, the **will** of the person. This is actually the measure with which all of a person’s words, works, and life are measured, for nothing is added to it nor taken away from it.

This overflowing love draws all of this into its own vessel. For whoever has this love, the good works of another person become much more their own share and joy than they are for the one who actually performs the works but lacks this overflowing love.

# 80.

## On the Fifth Sunday after Trinity.

A very subtle and insightful sermon on the true oneness of prayer, and on the equality that man has with God, such that he can be active and receptive <note>original: "wirkend... und gebräuchlich" — the idea that a person can perform outward acts while remaining an instrument for God's use</note> at the same time; that is, that the inner man has an unchangeable clinging to God within, in a perfect, pure, inward intention toward God. On the three stages through which man comes to the simple Essence, and to the most truthful confession of his own nothingness.
->*Be of one mind in prayer. 1 Peter 3:8–15. <note>original: "Estote unanimes in oratione"</note> \*)*<-

We read today in the Epistle for this Sunday that St. Peter said: "Beloved, be of one mind in prayer."

Children, here St. Peter touches upon the most useful, delightful, noble, and fruitful work that one can do in this time, and that is prayer. Now note what God is, and what the essence of prayer is, and what the manner of prayer is, and how one should pray, and what the place is where one should pray.

Now, what is prayer? The essence of prayer is an ascent <note>original: "Auf-gang" — a rising up or dawning</note> of the mind <note>term: "Gemüth" — a central concept in German mysticism referring to the seat of the soul's faculties, deeper than just the intellect, where one encounters the divine</term> into God, as the holy teachers say. The place where one should pray is in the spirit, as our Lord himself said. Now, concerning how one should pray, I will say a little: every good person, when he wishes to pray, should gather his outward senses into himself, and should look into his mind to see that it is well turned toward God. This manner may the person

When this prayer of the true inward spirit is achieved, then everything that served it is preserved and well-concluded, and this state goes far beyond outward prayer. 

The exception would be if a person were so well-practiced that the outward prayer could exist alongside the inward without any hindrance, and in true practice and reality—so that one remains unhindered by the other. That belongs to a truly essential, absorbed, and glorified person, in whom "working" and "using" <note>The author uses "Wirken" (active work/creation) and "Gebrauchen" (the enjoyment or fruition of the divine essence) to describe a state where spiritual activity and peaceful contemplation are perfectly integrated.</note> become one, and one remains unhindered by the other, just as it is in God. The working is found in the Persons <note>Referring to the three persons of the Trinity: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.</note>, while the using is attributed to the simple Essence.

For man’s sake, He became human and suffered; He offered His life, His holy soul, and His very self for us, inviting us to an unspeakable proximity to Himself. How the **Holy Trinity** <note>original: "Dreyfaltigkeit"</note> has waited for man, to be enjoyed eternally. 

When a person contemplates these things with deep internal insight, a great and tangible joy is born within them. If he did not do so, the blood might perhaps burst from his mouth (as has often happened), or the person would fall into a great distress and suffering...

# 81.

## On the Fifth Sunday after the Holy Trinity.

### The Second Sermon.

*How the spiritual little boat—that is, the inner mind of man and his intention—must be guided upward away from everything that is not God: first through holy contemplations, then through suffering-filled serenity <term>Gelassenheit: a core concept in German mysticism meaning "releasement" or "letting go" of the self and worldly desires to be open to God</term> in the deprivation of all comfort and sweetness, and finally how it sinks into the uncreated Nothingness—that is, what one can neither understand nor put into words. All very subtle and exceedingly high and lovely.*

->When the crowds pressed in upon Jesus, etc. Luke 5:1–11. <note>original Latin: "Cum turbae irruerent in Jesum etc."</note> *)<-

In this Gospel for the week and the season, one reads among other words that our Lord went into a little boat that belonged to Simon, and commanded him to steer the boat a little way out into the heights away from the shore. And He sat and taught the people from the boat, and said to Simon: "Lead the boat into the heights <note>original: "in die Höhe." While the biblical text usually refers to "the deep," the author emphasizes "the heights" to signify the elevation of the soul</note>, and cast out your net for a catch." Simon said: "Master, we have worked all this night and have caught nothing, but at Your word I will cast out the net." And when they had done this, they enclosed so many fish that the net began to break. Afterward, they filled the boat so full that it began to sink. Then St. Peter fell down before our Lord and said: "Depart from me, for I am a sinful man."

This boat, which our Lord commanded to be led into the heights, is nothing other than the inner mind <term>Gemüth: the seat of the soul's emotions, will, and thoughts</term> of man and his intention. This boat sails in the anxious, raging sea

## 82.

# On the Fifth Sunday after Holy
# Trinity.

### The Third Sermon.

How Christ truly sits in the inner depths <term>inner depths: (inwendigem Grunde) the "ground of the soul," the deepest part of the human spirit where God dwells.</term> of the obedient person, and there teaches and shows them His most beloved will. Concerning the highest perfection of transformed, yielded <term>yielded: (gelaſſen) a state of total surrender, detachment from self-will, and serene acceptance of God’s will.</term> people, who build neither upon their doing nor their leaving <note>meaning their actions or their omissions</note>, but purely upon their own nothingness, with a humble, yielded sinking into the abyss of the free divine will. Initially based on several words of today’s Gospel, as stated in the previous sermon.

Finally, based on a very profound interpretation of the words: <note>original: "Mittite in dexteram navigii rete"</note> **Cast the net on the right side.** John 21:6. This subject would be well-suited to be preached on the Wednesday of the Easter holidays. Yet, it all proceeds from one foundation, to be preached also on this Sunday; especially regarding the words: **Jesus, getting into one of the boats, which was Simon's, etc. Luke 5:1–11.** <note>original: "Aſcendens Jeſus in unam navem, quae erat Simonis etc."</note>

Dear children, one reads in the present Gospel that our dear Lord came to the sea, and went into Simon’s boat, and asked him to lead the boat a little way from the land; and He sat down there and taught the people, and said to Simon Peter: <note>original: "Duc in altum"</note> **Lead out into the deep**, and let down your net for a catch. Then Simon Peter began and said: Master, we have worked the whole night and have caught nothing; but at Your word, I will let down the net in Your name. And when they had done this, they enclosed so many fish that the net broke, and they were very nearly sinking because of it. Then Simon Peter stood up and fell on his knees and said to our Lord: Lord, depart from me, for I am a sinner. One reads that this Gospel occurred before our Lord's death. After our Lord’s death, they fished once again and caught one hundred and fifty-three large fish, and then the net did not break, and they did not sink.

Children, this Gospel <note>original: "Evangelium"</note> has much noble meaning enclosed within it. Any person who possessed a pure reason would find many good meanings, ways, and teachings therein, if they were only truly present within themselves.

This boat was Simon’s <note>original: "Simonis," the Latin genitive form of Simon</note>, that is, it belonged to the obedient, righteous person who is always obedient to God in truth. Now, what is the boat in which God truly sits? It is the ground of the inner man; there our Lord truly sits in His rest. Therefore, whatever person would always pay heed to this inner ground, from within and without, and would joyfully leave <note>meaning to let go of or detach from</note> all things for the sake of God’s will, and turn inward into their inner ground—to that person all truth of what to do and what to leave undone would become known. 

For this reason, it often happens that a person engaged in external works is frequently and greatly exhorted by God to turn deeply into the inner ground of their heart; and yet, the person often avoids or ignores this divine exhortation. In such a person, the humble, obedient Simon Peter is not to be found. For the disobedient person who avoids God’s exhortation, and for whom the will of God is not always sufficient, remains always in their own self-will, in their old habits, and in their own self-possession <term>self-possession: (Besessenheit) in this context, the state of being "possessed" by one's own ego, attachments, or stubborn will, rather than by God.</term>; in this state, the person becomes displeasing and disobedient to God. 

But the noble obedience of good, blessed, and righteous people, who are always humbly obedient to God, both inwardly and outwardly—that obedience is a noble virtue above all other human obedience. Therefore, if it should happen that a devout brother or a sister in a monastery <term>monastery: (Kloster) a communal residence for monks or nuns.</term> were standing in their choir <term>choir: (Chor) the part of the church where the monastic community gathers to sing the Divine Office.</term>, and were singing or reading, and they felt or noticed in their inner ground that God was exhorting or prompting them to turn inward, and if the good works they were then performing—the singing or reading—were hindering this inner turning, then that brother or sister should let the song drop, turn inward, and give themselves to God in that inner return, following His inner drawing to the very ground. 

However, if a person were able to accomplish the outward work along with the inward, then two would always be better than one, and that same song would then rise from the ground of the heart to the heights, before the face of God. Therefore, I tell you truly, if you knew how harmful and how worrisome it is,

...and it is a great danger that you ignore the noble exhortations of God, are disobedient, and resist. Therefore, when the chosen friends of God recognize this perilous, anxious life, their hearts might break and the marrow in their bones wither, seeing that many people, alas, stand in such peril and yet want to be certain of eternal life—even though Holy Scripture speaks thus: *The righteous person will scarcely be saved.* <note>original: "Der gerechte Mensch wird kaum behalten." Afterward, they arrive so low in heaven, far below those people who stood in even the very lowest degree of virtue.

They should act in the same way as a person who makes a crooked piece of wood straight: they bend the wood back further than is straight, and from that counter-bending, it then becomes straight. This is exactly what a person should do to their nature, the **outer, animalistic man** <note>The "animalistic man" refers to the lower part of human nature that is driven by physical senses and instincts rather than spiritual reason.</note>. They should bend themselves beneath all things that belong to God, and should completely break off from themselves everything that is not God, purely in spirit and in nature. With a pure confession of themselves and with a deep humility, they should bend beneath God and beneath His free will. Then, incline yourself before the mercy of God and complain to Him humbly with **St. Peter**: "Dear Lord, I have worked all the night and have caught nothing." 

Know this: everything that a person works without God is all "night," and in this, the person falls into sluggishness and lethargy, so that their nature becomes unfit for all good things; for it is dark and night around the person. In this state, you should exercise the outer man greatly with hands and feet, and through all this, the person should intend to come back into the **Ground** <note>The "Ground" (Grund) is a central concept in German mysticism, referring to the deepest, innermost center of the soul where it meets God.</note>, so that their entire life may be ordered in God; they should do all of this in the noble, honorable intention of God.

Children, our Lord spoke to St. Peter: "Lead the ship into the height." <note>This refers to Luke 5:4. While many Bibles say "into the deep," the Latin "in altum" can mean both deep or high; the author here interprets it as "the height."</note> That is: lift up your entire mind and all your powers into the height above yourself and above all sensory things. ### 83.

## On the Sixth Sunday after Trinity.

A precious sermon on the elements through which a person may be freed from the excessive **merchandising** <term>merchandising: (German: *Kaufmannschaft*) the spiritual state of performing religious acts or "good works" with the expectation of a reward from God, rather than out of selfless love</term> of their inner temple of the soul; that is, how one should remove from there the very ground and root from which distraction, discord, and unrest always spring in the heart. The first element is a secure, free conscience, whereby it is also explained what true repentance and confession are, and how one should find grace. The second element is that one should stand equal in all things, and how that is to be understood. The third is that one should hold oneself toward the justice and mercy of God.

The Christian Church reads on this day (as John writes) that the Passover of the Jews was near, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem. In the temple, he found sitting those who had sheep, oxen, and doves for sale, and the money changers. And he made a **scourge** <term>scourge: (German: *Geißel*) a whip; here used symbolically for the divine discipline or trials that drive worldly distractions out of the soul</term> out of cords and drove them all out of the temple, together with the sheep and oxen, and poured out the money of the changers and overturned the tables. And he said to those who had doves for sale: "Take these things away and do not make my Father's house into a house of trade."

Behold, children, now notice here the dignity of the soul, which is truly a house and a dwelling of God, wherein God would rather dwell than in heaven or on earth. The soul has more of the Divine within it than all the heavens, all physical temples, and everything that God ever created; for the heart of God is in the soul, with all His love and faithfulness, and with all His delight. For in all creatures, God seeks nothing other than how He may honor the soul, make it worthy, and bring it to blessedness. Since God is thus turned toward the soul with all His love and intent, God is more truly in the soul than in the heavens or in physical temples; for God works all His works in the soul, and works them for the

Now note, I have intended to speak of three parts: how a person should remove the ground with the root that creates such obstacles in people; and know that whoever does this will be quit and thus free of these merchants, so that they never occur to him again, and they leave the temple of his soul in peace; and of this be as sure as God lives.

An unclouded and untouched purity. But where purity is clouded, and the freedom of the soul <note>original: *Gemüthes*; referring to the seat of emotions, will, and inner disposition</note> is diverted <insert>out of its proper direction</insert> through attachment to the creature <note>original: *Creatur*; in mystical theology, this refers to any created being or thing as distinct from the Creator</note>, and through the accidental occurrence of evil in the practice of weaknesses, this must be washed away with true repentance. 

What is right, true repentance? Is it to behave miserably, and to cry and weep loudly? No, not at all! For it often happens that dissolute, negligent, and sinful people cry and weep loudly, and yet do not have right repentance; and conversely, some have complete, true repentance, and yet do not weep. Now note what true repentance is. Every creature loves God by nature more than itself, except for the sinner; he loves himself more than God. He proves this by seeking his own pleasure and satisfaction, and taking it from created things, no matter how much it grieves God. 

Because man now loves himself above all things, he searches and desires with great longing for what is familiar and good to him, and avoids what is painful and brings him ill. Therefore, because the sinful man well knows that through his sins he has lost eternal life and is ensnared and bound to hell and eternal torment, he feels sorrow and regret—and yet he is as far from right, true repentance as heaven is from earth. Here, man serves himself and not God, and therefore his regret does not help him, nor does it obtain grace for him, for he seeks grace where it is not to be found.

Whoever wishes to find grace must seek it where it is, which is in God. In God alone does one find grace, and not in created things, nor in creaturely formations <note>original: *Bildung*; the mental images or attachments to things other than God that "form" the soul</note>. Therefore, however much sorrow and regret you have for your own loss, it neither gives nor earns you grace, for you remain entirely centered on yourself and in creaturely formations, no matter how good the work might be that a person might perform; if the intention <note>original: *Meinung*; the inner aim or focus of the heart</note> is not withdrawn from the creature and does not adhere to God alone with all faithfulness, you will find no grace, for grace is in God, not in created things. But if, in every work, God's honor and His praise are intended with all repentance, God accepts that work, as He says Himself: "Whatever you do to the least in my name, that is done to me."

According to this sense, you have and you take as much grace as you yourself want, for you love God, suffer, avoid, and work through Him and in Him, as much as you want. Thus a person finds grace, and he alone has right repentance, who is sorry out of faithfulness and love that he has angered and dishonored the sweet, good God. Even if there were neither hell nor the kingdom of heaven, he should nonetheless be no less sorry that he had ever acted against God. That is true repentance, even if the person could not weep.

* 19

Several people, who believe they love God very much (as it seems to them) when they are at rest and engaged in noble works or in noble places, act as if they were giving God **leave** <note>original: "Urlaub"; here meaning permission to depart or taking a temporary break from a relationship</note> when they must depart from those things or are hindered in them. They wait until they return to their rest or to the specific manner of devotion they have chosen for themselves. See, in truth, as long as you seek God through specific manners and places, you will never gain right peace, nor find God in truth. It may well seem so to you, but it is merely the manner you have adopted, in which you have sought only yourself. All such people feel great joy in the church in the morning and hurry to get there quickly, exactly as if God were not at home, nor on the street, and as if God could be found nowhere but in the church. In truth, if you go there with such a hurried spirit, you will find such a hurry there that it will harm you and become a burden, and you will not find God there either. Now, they may perform a good work, or say a prayer—perhaps now to God, now to a saint—and they hurry and rush from one thing to the other, and thus everything becomes hurried, the last thing just like the first. Therefore, they find rest nowhere, nor God in truth.

A person should hold their **disposition** <note>original: "Gemüth"; the deep inner seat of emotions and will</note> so entirely and completely toward God in every single work, that the "image" of the work fades away from the person, and God alone remains in the **intellect** <note>original: "Vernunft"; the higher faculty of the soul capable of perceiving divine truth</note>. In this way, one should seek grace and belong entirely to God in every single task, whatever it may be. Whether it be a woman tending to or caring for her house, or the household servants, or whatever work it is: in that moment, surrender yourself to God and belong to Him entirely. God—who watches day and night with all His wisdom and great diligence, waiting to see how He might draw a person to Himself and when He might find them ready—is not concerned with specific places or manners. Furthermore, you know little of the circumstances in which God wishes to meet you and where you shall find Him. Therefore, be the same toward God in every situation, however it falls, and wait for God within it, and belong to Him as if it were the very best thing. In truth, it *is* the best. You should never think that you are missing anything in this, for with God, no one can ever miss anything. Thus, the person misses nothing who is constant toward God in all things, in all manners, and in all places, and is entirely focused—at the very least in their intention—upon Him. ...and without this, one is never satisfied. Thus one finds God and peace rightly and in truth, and nowhere else. Whoever does not seek and **intend** <note>original: "meinet"; in this context, it refers to the inner direction of the heart and will toward a specific goal</note> God in all things, will never find Him rightly in any one thing. Whoever does not belong to Him in all manners, in truth, will not belong to Him in any one manner. In this, examine yourself.

A person should intend God in all things, and should not pay heed to the **manners** <note>original: "Weisen"; the specific methods, rituals, or external forms of devotion a person might prefer</note> through which they come to God. Just like one who wished to go to Rome should not heed nor look at how the road is uneven—at one time straight, then crooked, for a while uphill, and the next while into the valley. If they were to lose their peace because of this and try to avoid all these paths, they might perhaps never arrive there in the end. Likewise, a person should desire God in all manners, and should not heed the paths by which they go, or how those paths change. Whoever does not seek, find, or receive God at home or on the street, never received Him rightly in the church; that is certain. Children, in this **equality** <note>original: "Gleichheit"; a key mystical concept referring to "equanimity" or a state of inner detachment where all external circumstances—whether pleasant or difficult—are treated with the same calm spirit</note> there would be joy upon joy. But how should a person come to this, so that they may win this equality? I will tell you: learn that you must be able to renounce yourself, and that you should seek nothing of your own in any things; seek only God and His honor in all your works. How do you achieve this? You do it by taking notice of yourself wherever you find yourself, and leaving yourself right there. Learn to overcome yourself often in many things, and thus this virtue will become yours, and not otherwise. No one can give you this, nor teach it to you otherwise, and no one can know it of you but you alone—whether you intend God, or your own self in your affairs. He has peace who thus stands in "equality," and he stands in equality who does not seek his own.

Thirdly, a person should hold themselves equally toward the justice and the mercy of God. Now, one finds people who greatly desire and love God's mercy, and greatly fear His justice. Tell me, dear child, what has His justice done to you? Know for truth: what God does out of mercy, He also does out of justice. Conversely, what He does out of justice, He also does out of mercy. Justice compels God so that He must be merciful, for He is our...

<summary>Tauler uses an analogy of a journey to Rome to argue that the specific "path" or method of devotion is less important than the destination, which is God. He introduces the concept of spiritual equanimity, arguing that God's justice and mercy are inseparable and should both be embraced with the same spirit.</summary>

Father, and we are His children. Thus, it is His justice <note>original: "Gerechtigkeit"; in this context, it refers to God's righteous order and the "fairness" of His dealings with humanity</note> of necessity that He take heed of us, and show us faithfulness and love, as He indeed does and has done. One should also love and desire God's mercy <note>original: "Barmherzigkeit"</note> in such a way that God may exercise His justice upon us, according to all His worthy will, praise, and honor.

If a person is to overcome and attain this, they must be empty and void of all self-will <note>original: "Eigenwillens"; the individual ego or personal desire that opposes the divine will</note>, so that the person seeks and desires the most beloved will of God so much that whatever God does with them and with all creatures <note>original: "Creaturen"; refers to all created things, both living and inanimate</note> pleases them. To whoever the will of God tastes pleasant, everything pleases them just as well—what God does according to His justice, as what He does according to His mercy toward them and toward all creatures. To a truly loving person, everything that God wills pleases them well, whether it be love or suffering, in themselves and in all creatures. If it is God’s will, then let it also be your will, as we also pray daily:

> Lord, your will be done,

and that should also be our will: that God’s will happens in all things. We should rejoice in His will and all His works which He works in us, whether out of His mercy or out of His justice. If this [disposition] were truly our own, we would be in a state of blessedness <note>original: "Seligkeit"; a state of perfect spiritual peace and divine happiness</note>.

> That this may happen to us, may merciful justice and just mercy help us. Amen.

<summary>Tauler concludes that spiritual peace is found by surrendering "self-will" and accepting God's justice and mercy with equal gratitude. He argues that true blessedness consists in wanting exactly what God wills, whether that brings joy or suffering.</summary>

# 84.

## On the Seventh Sunday after Trinity, or on Corpus Christi, or Maundy Thursday.

### The first sermon.

->Speaks very devoutly of the great benefits and powers that the holy Sacrament of the Altar <note>The Eucharist or Holy Communion</note> works in man, etc.<-

> Behold, I am with you always, even unto the end of the world. Matthew 28:20. <note>original Latin: "Ecce ego vobiscum sum, omnibus diebus usque ad consummationem seculi."</note> *)

This was the last word that our dear Lord Jesus Christ spoke to his disciples when he departed from them on the day of the Ascension. For the faithful Son of God saw the sorrowful distress <note>original: "Jammer"; a strong term for misery or lamentation</note> of his disciples' hearts, which they felt because he was now to depart from them. So that he might comfort them—and not only them, but also all his chosen ones who would feel a great longing and distress in this misery <note>meaning the "vale of tears" or earthly life</note> after him—he spoke this word. He reminded them of the overflowing love that flowed from the depths of his divine heart at the Last Supper, when he left us the holy, physical pledge: the overflowing presence of his holy body. Then he spoke at the very last, as he was about to depart from them immediately: "I am with you every day until the end, so that all things may be fulfilled"; as if he wished to say: "See, children, just as I have left myself to you, so your distress may rightly be turned into glorious joy; that is, that I will remain with you on earth with the presence of my body <note>original: "Leichnam"; in this context, it refers specifically to the Real Presence of Christ in the bread and wine</note> until the end of the world." Therefore, perceive with all the powers of your soul the overflowing sweetness of the heart from which this gift flowed; perceive the dignity of the gift of my holy body, which I will leave on earth, and perceive also the manifold benefit which you [will receive] on earth...

[you shall] have from me, which you shall receive from this fruitful gift. Let this word be right for you, as if it were now being spoken to you by your faithful Bridegroom, Jesus Christ, as if he were saying:

> "Behold, child, see how gratefully you receive this great gift from me—that I desire to be with you through the presence of my body <note>original: "Leichnam"; in this medieval context, this refers to the physical body of Christ present in the consecrated host</note> until you have departed from this world. Observe with what purity you have adorned the house of your heart, keeping it prepared and clean so that I may dwell within it. Observe with what a bond of love I have bound myself to you and you to me through this gift, and how I have joined myself to you with willing faithfulness in a constant indwelling."

When the soul considers that his body, his blood, and his soul—united with the Godhead—are truly present there; he who, with his divine presence, fills the kingdom of heaven and all that is in it with joy; and that he wishes to grant you everything you seek in him for your salvation, and everything you need or could ever desire—then you may indeed often be filled with comforting confidence and with an inward, sweet peace of heart and soul. When you have received him with great desire, you may say:

> "I see that every good thing has come to me with him; that is, with the eternal wisdom of Jesus Christ, whose soul and body <note>original: "Leichnam"</note> are united with the Godhead."

Among other benefits that have come to me from him, three kinds of good have come to me especially. The first is that he wishes to forgive my sins all the better and make me clean from all stains. The second is that he makes me die to myself along with him, standing against every temptation of every vice, and makes me fruitful in the exercise of virtue. The third is that I have united myself with him, and he has united himself with me. See, when a person has received the holy body and blood and has offered it to the heavenly Father upon the altar of his heart, then his conscience and his soul are washed and purified from the stains of sin. As John says in the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation 7:14</note>:

> "They washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the living Lamb, Jesus Christ, all the days of their lives,"

for this is the pledge of love by which the soul is released from the bonds of all its guilt; it is the consuming fire that, by its presence, consumes and drives away all the stains of the soul—which are the sins. Ambrose <note>Saint Ambrose of Milan, a 4th-century Church Father known for his writings on the sacraments</note>

[He] says thus: As often as a person receives our Lord, so often are his sins forgiven him. Therefore he has left himself to us, so that we should offer him to the heavenly Father for our debt <note>original: "Schuld"; in this context, it refers to the spiritual debt incurred by sin</note> as a sacrifice. So pleasing is this sacrifice of his only-begotten Son that he forgives us our sins. Therefore he gave himself in the form of food <note>original: "förmlichen Speise"; likely referring to the physical "form" or "accidents" of the bread in the Sacrament</note>, and wished to take this upon himself so that he might spiritually feed and strengthen man with himself in all his illnesses.

Especially, this food strengthens [us] in three illnesses and infirmities which God so often finds in man. The first is that man, by his own power, is so little able to withstand the temptations of the enemy and the lack of virtue. The second is that he increases so little in virtues and in holy, good exercises, but rather the enemy becomes stronger in these matters. The third illness is that man remains so unsteady in the struggle against evil and in the increase of good. In order that he might come to our aid, he gives himself to us in a spiritual manner and food, so that it may strengthen us toward true virtue. Therefore he spoke: "My flesh is food indeed" <note>John 6:55</note>. 

Therefore, a person should look within himself to see if he finds himself perhaps infirm. As often as he is overcome—whether it be with impatience, or sloth, disobedience, pride <term>Hoffart: an archaic German term for arrogance or spiritual vanity</term>, ill-will, and many other things that create a barrier between him and his God—and the person finds himself in such sickness, then he should desire from the bottom of his heart to be strengthened with great humility. He should have a burning, great desire for the great, holy, heavenly food, which alone can strengthen his soul until he overcomes all his infirmity with the help of God. Now, the devils must all flee wherever the Lord possesses the fortress <note>The "Burg" or fortress is a common medieval metaphor for the inner soul where God dwells</note>, and all their storming is of no use there; and all those who rarely go to this food become sickly, and the strength within them diminishes—whether it be toward God, or in devotion, or in the virtues of good works and practice, and in inward works. The person becomes heavy, slothful, and cold toward all good things; he decreases in the strength of the soul and in its health when it is rarely fed with spiritual food, with our Lord’s body <note>original: "Leichnam"; used here in the medieval sense of the living, sacramental body of Christ</note> in a state of devotion. In the same way that the strength and health of the body diminishes from long deprivation <note>original: "Entbrechung"; a lack or absence of sustenance</note> of physical food, so too does the strength of the soul diminish from long deprivation of spiritual food and power. Therefore the Prophet says:

"My heart is withered, for I have forgotten to eat my bread." My heart is rightly withered of all devotion and starved of the spiritual strength of all virtuous, good works, because I have for so long abstained from my bread which God left to me for my food on earth, which I should have applied to the strength of my soul.

Therefore know, when a person finds himself in such spiritual sickness, he should first flee to our Lord, to his holy Body <term>Heiliger Leichnam: literally "holy corpse," this refers to the consecrated Host or the physical presence of Christ in the Eucharist</term>, so he will become joyful, strong, and alive to all good things. David says: "God sent his word and made them healthy." <note>Psalm 107:20</note>. The Word is his only-begotten Son, Jesus Christ, the Host and the sacrifice which the heavenly Father daily sends to us through the priest's hands, which makes our soul healthy, and which is sent back to Him for all our sins and distress. Therefore, when the Mass is over, they sing: *Go, it is sent* <note>original: "Ite missa est"; the traditional Latin dismissal of the Mass</note>: Go, she is sent, as if he were saying: Go forth joyfully and praise God, for the Host of the heavenly sacrifice, which the heavenly Father sent to us all for our sins, is sent back to Him.

Thus, when a person stands before our Lord’s Body, he should let himself be right in his thoughts, as if our Lord were speaking to his heart: "I am your teacher, and a constant, faithful companion in your misery. I am here with you so that, by my presence, I may remind you of my suffering, my life, and my death, all of which I bore on earth for the sake of love for you. Think of how patiently I suffered for you, how gently, how willingly; and think of my poverty, my lack of natural things <note>referring to Christ's lack of physical comforts or basic necessities</note>. Think of all the misery, labor, fatigue, disdain, scornful words, hard blows, and pain even unto death, and that I intended all my works and sufferings for you, and not for myself, so that this reminder may soften your heart and kindle it in my love, and that love may lead you to follow me, and that you also, for my sake, might forget sweet comfort and endure all your suffering and labor gently, and that..."

...[that] you suffer in all your sufferings for nothing other than me; that is, you intend me, and you place me upon your heart as a seal of love, for love is stronger than death, for I am with you. In this eternal divine love, he has so drawn us to himself that he is truly in us, and we are in him. Therefore eat and drink me; that is very necessary for you. "The bread," says Christ, "that I shall give for the life of the world, that is my flesh," which is the life of the soul when one receives it well in the Sacrament. No one can do this unless he be first in the grace of God; for just as Christ’s Body <term>Leichnam: literally "corpse" or "physical remains," used here to emphasize the real, physical presence of Christ in the Host</term> is a life of the soul in grace, so is it also a death of the soul outside of grace. Grace and love do not leave the soul within itself, for grace and love transform it into that which it loves. Of this Augustine says: "My soul is more truly where it loves than where it gives life to the body." <note>A famous medieval attribution to St. Augustine: "Anima magis est ubi amat, quam ubi animat."</note> Now, when the soul receives the Body of Christ in love, it is transformed into the Body of Christ—indeed, into Christ altogether—and beyond all that...

into his Godhead <term>Gottheit: the divine essence of God, often distinguished in German mysticism from the "God" of the Trinity as the absolute, undifferentiated source</term>. Therefore, let grace and love not allow the soul to live within itself, for it is the nature of love to carry and shape the soul beyond its natural state into the bottomless Godhead, so that it no longer knows of itself, nor feels within the spirit, for it finds itself hovering in Christ’s nakedness <note>original: "Blosheit"; a mystical term for being stripped of all earthly attachments, images, and self-will</note>. So then the soul says with Paul: Christ is my life, and dying is my gain <note>original: "Christus ist mein Leben, und Sterben ist mein Gewinn"; a translation of Philippians 1:21, "Mihi vivere Christus est et mori lucrum"</note>. This is a noble dying, where the soul dies to itself so that it may live in its beloved Christ, who is essentially Life, and in whom all creatures live eternally.

For this reason, my advice is that you, in the grace and love of God, go often to the Body of our Lord <note>original: "Leichnam"; while literally "corpse," in this context it refers to the consecrated Host or "Corpus Christi"</note>, which is eternal life. Our Lord himself spoke: "Whoever eats of the bread that I give shall live eternally," <note>A reference to John 6:51</note> for he shall be transformed into a life that is God, and where the life of all creatures is made in their clarity <note>original: "Klarheit"; refers to divine radiance or the glorified state of the soul</note>, which shall never have an end; for all souls will be transfigured with the light of the Godhead. Therefore, I advise you to go often to the holy Body of Christ.

The second reason is: because love and grace are always increased, and grow so much that the smallest degree of grace (given to the soul as often as one receives the Sacrament) is increased incomprehensibly high; and even if the soul had no grace at all, this would be enough for its salvation. For as often as one receives the Sacrament, God gives a new degree of love, and to that degree responds a new degree of a new radiance in the Godhead; that is a greatness of worth beyond all grace. Therefore, do not let yourselves be drawn away again, nor be talked out of it, by any temptation or sickness, regarding the usefulness and blessedness of the Sacrament.

The third reason why I advise going so often to the holy Sacrament is that all temptations, spiritual and natural, are moderated and satisfied in the Sacrament, so that a person comes into a stillness and into a peace of the body outwardly, and every inclination to sin is bound. Furthermore, daily sins are washed away, as well as other great sins that one does not know of, yet would gladly confess and do penance for if one knew them. Yes, how often? I answer with St. Augustine <note>original: "St. Augustino"</note>:
> To go to the Body of God every day, I neither praise nor blame; but to go every Sunday, I advise all people who do not have an intention to do evil, and I advise it with certainty.

You may well object to me: "Ah, Lord, I find myself so unprepared, and so sluggish, and without any desire or fervor <term>Innigkeit: a key term in German mysticism referring to a deep, heart-felt, and internal devotion</term> from within; also, I have such great fear because I am not well-suited." Ah, who is certain that they are in the grace of God? Truly and without any doubt, there is no human who knows that. Therefore, by the mercy of God, do what I advise you: hope that you are in the grace of God, and strive to work all virtue according to your power, and go every Sunday to the Body of God. Truly, I hold that it is better, and more praiseworthy for the soul, to receive the Body of God at a meal <note>referring to the "Lord's Supper" or Communion</note> than to have heard a hundred Masses, a hundred sermons and preachings. Also, some masters <note>original: "Meister"; likely referring to scholastic theologians or "Masters of Sacred Scripture"</note> wish to say:
> Whatever person goes once to the Sacrament without mortal sin <term>Todsünde: a grave sin that "kills" the life of grace in the soul according to Catholic teaching</term>, that person receives more love and grace than if they had gone on a pilgrimage three times across the sea to the Holy Sepulcher <note>The tomb of Jesus in Jerusalem; a major medieval pilgrimage site</note>.

Therefore, do not be frightened, and happily follow my advice with good hope; for all anxiety and fear and sluggishness shall be diminished in you, and the taste and the inwardness within shall be increased in you.

Now look at the priests, who hold Mass every day and receive God’s Body; without doubt, they do not have a particularly great fervor for the Sacrament every day; they are not all willing to do it, nor are they particularly holy of life; nevertheless, there is no day, when they have spoken their confession and [receive] our Lord's Body

have received, they receive a special grace of a degree of love and grace more than they had before. Now you might say: "Yes, Lord, they are priests, and I am not." You should be certain of this: that it helps them nothing, nor protects them, that they are priests, for the priesthood does not make them better or holier (ah, no!); rather, it is solely through the office of their priesthood that they have the ability to handle and consecrate <term>consecrate: the ritual act of turning the bread and wine into the Body and Blood of Christ</term> God's Body <note>original: "Leichnam"; while literally "corpse," in this context it refers to the consecrated Host</note>, but you cannot do that. Your life may well be better than their life; if you then receive the Body of Christ, you receive more grace in the Sacrament from God than the priests do.

St. Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas (c. 1225–1274), a preeminent medieval theologian and philosopher whose writings defined much of Catholic doctrine</note> says: This is a true preparation for the Sacrament: that a person do what is within them. To this belong three parts: first, that they leave and shun the works of sin; the second, that they have a firm will to do sin no more; the third, that they apply themselves to all good works, as much as is possible for them to do, to the honor of God.

In the Sacrament (one should know), a person receives five special things; the first is the Body which the Son of God received from Mary the Virgin. The second is the Blood of God, which Christ shed on the holy Cross. The third is the Soul of Christ, which God the Father sent from His fatherly heart into the Body of Christ. The fourth is the life of Christ with the Body. The fifth is the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and it is the Holy Trinity <term>Trinity: the Christian doctrine of one God in three divine persons: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit</term> all at once.

Therefore, know in the first part: when you receive the Body of Christ, you become a partaker in all the good deeds <note>original: "Wohlthat"; benefits or merits</note> that Christ earned in His life, in His passion, and in His death, and all the good that has ever happened since Adam's time <note>referring to the beginning of human history</note>, and shall yet happen, until the last chosen person. Secondly: when you receive the Blood of Christ, you are cleansed from all sins—even if there were perhaps mortal sins that you did not know of, provided you had the will to confess them and do penance <term>penance: the practice of making amends for one's sins</term> for them if you did know of them. Thirdly: when you take the Body of Christ and send the precious pledge of Christ's Soul into the lap of the Heavenly Father, He will forget all the sins that you have ever committed before His eyes. Fourthly: when you receive the Sacrament,

It further enumerates the five divine elements received in the Host and the spiritual benefits they provide, including the forgiveness of forgotten sins.</summary>

that is, life with the Body of Christ; in this way you are transformed into God, just as food and drink are transformed within you, and from this you receive the strength to resist all wickedness and to perform every virtue. Fifthly, when you receive the Body <note>original: "Leichnam"; while literally "corpse," in this context it refers to the consecrated Host</note> of Christ, in which the Holy Trinity <term>Holy Trinity: the Christian doctrine of one God in three persons: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit</term> resides, you are filled with all the grace of the Holy Trinity, for nothing may fill or satisfy the soul except God Himself alone. St. Bernard <note>St. Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153), a highly influential Cistercian abbot and mystic</note> says of the Holy Sacrament thus: The Body of Christ is medicine <note>original: "Arzney"</note> to the sick, a day's journey <note>likely referring to "viaticum," the Eucharist given to those traveling toward death or through the journey of life</note> to the wretched; it strengthens the weak, it brings joy to the strong, it heals the wounded, and preserves health in body and soul. The person who gladly and fruitfully receives God's Body becomes stronger to endure mockery, more patient under punishment, more diligent in work, more joyful in love, more cautious in all things, more ready for obedience, and more devout in thanking and praising God.

Now, whoever wishes to approach the Sacrament fruitfully should do so with repentance for their sins, with purity of body and heart, with longing devotion, with remembrance of the love, the suffering, and the death of Christ, and with a ready, swift, good will toward all the virtues of perfection. This is my advice and my teaching. That we all may accomplish this, may God from heaven help us. Amen.

### 85.

# For the same Sunday, or the Feast of Corpus Christi <note>original: "Frohnleichnam," the feast celebrating the Real Presence of the body of Jesus in the Eucharist</note>, or for Maundy Thursday <note>original: "grünen Donnerstag," the Thursday before Easter commemorating the Last Supper</note>.

->The second sermon on the Holy Sacrament.<-

Which people should or may receive the holy sacrament. How they benefit from it, and how they should prepare and prove themselves through the work of true repentance, both outwardly and inwardly. Also, how one may come to the true purity of virtue, thoughts, and heart.

> Let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread, and drink of that cup, etc. 1 Corinthians 11:28–32. <note>original: "Probet autem se ipsum homo, et sic de pane illo edat etc."</note> *)

St. Paul writes: Every person should prove <note>or "examine"</note> themselves before they go to the holy sacrament; that is, they should take notice of themselves, observing with what fitting exercise or devotion their heart may approach this most worthy, noble food. For it is good for some that they go often to the sacrament, even if they have no great inward desire for it, so that they may thereby keep their common habits and ways in good order and maintain the intention of turning away from sins. Indeed, those who are such, even if they occasionally feel themselves not entirely well-disposed or prepared, or without any desire, they should not for that reason refrain from it.

Excepted are those people who live according to their own will, without the ceasing of sin; these should not go to it. Also those who wish to be seen by others <note>meaning those who take communion for the sake of appearances or status</note>, and remain arrogant in themselves and in their own will, full of gossip and judgment, impatient and unpeaceful in their mind, full of scolding and grumbling, lustful in their body, and cunning and sharp of mind. Whether such as these, being equal in all these failings, should ever take the Body of God <note>original: "Leichnam Gottes"; referring to the consecrated Host</note>, we leave to their own discretion. I would well advise them that they should not go to it, for it seems to me they receive more harm from it than benefit. The more they do so, the worse and more wicked they become within, and thus they wander away from all right virtues.

Such a person is not without great inwardness, even if their outer self feels very sluggish, cold, and lacking in outward devotion. That matters nothing, for these feelings belong to our physical nature. But if the **inward will** is not righteous, then everything else is worth little.

This work of penance consists first in the reduction of food and drink, wearing rough clothing, sleeping on a hard bed, fasting, keeping vigils, and so on. One certainly finds many seemingly good people who possess many outward, praiseworthy, and noble graces, virtues, and **inwardness** <note>original: "Innigkeit," a deep, internal devotion</note>, but they base everything upon experiencing and feeling, and not upon the mind or the essence. The purity of virtue comes from other exercises, such as a person subduing his thoughts and resisting all useless whims; afterward, he should occupy his senses with the life of Christ, with His words and works, and with the Holy Scripture. He should do this constantly—now this, now that—and by this means all useless and foreign worries and anxieties that make the heart restless flee from him. Look, by this means one attains purity of thoughts. Then a person should strive for **purity of heart**, so that his heart is clean from all evil intent, from all evil sensory lust and sinful desire, so that these things are inwardly painful to him and truly repulsive <note>original: "widermüthig," meaning contrary to one's spirit or loathsome</note>, so that he cannot adapt or subject himself to anything that is sinful or evil.
