# 86.

## On the Eighth Sunday after Trinity.

Concerning the inner intention and prompting of the Holy Spirit, through which He brings a person onto the right path; concerning two things of God which are the most beloved among them. How we should take care so that our good fruits—that is, everything good we do—do not become worm-eaten <note>A common historical metaphor for good deeds corrupted by pride or selfish motives.</note>. Concerning four good pieces that serve this purpose; and finally, which people are worked upon or driven by the Spirit of God.

> <note>original: "Qui spiritu Dei aguntur, hi filii Dei sunt. Pauli ad Rom. VIII. v. 14."</note> Those who are driven or moved by the Spirit of God, they are children of God.

Every work that all humans and all creatures could perform, or should perform, until the end of the world without the grace of God—all of that together is a pure nothing, no matter how great a work one might perform, compared to the smallest work that is performed by God in a person through His grace, and the fact that the person is worked upon by God. Just as God is better than all creatures, so too are His works better than all works or methods or rules <note>original: "Aufsätze," referring to self-imposed religious regulations or formal structures.</note> with all the pleasantness that all humans might imagine. Now, the Holy Spirit often comes into a person and admonishes him, and drives him into his **inner ground** <term>inner ground: In the tradition of German mysticism, the "Seelengrund" is the deepest, most central part of the soul where God dwells and interacts directly with the individual.</term>, or speaks through teachers, and acts as if He says: Dear human, if you would only leave yourself to me, and if you would follow me alone, I would bring you onto the right path; I would work within you, and I would work through you myself. Oh, children, it is a tragedy that there is so little of anyone who would follow or listen to this wise, good counselor; instead, everyone stays stuck in their own rules, and their own adopted methods, and in blind, sensory works and opinions, which hinder the influence of the Holy Spirit so that one neither hears nor understands His language, nor gives Him place and room for His work. Therefore, it is quite necessary to say that one can reach the point of hearing the Word in no better way than with stillness, with listening, and with silence. If God is to speak—

The apples, as they lie there, look just as beautifully made as the good ones, before they are touched, picked up, and handled.

### 86. b

## On the Ninth Sunday after Trinity.

In this following sermon, every devout person is instructed how he should arrange and direct his life, externally and internally, so that he may come to right detachment <note>original: "Gelassenheit"; a central term in German mysticism referring to a state of letting go of self-will to be filled by God.</note> and the inward peace of his heart, and to a true, pure union with God.

> Reveal your way to the Lord, and hope in Him, and He will act, etc. Psalm 37:5. <note>original Latin: "Revela domino viam tuam, et spera in eo, et ipse faciet etc."</note>

The prophet says in the Psalter: Reveal your way to the Lord and hope in Him; He will make it well. Every person should take these words to heart, for everything a person needs for a godly life can be found here as a path, for whoever can seek it. Reveal your way to our Lord, and hope in Him; He will make it well.

Children, now I wish to say here what and of what kind your practice should be, outwardly and inwardly, in spirit and in nature. When one has good wine, one must have a good barrel in which to keep the wine; and therefore, a completely orderly nature <note>Tauler uses "nature" here to refer to the physical body and its natural functions.</note> creates a good, orderly foundation for good works and practices. These same practices consist of fasting, vigils, and silence. How then should the fasting be? It should be that those people fast who can well endure it, without any hardship or ruin of their nature. These same people may and should fast; therefore, I do not compel them with it here, but leave it to their own free will. But this should be your manner: that in the morning you eat your necessities well, however good the food may be that is necessary and useful for nature, and I allow that to be good for all good people. In the evening, eat and drink little; that is useful to the spirit and to nature. Furthermore, the spiritual person should always—

Therefore, turn your inward **ground** <term>Grund; the "Seelengrund" or the deepest, most essential part of the soul where the human meets the divine.</term> toward Him, and speak with the Prophet: **My face has sought You; Your face, Lord, will I seek** <note>original: "Exquisivit te facies mea, faciem tuam domine requiram"; a reference to Psalm 27:8.</note>; that is to say: Lord, my face seeks You; Your countenance, Lord, I shall search for, and there turn your ground toward the divine countenance.

For when the inward, unnamed Good offers itself within, then at once everything that has a name within the person offers itself along with it, and responds [corresponds] to that which is in God; and everything that is unnamed and unknown, and along with it everything that has a name in God, offers itself in turn to the person in the inward ground of the soul.

For this, it is useful and helpful to a person that the outer man be at rest, that he sit and keep silent, and not have outward unrest in his body through outward works. Children, for the sake of this quiet, inward chamber, God shall give you eternal life, and moreover, Himself eternally.

Children, now follows the next verse, which says: **And He shall bring forth your righteousness as the light** <note>original: "Et deducet quasi lumen justiciam tuam," from Psalm 37:6.</note>. That means: He shall shine like a light upon your righteousness. What is our righteousness? It is that we know ourselves. As St. Bernhard <note>St. Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153), a Cistercian abbot and influential mystic who emphasized self-knowledge as the first step to knowing God.</note> says: The highest and best knowledge, and that which is closest to the eternal God, is that we truly and completely know ourselves. He shall shine like a light upon your righteousness. Your righteousness is worthily maintained by the keeping of your Order, and especially by your silence. Therefore, you should be diligent in keeping your silence. Keep yourselves completely free of all people—

### 87.

# On the Tenth Sunday after the Holy Trinity.

## The First Sermon.

How every Christian should specifically perceive what their office <note>In this context, "office" (German: *Amt*) refers to one's specific vocation, duty, or spiritual calling in life.</note> might be, to which God the Lord has called them; and how they should and may act in such a way that God is honored therein, their neighbor is improved, and they remain peaceful in their conscience. Which people they are to whom God gives the discernment of spirits.

-> There are varieties of activities, but it is the same God who works all things in all. <-
<note>original Latin: "Divisiones operationum sunt, idem vero Deus qui operatur omnia in omnibus."</note>
-> 1 Corinthians 12:6. *) <-

St. Paul says in the Epistle: There are divisions of works, and one Spirit works them all together for the fruit and benefit of mankind. But it is all one Spirit; the same works all things in all things. To each is given the revelation of the Spirit for his benefit and fruit. To one is given the word of knowledge <note>original: "Rede der Kunst"; here referring to the spiritual gift of wisdom or the ability to teach complex truths.</note> in the same Spirit. And he names many differences of gifts, and all this is worked by one and the same Spirit. And he speaks much for the confirmation of faith.

In times past, the Holy Spirit worked very great, wonderful things in His friends for the confirmation of faith; these were great signs of manifold prophecies, the shedding of the blood of the saints, and their suffering in death. This manner <note>i.e., the era of spectacular miracles and martyrdoms used to establish the early Church.</note> is now no longer necessary. Yet know that, alas, there is as little true, living, active faith in some Christian people as there is in heathens and Jews.

Now let us take before us the words of St. Paul: There are divisions of works and of services, and one and the same Spirit works them all. Children, you see outwardly that there is one body, and the same has many members and many senses, and each part of the members has a particular office and work, such as the eye, which

Whoever serves God according to God’s will, God will answer according to that person’s will; but whoever serves God according to their own will, God shall not answer according to the person’s will, but according to God's own.

Be sure of this: any peace is false unless it comes from practiced virtue; you must be exercised both inwardly and outwardly. But the peace that comes from within, no one can take away. These people have appeared to lead a spiritual life for forty years, and yet today they still do not know how or where...

### 88.

# On the same Sunday.

## The second sermon.

Today’s Gospel conveys a spiritual, intelligible, and useful meaning; specifically, it speaks of two kinds of people who, through the "commerce" of their own will, are occupied with created things. Some of these are harmfully quiet and satisfied within themselves; others, by contrast, are restless yet negligent. We shall see how one may recognize the difference between the elect and the non-elect in this aforementioned spiritual commerce.

*When Jesus drew near to Jerusalem, seeing the city, he wept over it, etc. Luke 19:41.* <note>original Latin: "Cum appropinquaret Jesus Hierosolymam, videns civitatem, flevit super illam etc. Luc. XIX. v. 41."</note> \*)

**A**s our Lord approached the city of Jerusalem, he looked upon it and wept over it, saying: "Jerusalem, Jerusalem, if you only recognized the things that are near to you, you would also weep. For your enemies will come and surround you, and destroy you, and will not leave one stone upon another within you." And he went further into the Temple and cast out and struck those who were buying and selling there, saying: "My house shall be a house of prayer, and you have made it into a den of thieves." <note>German: *Mördergrube*, literally "a pit of murderers."</note>

This city, over which our Lord wept, is first of all Holy Christendom. Secondly, it represents worldly hearts, over whom our Lord weeps, and for whom it is right to weep; indeed, all people together can never weep enough for them, for they do not know, nor do they wish to know, the days of their visitation. <term>visitation (German: *Heimsuchung*): a theological term for a time when God draws near to an individual or a people, either for grace or for judgment.</term> They were in Jerusalem in great joy and peace at the time when Christ wept over them. Who are these people? All those who live according to the pleasure and desire of their external senses; these are in great peace as long as they have enough goods—power, friends, relatives, property, honor, and whatever their heart desires. They have great joy and peace, following every delight and bliss of their heart, as if they were to live forever. They confess well, they pray well, and it seems to them that they are doing well...

...they are so set in their ways that if anyone speaks a single word against them (even if it were for their own good), it would be completely wasted. Do not take these as my words, but as the words of St. Gregory in his homily. <note>likely referring to Gregory the Great's *Homiliae in Evangelia*, specifically Homily 39 which discusses this passage of Luke.</note>

It is the soul and the body of man, which are more truly a temple of God than any temple ever built of stone. St. Paul says: "The temple of God is holy, which you are." <note>1 Corinthians 3:17</note> When our Lord wishes to enter this temple, he finds it has become a house of murder and a house of commerce. ...which they do not have, and thus it becomes a trade. Who, then, are the merchants? They are those who give what they have in exchange for that which they do not have. Since a human being possesses nothing more truly their own than their own will, and they use it to buy enough temporal things—of whatever kind they may be—they therefore give [trade away] their own will. Thus, they seek pleasure in food, in clothes, in jewels, in the pleasing of themselves and of other people wherever they can; indeed, at last they must also have a "spouse" <note>original: *Gespons*. In this context, it refers to an intense emotional attachment or a person who displaces God as the soul's primary focus</note>. "Oh, dear Lord," (they say), "it does no harm; it is a spiritual love. We must enjoy ourselves, we must have pastimes, we do not want to go without them." Now, you should know this from me: you are making such a trade as long as you give your free will for these things and persist in this state, and because of it, God will always become more distant and foreign to you. **St. Bernard** says: "Divine comfort is so delicate that it can in no way exist where one receives other [worldly] comforts." "Oh, dear Lord, we are spiritual people, we belong to a religious order." Now, go ahead and wear all the cowls and hoods you want; if you do not do what you are rightfully supposed to do, it helps you not at all.

Once in times past, a man did wrong and put on a monk's cowl, yet kept his wrongdoing; the devil came and took the man, and tore him into a hundred pieces, but left the cowl whole, and carried the man away, body and soul, as people watched. Therefore, beware all the more of how full the world is of these "merchants"—among laypeople, among monks, and nuns. Oh, what a vast subject this is (for anyone who would pursue it), how everyone is full of their own will—full, full, full! That is why one sees few strong men who take God's cause upon themselves; instead, those who do so are called by "poor women's names" <note>original: "arme Frauen-Namen". > Our little bed is flowered; it is full of heavenly images and thoughts.

If the temple were cleared, and if the commerce and the fantasies that trouble the temple were cast out, you could become a temple of God—and never before, no matter what else you do—for then you would have peace and joy in your heart. Nothing would ever confuse you again, whereas now you are constantly entangled, living in distress and suffering. Elsewhere it is written: Our Lord God showed the prophet Ezekiel the temple in Jerusalem and said:

> Dig through the wall or the masonry into the temple of Jerusalem.

When the prophet did this, he found a daughter <note>In this context, the "daughter" represents the human soul</note> with many gruesome images and said:

> Lord, there are gruesome images in here.

Then our Lord said:

> The daughter painted these gruesome images herself, and thus she has made herself what she is.

This daughter with many vain images is a person with a disordered mind <term>Gemüth: the inner disposition or "heart" of the soul</term>; therefore, she must also suffer much disordered sadness.

By this, one should recognize the difference between the chosen <term>Erwählten: the "elect" or those who respond to God's grace</term> and the non-chosen. The chosen can never find perfect rest in disordered things, even though they may sometimes lose themselves a bit, becoming spiritually dry and casting all divine things behind them. These people finally come to true repentance, weeping for their indulgent, disordered lives, and so they are ultimately saved; though it may take them a long time. and this is an immeasurable, great grace from...

...of the goodness of God; he to whom God grants this is truly blessed, in that he is admonished and warned, whether inwardly or outwardly. The blame is that the way is troubled, lead astray, and covered with other images <note>mental distractions or sensory impressions that block spiritual sight</note>, so that the Word cannot come to its rightful place. Unless the ways are cleared, and the strange satisfactions and the created images are driven out, the truth will not be understood. If one preaches the truth today, and tomorrow the very same truth, and as often as that happens, one should hear it with love and with diligence. For a new truth is always hidden within, which is always to be found and is never entirely understood. 

Specifically, much is given to those who approach with a bare soul <note>original: *bloßer Seele*; a "bare" or "naked" soul is one that has been stripped of all attachments to the self and the world, a state of total spiritual receptivity</note>, for much of God's Word is lost and misunderstood by those who are not yet bare. It enters the senses and the fantasies, and goes no further into its own rightful place because of these hindrances. If these hindrances were gone, and if the merchants <note>referring to the biblical story of Jesus cleansing the Temple (Matthew 21:12-13)</note> were driven out and the temple cleared, it would immediately become a house of prayer in which God should dwell. What that prayer and petitioning truly consist of shall be spoken of further. That we may thus drive out [the world] and leave the merchants behind, so that our house becomes pleasing to God—may God help us. Amen.

## On the Eleventh Sunday after Trinity.

How a person should be prepared to receive the holy Sacrament of the Altar <note>The Eucharist or Holy Communion</note> often and frequently, as the members of religious orders are accustomed to do. For this reason, they are especially exhorted and instructed in this sermon with many discreet teachings, which may be suitable not only for them but for all Christians.

<margin>*) Serm. L. 1498. f. 154; 1508. f. 123; 1521. f. 97; 1523. f. 84; 1543. f. 175; 1565 f. 137; 1548. p. 276; 1552. p. 367; 1621. p. 817; Arndt p. 223.</margin>

> Two men went up into the temple to pray, etc. Luke 18:10. *) <note>original Latin: *Duo homines ascenderunt in templum ut orarent etc. Lucae XVIII. v. 10.*</note>
> Two men went up into the temple to pray; among them, one was a hypocrite <note>original: *Gleißner*; literally one who "shines" with a false outward appearance of piety</note>, and the other was an open sinner.

This temple is the **ground of the soul** <term>ground of the soul: *Grund der Seele*, a key concept in German mysticism referring to the deepest, most essential part of the human spirit where God dwells directly</term>, in which the Holy Trinity dwells lovably, works nobly within, has richly placed all its treasure, takes its play and its delight therein, and makes use of its noble image and likeness here. One should go into this [temple] to pray, and there must be two of these "men." That is, the **outer** and the **inward man**, if this prayer is to happen rightly. What the outer man asks for without the inward man is of little use, or nothing at all. Now, dear brothers and sisters, for this right and true prayer, there is no better or more useful help for true progress than the tender **Body of our Lord** <note>original: *Frohnleichnam*; meaning the "Body of the Lord," specifically referring to the consecrated bread of the Eucharist</note> Jesus Christ, that a person should receive it temporally <note>regularly during their time on earth</note>, and be renewed therein at once, and be born again through it. That this grace is permitted to you, you should rightly and especially thank God, and you should make use of it above all things. For nature is now so sick, and in the world so inclined toward flaws, that a person truly needs some great help and support to pull them up again and sustain them; that is, the divine food above all things.

Now, one of these men was a Pharisee—that is, a "separated" hypocrite—and the other was a tax collector—that is, an open sinner. He stood from afar and did not dare to lift his eyes toward heaven, and spoke: Lord, have mercy on me, a po— <note>The text breaks off mid-word at the end of the page; the full phrase in German is *armer Sünder*, or "poor sinner."</note>

...[if he were such a] sinner, it would go blessedly for him. I wish that I acted in truth as this one did, and always looked into my nothingness; that would be the noblest, most useful way one could have. This way brings God to man constantly, without any medium <note>without mediation; directly</note>. Where God comes with His mercy, there He comes with His whole being, and with Himself.

Now this sinner’s way <note>The humble attitude of the Tax Collector/Publican</note> enters into some people, and they want to flee from God by confessing their sin, and [flee] from this holy Sacrament, and say they dare not take it. No, dear brothers, you should go to it all the more gladly, so that the sins fall away, and you should say:

-> Lord, come soon, before my soul dies in sins. <-

Know in truth, if I found a person in the Tax Collector’s way <term>Tax Collector's way: an attitude of extreme humility and recognition of one's own unworthiness before God</term>, who truly held himself for sinful, while longing to be good, in humility, and had a reverent fear, and gladly wanted to live according to God’s dearest will, and turned from the possession of the creature <note>attachment to created, worldly things rather than the Creator</note> as much as he was able, I would gladly give that person our Lord’s Body <note>original: *Frohnleichnam*; the consecrated host/Eucharist</note> every other day with a good conscience. I will prove this with Holy Scripture. When we were plunged into holy baptism and bound to God, we gained all rights to the holy Sacrament, and all creatures cannot take that right from us, unless we take it from ourselves.

Dear sisters and brothers, it is not necessary that one has had great feelings <note>intense emotional or "sensible" spiritual experiences</note> or performed great outward works; it is enough that one is specifically without mortal sin, that one longs to be good, stands in humble, reverent fear, and confesses oneself unworthy of it; this is necessary and very useful. If the person then wished to remain so that he stayed without heavy sin, it is of great necessity that he be fed with this noble food. It draws him further into the endurance of a spiritual life. Therefore you should not easily draw back because you acknowledge your frailty; you should hasten all the more to go to this grace. For from it comes all strength, holiness, all help and comfort and sweetness, and it lies within it. You should not condemn those who do not do it <note>receive the Sacrament frequently</note>, and the others should also not be condemned by those who do not go to it, for St. Augustine says:

-> No one should condemn another for anything he does. <-

It would be then, that

...[unless] the holy Church had condemned him, both spiritually and temporally. It would be different if a person appeared, inwardly and outwardly, in a proud and haughty spirit, and willingly practiced those creaturely things that hinder him—whether such people truly approach [the Sacrament], we shall leave to the judgment of their masters <note>their spiritual superiors or teachers</note>; let them see to it whether they do so safely. Children, you should not judge all this, so that you do not become like the Pharisee, the hypocrite <term>hypocrite: original *Gleißner*, meaning one who shines outwardly or puts on a false show but lacks inner truth</term>, who exalted himself and condemned the one standing behind him. Guard against this as you would against the eternal loss of your soul. Do not fear if your weaknesses <note>original: *Gebrechen*; infirmities or moral failings</note> are pointed out to you; but guard against these dangerous failings of judgment.

Some time ago, when I saw the holy brothers who strictly kept the Order <note>The Dominican Order, known for its rigorous rule</note>, I would also have gladly done the same; but our Lord did not want that, for I recognized myself as sick. I fear I might have fallen into the Pharisaical way, with self-complacency; but you should not be afraid; for our Lord is so faithful that He often leaves a well-intentioned person in noticeable weaknesses all his life, so that he may be humbled within himself and also by those who associate with him, and thereby be directed toward his own nothingness. Therefore, a person should not cease to go forward with more joy and love and say: "Lord, I am not worthy that you should come under my roof <note>original: *Dach*; a reference to the words of the Centurion in Matthew 8:8, used in the liturgy of the Mass</note>, into my heart, but relying on your groundless <note>original: *grundlose*; in mystic theology, this means "unfathomable" or "bottomless," referring to God's infinite nature</note> mercy, and on the rich treasure of your worthy merit, I approach." For I lack repentance, love, and grace; I find these entirely in you; there one finds virtue, desire or longing, and goodness.

Children, these dangerous ways—because of which the Heavenly Father was so angry that He wished to destroy this whole world in the time of our father *Dominic* <note>Saint Dominic (c. 1170–1221), founder of the Order of Preachers to which the author likely belongs</note>, until he pleaded with Him—these same ways and failings have now risen up again. We do not know how it will go for us; we have great need to find a way by which we might soften the merciful God. For this, nothing is better than that a person give up and cast back all things, and unite himself inwardly with God in the Holy Body of our Lord <note>the Eucharist</note>. Dear brothers and sisters, you should do this with all diligence, if you can achieve it, and that at the right time with your senses, if you find within yourselves that you would gladly [praise] God...

...lived [more purely], and where you fall short of this, let it be a sorrow to you; may you gladly flee those causes that might hinder your purity, as far as you are able. In your **holy Order**, in which you are and I also am—to which we are invited and in which God has called us away from this sorrowful world—we should wait for Him and live for Him alone with whole faithfulness. Now, take note of this worthy calling often, so that you may acknowledge your own progress and be acknowledged by others. You should be very diligent in the fruitfulness of this entry into the holy Order and in all your **rules** <note>original: *Geseßen*; refers to the statutes or regulations of the monastic life</note>; not that an old brother or an old sister must fast, keep vigil, or perform outward works beyond their strength. If you conduct yourselves thus, no one can truly recognize or fathom the fruit and the benefit that comes from it.

Second, the words that one speaks should be sweet, kind, and peaceful; and if a harsh word escapes you, let there be an immediate humble confession and submission regarding it before God and before men. If someone approaches you with harsh words, you should respond with nothing but a sweet, kind countenance, and one word or two, and no more.

You should observe your **inner ground** <term>inner ground: original *Grund*, a central concept in German mysticism referring to the deepest part of the soul where the human meets the Divine</term>, that you possess, have, or use no thing with attachment <note>original: *Lust*; here meaning a craving or misplaced desire for ownership</note>, or for your own self-pleasing or that of someone else—whether it be clothes, books, jewels, or company. Everything that you truly require in an honest, orderly way—be it clothes or furs, as much as you need of these or other things for your necessity—that, God and the Order grant to you willingly.

You should have **brotherly love** among one another, and a humble submission, one to another in love and in kindness; you should not show heavy gestures, nor coldness toward one another, nor anything that may disturb your peace. You should practice virtuous works among one another in love, and friendly offer yourselves for service to one another—not only to your own friends, but to every sick or old brother or sister. You should joyfully take the work and the burdens out of their hands and carry them for them. If you only do this for your own [favorites], God does not accept it; even the heathens do that, as **Christ** speaks in the **Gospel**.

If you are also attacked or mocked for a good **spiritual exercise**...

...or despised, you should not answer for it, nor complain. Observe **silence** <note>original: *Silentium*</note>, that is your stillness in the choir and in all forbidden places. In the choir, you should stand with great reverence (for our Lord's body is truly present there in truth), with downcast eyes and with a heart turned toward the presence and face of the eternal King. If a maiden stood before a king and she knew that he was looking at her specifically, if she were sensible and rational, she would keep her composure firmly and stand in a most orderly and modest manner. How then should a person stand with all their strength, inwardly and outwardly, before their Lord and God, and before their chosen spouse <note>original: *Gemahl*; Tauler uses this bridal imagery to describe the soul's intimate relationship with Christ</note>, who gazes upon them without ceasing, both within and without? O, dear sisters and brothers, you should sing and read your **liturgical hours** <note>original: *Zeiten*; the scheduled daily prayers of the Church</note> with great devotion and with a focused heart, as much as you are able. But know, for the peace of your conscience, it is sufficient by way of commandment that one speaks the words; even if the mind is not present, one does not need to repeat it elsewhere. One truly fulfills the obligation with the words, provided the person does not intentionally think of anything contrary to the words.

Now the Gospel says: *By their fruits you shall know them.* Therefore, these are your outward fruits, by which you shall know yourselves and be known. In this manner, no one is too sick or too old; let there be love and faithfulness among one another, and patience and gentleness. A person could possess these even on a sickbed, no matter how ill they might be. You should also recognize your inward fruit; that is, that you keep yourselves **detached** <term>detached: original *abgeschieden*, a central term in German mysticism referring to a state of being "cut off" from worldly distractions to be open to God</term> from everything that is not God, and you should flee from wasting your time. You should gladly remain in union, and there unite yourselves solely with God, and climb upon the blossoming tree of the worthy suffering of Jesus Christ, and into His glorified wounds, and then climb further to the height of His most venerable Divinity, and you shall go in and out and find full pasture. Through these fruits of such a life, you shall partake of the grace of the worthy Sacrament <note>The Eucharist or Holy Communion</note> with great benefit and progress. If this way does not please those good brothers and sisters (who refrain from this out of fear, which is also good), and if suffering should then fall upon it, or heavy...

Above all things, one should practice active love; this is useful and fruitful beyond all measure. This means that a person should be grateful for the manifold good that God has done for them and for all people. They should turn with all their strength toward the great signs of love that God has shown them in every way and through every work, and especially within their own life and suffering. In response, they should offer up their own smallness, unworthiness, and nothingness, and invite heaven, earth, and all creatures to help them give thanks and praise, because they cannot do it alone.

Whatever you have ever received from God, you should not claim it as your own property or with any sense of entitlement; offer it all back to Him at once. Hold onto nothing of it as your own, except for your pure nothingness and poverty. Furthermore, let go of your questioning and disputing about whether it is God who is drawing near to you and offering Himself to you within. Stand alone upon your smallness, and upon your pure poverty and nothingness—which is what you are in truth—and leave to God what is His. 

Turn yourself back into your **Origin** <term>Ursprung; a central concept in German mysticism referring to the soul's essential source in God</term>, just as our Lord Jesus Christ, with all His powers, was always turned toward the Father, in both the highest and the lowest parts of His being. Whosoever follows this example most closely is the very best of people. For a person cannot easily or quickly fall away from this state, unless they fall into inconsistency and become somewhat less pure. In that case, the person should begin again with bottomless humility, looking inward once more and sinking into the Origin. All this is accomplished through the life and suffering of our Lord, through which everything becomes higher, more essential, more divine, and truer—and all this through the diminishing [of the self]...

## 90.

# On the Twelfth Sunday after Trinity.

### The first sermon.

How a person is prepared through the old covenant for the new; that is, through much labor and suffering (which the old covenant signifies) one must dispose and prepare oneself in true **inwardness** <term>Einkehrung; the act of turning one's attention away from the external world toward the soul</term> and **detachment** <term>Gelassenheit; a central mystical concept of letting go of self-will and worldly desires to be receptive to God</term> for the gentle yoke of the new covenant, where God helps him carry the weight, and makes all suffering light and effortless.

*The letter kills, but the spirit gives life.* <note>original Latin: "Litera occidit, spiritus autem vivificat."</note> 2 Corinthians 3:6. \*)

There are two ways of life among the **friends of God** <term>Gottesfreunde; a 14th-century mystical movement that emphasized a direct, personal relationship with God</term>: one was the old marriage [covenant, testament, law], the other is the new marriage. All people who were to be saved had to keep the old laws, with all their customs, until the Lord Christ was born and the new marriage arrived. The old marriage served as a path and a model for the new marriage. If a person looks the old marriage directly in the eye, they are prepared through the old for the new. Everything that is intended to receive something must first become receptive. The old marriage has much stricter and sharper judgments, and a far more severe demonstration of the **justice of God** <term>Gerechtigkeit Gottes; here referring to God’s strict adherence to moral law and punishment for sin</term>, and a dark, distant hope of **redemption** <term>Erlösung; the act of being saved or set free</term>. The gates were closed to them for a total of five thousand years <note>A traditional medieval calculation of the time elapsed between the Fall of Adam and the birth of Christ</note>, so that with all their suffering and their hard works they could not enter into eternal life; they had to wait long and heavily before the new marriage came, which is peace and joy in the **Holy Spirit**. Now, whoever wishes to reach the new without doubt must first be united with the old. A person must suffer, and carry heavy burdens, and bend humbly under the mighty hand of God; they must suffer inwardly and outwardly, from wherever it may come, whether it is deserved or undeserved.

Dear children, take care, for things must be very different for this matter,

# 91.

## On the Twelfth Sunday after Trinity.

->The Second Sermon.<-

What makes a person deaf or hinders them so that they cannot hear or understand the divine **in-speaking** <term>Einsprechen; the mystical concept of God's internal communication or "whispering" directly to the soul's essence</term> of the eternal Word, and how one may resist such temptation and prevent it. Concerning divine love, by which one may recognize and feel it; also how a person should practice this both outwardly and inwardly. Concerning the fingers of Christ, which signify the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, through which a person hears the truth once more. **He has done all things well** <note>original: "Bene omnia fecit etc."; Mark 7:37</note> etc. Mark VII. v. 37. *)

In the **Gospel** <gloss>the liturgical reading from the New Testament</gloss> of this time, we read that our dear Lord went from one region to another. There, a man was brought to him who was born deaf and mute; this was a necessity, for whoever is born deaf must also be mute; because he has never heard, he does not know what talking or speaking is. Into this deaf man's ear our Lord thrust his finger, and placed his saliva on his tongue, and said: **Be opened** <note>original: "Thue dich auf"; translating the Aramaic "Ephphatha" used in the biblical text</note>. When the people saw these works, they came and spoke of a great wonder: He has done all things well, He has made the deaf to hear and the mute to speak.

Now, one must note here what it is that makes a person so deaf. From the moment that the first man <note>Adam</note> offered his ears to the in-speaking of the Enemy, they became deaf to spiritual hearing, and we all after him. Thus, we cannot hear nor understand the lovely **in-speaking** <gloss>Einsprechen</gloss> of the eternal Word. Yet we know that the eternal Word is so unspeakably near to us within our **ground** <term>Grunde; the "Seelengrund" or the deepest, most essential part of the soul where God dwells</term> that a person’s own self, their own nature, their thoughts, and everything one can name or say or understand—none of these are as near, nor as internal, as the eternal Word is within a person. It speaks without ceasing within the person, yet the person hears none of this due to great deafness,

---

*) **Sermon** <note>original: "Serm." (Sermo)</note> LII. 1498. f. 160; 1508. f. 127; 1521. f. 101; 1523. f. 87; 1543. f. 178; 1565. f. 139; 1548. p. 282; 1552. p. 373; 1621. p. 833; **Arndt** <note>Referring to Johann Arndt’s influential 17th-century edition of these sermons</note> p. 231.

<summary>In this sermon, the author uses the miracle of healing the deaf-mute man to illustrate humanity's spiritual deafness toward God's internal Word. He emphasizes that although God's presence is more intimate to us than our own thoughts, we remain unable to hear Him because of the spiritual legacy of the Fall.</summary>

which has possessed the person. Whose fault is that? I say this: something has fallen over the person’s ears that has blocked his ears, so that he does not care to hear this Word; and he is so blinded by it that he has become mute, so that he does not recognize himself. If he wished to speak of his **inwardness** <term>Inwendigkeit; the internal spiritual reality or the "ground of the soul" where God dwells</term>, he could not do it, for he would not know where he stands, and would not know his own way. This is the cause: the enemy has **whispered** <term>eingeraunt; a subtle, deceptive murmuring intended to mislead the soul</term> to him, and he has listened to him, and from this he has become mute and deaf. 

What is this harmful whispering of the enemy? It is all the **disorder** <note>In this context, "disorder" refers to anything that disrupts the soul's proper orientation toward God</note> that appeals to you and speaks to you, whether it be through love for or opinions of **creatures** <term>Creaturen; in mystical theology, this refers to all created things—people, objects, or status—as opposed to the Creator</term>, or whether it be the world or what clings to it: wealth, honor, friends or relatives, and your own nature, or whatever you imagine as the love or favor of creatures—with all of this he performs his whispering. For he is always with the person and notices what the person is inclined toward, inwardly or outwardly—that is, now toward love, now toward sorrow—and he immediately leans in, looks at the person with it, and suggests it to them. And the **images** <note>mental representations or distractions that pull the mind away from God</note> that the person has of these things flow before the ears of his inwardness, so that the **Eternal Word** <note>The Logos or the voice of God within the soul</note> cannot be heard by him. If the person would quickly turn his ears and his mind away from it, the **temptation** <term>Anfechtung; a trial or spiritual struggle</term> would be easy to overcome; but because the person offers his ears to it so much, looking at it and "tasting" it with the enemy, he is nearly defeated, and the temptation is at its most difficult. But as soon as you courageously turn your ears away with your heart, you have nearly overcome, and this allows you to hear the inward Word and takes away this deafness.

Not only worldly people have this deafness, but also **spiritual people** <note>meaning those in religious orders or the clergy</note> who are turned toward creatures with love and with their own opinions, and are possessed by them. The devil has noticed this and suggests these images to them when he finds them inclined toward them. Some are made deaf by their own self-devised rules and by their **assumed practices** <term>Angenommenheiten; specific spiritual exercises or dispositions that a person adopts by their own will rather than by God's guidance</term> in sensory activity, and that with **attachment** <term>Eigenschaft; literally "property-ness," referring to a self-centered clinging to one's own will, works, or spiritual experiences</term> and with outward ways which they have taken on with their senses from creatures. All of this flows before the person’s ears, so that the Eternal Word can neither be heard nor understood in the person in any way. It is indeed true that a person must have a good, inward disposition without attachment, whether it be...

# 347

Prayer, or holy contemplation, and many similar practices, are intended to awaken **nature** <note>here referring to the person's physical and psychological faculties</note> and keep it alert, so that the spirit might be drawn up and the person enticed toward God. This should be done without any **attachment** <term>Eigenschaft; in mystical thought, this refers to "self-hood" or the desire to possess spiritual experiences and deeds as one's own property rather than God's</term>, so that the person may focus more on an inward listening for the inward Word and the inward whispering. A person should not act like those stagnant people who, until their death, remain fixed in their outward ways and seek nothing further. When God wishes to speak into their souls, there is always something rushing into their ears so that His Word cannot be heard. Children, these external means are so strangely numerous, and people are so entangled in these ways, that in the end, there will be nothing but misery when all things are revealed.

Now, the Word is spoken into no one's ears unless they possess divine love; for the Gospel says: *If you love me, you will hear my words.* <note>original: "Liebet ihr mich, so höret ihr meine Worte." A paraphrase of John 14:23</note> Now **St. Gregory** <note>Gregory the Great (c. 540–604), a Pope and Doctor of the Church whose writings on the contemplative life were highly influential in the Middle Ages</note> says: "If you wish to know whether you love God, take notice of what happens when distress, tribulation, and suffering fall upon you, whether from within or without." It may come from an internal pressure so great that you do not know which way to turn, where you stand, or how to distinguish one thing from another. If you then remain—despite the outward storm of suffering, unforeseen circumstances, and great pressure—peaceful and undisturbed in your **ground** <term>Grund; the deepest, most essential part of the soul where the human meets the Divine</term>, so that you do not fall into the failing of restlessness in your words, works, or gestures, then there is no doubt: you love God. Where true love really exists, a person remains neither puffed up by love nor terrified by sorrow; whether things are taken from you or given to you, as long as your Beloved remains, you are at peace inwardly. Even if the "outer man" weeps, that must be endured, as long as the "inner man" remains at peace and is well-contented with the will of God. If you do not find this within yourself, then in truth you are deaf, and the eternal Word is not truly heard within you.

You shall also recognize whether you have real love by this: that you practice gratitude for the great good that God has done for you and all **creatures** <note>referring to all created beings and things</note> in heaven and on earth, and for His **holy humanity** <note>referring to the Incarnation and life of Jesus Christ</note>, and for the manifold gifts that flow from Him without ceasing to all people.

<summary>This page explains that spiritual practices should lead to "inward listening" for God's Word. It identifies the true test of divine love as maintaining inner peace during suffering and practicing constant gratitude for God's gifts.</summary>

Your practice should be universal, in love for all people—not only for your own circle, but for all people, whether they be priests, monks, nuns, or **Beguines** <term>Beghinnen; laywomen in the Middle Ages who lived in religious communities but did not take formal vows</term>, of whatever life or manner they may be. It must be a genuine love. You should not love yourself or your own interests with a selfish love. This genuine, universal love is useful beyond measure. Know, children, that where the true, transfigured **Friends of God** <term>Gottes-Freunde; a 14th-century mystical movement in the Rhineland that emphasized a direct, personal relationship with God</term> are found, their hearts melt out of love for all people, both the living and the dead; and if these people did not exist, we would be in a bad way. <margin>From: "Know, children — in a bad way" from the 1498 edition.</margin> You should also let your love shine outwardly as far as you are able, through gifts, comfort, help, and counsel. Although you must attend to your own necessities, if you find yourself unable to help others, you should always stir up your love so that you *would* do so gladly according to your ability if you could. These are the true signs of love, and proof that a person is not "deaf."

Now our Lord comes and puts His finger into the person's ears, and lays His saliva upon the person's tongue, and then he shall speak. <note>A reference to the healing of the deaf-mute in Mark 7:33-35, interpreted here as a spiritual awakening</note> Oh, children, wonders could be told of this! But here we consider the **Seven Gifts of the Holy Spirit** <note>Traditional Christian virtues: Wisdom, Understanding, Counsel, Fortitude, Knowledge, Piety, and Fear of the Lord</note>, which are given to the person through this divine touch, and then the person will hear in Truth.

First, the spirit of **Fear** is given. This can strip a person of all self-will; it teaches him to flee from and abandon all things, including all disordered pleasures and self-conceit. Second is the spirit of **Gentleness** <note>Milde; often corresponding to the gift of Piety</note>, which makes a person sweet-tempered, kind, and merciful; he does not strike down the work of others with his own harsh judgment, and it makes him peaceable. Third, the third finger is given, which is the gift of **Knowledge** <term>Kunst; here referring to the gift of 'Scientia' or spiritual discernment</term>. By this, the person becomes "knowing"—that is, he is tested inwardly on how he should conduct his inner life according to the most beloved will of God. The fourth is **Divine Fortitude**. Through this gift, a person becomes so "God-formed" that it becomes easy and a small thing for him to suffer, to act, and to let things be for the sake of God. The fifth is the spirit of **Counsel**; those who wait for this and follow it become tender, loving people. After these come two large, long fingers, which are Under- <note>The text breaks off here, likely continuing with "Understanding" (Verstand) and "Wisdom" (Weisheit) on the following page</note>

### 92.
# On the Thirteenth Sunday after Trinity.
## The first sermon.

Concerning the **inner vision** <term>inwendiges Gesicht; the spiritual capacity to perceive divine truths or the presence of God within the soul</term>, and how it is so miserably blinded in many people, covered and glazed over with the thick scales of willful failings and natural attachments. That we should look most highly upon our own nothingness and frailty; how one should usefully employ temporal necessities, and fruitfully view and contemplate the suffering of Christ; and what good deep humility can bring to a person.

> Blessed are the eyes that see what you see. Luke 10:23. <note>original Latin: "Beati oculi qui vident quae vos videtis."</note> *)

We read that our Lord once rejoiced when he gazed inwardly at those who were chosen by his heavenly Father, and said: I thank you, heavenly Father, that you have hidden these things from the great and wise of this world, and have revealed them to the little ones. Then he turned to his disciples, and looked at them, and began the Gospel that is read during this week: "Blessed are the eyes that see what you see, for many kings and prophets desired to see what you see, and did not see it." Then a master of the law <note>A scribe or lawyer specializing in Jewish religious law</note> came and wanted to test our Lord, and thereby catch him in an error, and asked him and said: "Master, what shall I do that I may possess eternal life?" Our Lord answered him kindly (and yet knew well that his intention was false) and said: "How do you read in the law?" Then he said: "That one should love God with all one's heart and—"

...soul, and with all your strength and mind, and your neighbor as yourself. Then our Lord said: Do this, and you shall live.

Now let us take the first word: "Blessed are the eyes that see what you see." Man has two kinds of eyes: outward and inward. If the inward eye were not there, man would be a wretched, sickly thing with only outward eyes, and man would be like an animal. How can it be then that noble Reason (which is the inward eye <term>inwendige Auge; the spiritual intellect or the "eye of the soul" capable of perceiving divine truth</term>) is so miserably blinded that it does not see the true light? This great, piteous harm has come about because a thick, coarse skin and a heavy hide have been drawn over it; this is the love and obsession with created things <note>original: "Liebe und Meinung der Creaturen." In medieval mysticism, "creatures" refers to anything created—people, objects, or the self—as opposed to the Creator</note>, whether it be the person themselves or something belonging to them. Because of this, man has become blind and deaf, regardless of his station, whether worldly or spiritual.

With this blindness, they go to receive the precious Body of our Lord <term>Frohnleichnam; the Eucharist or Holy Communion</term>, and the more they approach it, the deafer they are, the blinder they become, and the thicker the skin grows. Children, why do you imagine it is that man cannot come into his "Ground" <term>Grund; the deepest, most essential center of the soul where the human meets the Divine</term> in any way? The fault lies in the fact that many a thick skin has been pulled over it, as thick as an ox's forehead, and this has so covered his interior that neither God nor he himself can enter; it is overgrown. 

Know that some people may have 30 or 40 skins—thick, coarse, black skins. What are these skins? It is every thing to which you willfully turn: whether it be wantonness in words or works, favor or disfavor, pride, self-will, seeking pleasure in anything without God, hard-heartedness, frivolity, or carelessness of conduct. These and the like create all those thick skins and great barriers that blind a person's eyes. 

As soon as a person looks upon this with sorrow, and humbly confesses his guilt to God, and has the will to improve according to his ability, immediately all becomes good counsel around him, and the skins fall away. But for some people, whatever they are told does not go to their heart, as if they were asleep. Thus, the hides have grown over their eyes and ears; they will not let go of their idols <term>Abgötter; false gods or internal attachments that replace God</term>, whatever they may be. They act like Lady Rachel, who went and sat upon her idols <note>A reference to Genesis 31:34, where Rachel steals and hides her father's household idols by sitting on them</note>. The images that one has of these things create obstacles and thick hides, and they fall upon them...

**"Blessed are the eyes that see what you saw."** <note>A reference to Luke 10:23</note> A person who has their senses about them could easily notice in themselves that worldly, extravagant hearts find such delight in created things <note>original: "Creaturen." In this mystical tradition, "creatures" refers to anything that is not God, including people, physical objects, and the self</note>, which are actually nothing of themselves. How much more wonderful, then, must He be, from whom all these wonders have flowed. Our Lord said that his disciples were blessed because of what they saw. If we truly take note of it, we should be even more blessed, for we see much more of our Lord Jesus Christ than the disciples did. St. Peter, St. John, and the others saw a weak man walking before them, but we acknowledge him in holy faith as a great, mighty God and Lord of Heaven and Earth, who made all creatures out of nothing. If we look upon this rightly, then our eyes are eternally blessed.

Dear children, the great Doctors and the Lecturers <term>Lesemeister; scholastic masters who taught by reading and commenting on texts, often contrasted by mystics with the "Lebemeister" or masters of living</term> dispute whether knowledge <note>original: "Bekenntniß." Here meaning intellectual recognition or the cognitive act of "knowing" God</note> is greater and nobler, or love. But we will say nothing of the Lecturers here. When we arrive there [in the afterlife], we shall see all things clearly in the Truth. Our Lord says: **"One thing is needful."** <note>Luke 10:42, from the story of Mary and Martha</note> Now, what is the one thing that is needful? That one thing is that you recognize the "Nothingness"—that this is your own, what you are, and who you are of yourself. It was for this one thing that you caused our Lord such agony that he sweat bloody sweat. Because you would not recognize this one thing, he cried out on the cross: **"My God, my God, why have you forsaken me!"** <note>original: "Mein Gott, mein Gott, wie hast du mich verlassen!" (Matthew 27:46/Mark 15:34)</note>—so that the "One Thing" that is needful should be so completely forsaken by all men! 

Dear children, let go of everything that I and all teachers ever taught, and all active reality and contemplation, and contemplate and learn this one thing alone: that this [Nothingness] becomes yours; then you have worked well. Therefore our Lord says: "Mary has chosen the best part." In truth, if you could attain this one thing alone, you would have attained not just a part, but the whole of it. This "One Thing" is not like how some people might speak of their "nothingness" rationally and thus "humbly," as if they essentially possessed the noble virtue of humility, while in their depths they are still larger than the Cathedral or the Minster. They want to be great and appear great; they deceive others, and most of all themselves. For they are the ones who truly remain in deception.

Now let us speak of the **outward person.** See for yourself: what are you, and from what did you come? From a filthy, rotten, evil substance <note>original: "Materie"</note> that is unpleasant in itself and to all people. Now, what have you become? An unclean, stinking vessel full of foul flavor [smell] <gloss>odor</gloss>. No matter how noble, how pure, or how beautiful the food and drink that enters you, it will become an intolerable stench within you. And no one loves another so much (even those who have often risked their eternal lives for love and dared to be eternal **brands of hell** <term>Höllenbrände; those consumed by the fires of hell, suggesting that even intense human love cannot overcome the physical repulsion of death</term>) that, if the other dies, they could bear to have them near. They flee from them more than from a dead dog. 

Now God has set all things against man: the heavens, the sun, the stars. Now you shiver, now you are too hot, now too cold; now it frosts, now it snows, now it rains. Now you are healthy, now sick; now well, now ill; now in sorrow, now in joy; now hunger and thirst. Now the animals, the worms, fleas, and lice, and many such things; and from all of these, you often cannot defend yourself. Now see how the wild animals are more glorious in their nature; their clothing grows upon them, and it is enough for them, whether it be warm or cold. You must borrow your clothes from them, and in that very poverty you take pleasure, satisfaction, and **pride** <term>Hoffart; a specific type of spiritual arrogance or vanity, often related to external status</term>! Is it not an unspeakable blindness? 

The cattle are satisfied with food, drink, clothes, beds, and shelter, just as God has made for them. Now see what marvels <note>original: "Wunders"</note> are required so that your poor nature may be sustained, and yet one takes great pleasure in this and commits great failings through the use of dead animals. In former times, when the saints had to eat, they wept; and when they had to die, they laughed. 

Now consider further your **nothingness** <note>original: "Nichts." In this mystical tradition, "nothingness" is the goal of humility—stripping away the "self" so God can act through the soul</note>. What misery do you have in your nature? Do you pray gladly? Do you keep watch gladly? Do you fast gladly? Do you weep gladly? What comes of this? What you wish to do, you do not; and what you do not wish to do, that you do. <note>An allusion to the Apostle Paul’s lament in Romans 7:15 regarding human frailty</note> What marvels often arise within you from many strange **temptations** <term>Anfechtung; a spiritual trial, inner conflict, or "assault" on the soul</term>, so that many a failing is permitted over you by God, both inwardly and outwardly. Do you take no heed of this? Oh, if only you would learn this one thing—that is and would be necessary for you. Be at peace; God ordains it all for your best, so that through all of this you might arrive at your **nothingness**. This is perhaps better for you than if you stood amidst great things. Thus people come upon you with ghastly gestures and heavy words, and the great, rational ones with subtle, lofty words,

For the created abyss <note>Tauler often uses the term "abyss" (*Abgrund*) to describe the infinite depth of the human soul which mirrors the infinite depth of God</note> leads downward because of its depth, and draws the uncreated, deep abyss into itself, and there becomes a single One, a Nothingness within another Nothingness. This is the Nothingness of which St. Dionysius <note>referring to Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-century theologian influential in Christian mysticism</note> speaks, saying that God is none of those things that one might name, understand, or grasp. There the spirit becomes so detached <term>gelassen; a state of yielding or "letting be" where the soul releases its own will to God</term> and humble that if God wished to make it nothing at all (if it were possible to become nothing), it would gladly do so out of love for the Nothingness into which it has sunk; for it knows nothing, loves nothing, and tastes nothing but the One. These eyes that see in this way are truly blessed, and of them our Lord might well speak: Blessed are the eyes that see what you see. May God the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit help us to become blessed with a true vision of our own nothingness. Amen.

## 93.

# On the Thirteenth Sunday after Trinity.

### The Second Sermon.

Concerning the path that leads man to true blessedness. How one should love God with the whole heart, the whole soul, all strength, and the whole mind; what the mind is, and concerning its blessed nobility and its eternal inclination and attraction toward God. If the soul could see its own essence and all its powers, what great wonders and goodness it would find and see there.

## On the Fourteenth Sunday after Trinity.
<note>The "Fourteenth Sunday after Trinity" is a specific day in the liturgical calendar, occurring in late summer or early autumn. In the Lutheran and Catholic traditions, the readings often focus on the works of the Spirit versus the flesh.</note>

*How we should put on a new man and be formed and transformed according to God, especially with four qualities in which we become like God.*

Dear children, if we are now to walk in the Spirit, we must make a free, steadfast turning away from all sinful failings and from the disordered love and pleasure of all creatures. We must turn our soul with all its strength lovely toward God with constant prayer, with detachment <term>Abgeschiedenheit: a core concept in German mysticism meaning an inner "cutting away" from worldly distractions to be alone with God</term>, and with virtuous, modest exercises, through a submissive watching of the body under the Spirit. In this way, we put on a new man, who is formed after God.

This likeness <note>German: *Gleichniß*. Even the souls that must be in hell without end still possess this image of His likeness, which can never be wiped out. Now we read of four things that are in God, in which we should likewise be formed according to God. The first is that God is invisible, for we read that no mortal eye can see God. Now, we should be like God in this respect when we come to the spiritual life: that henceforth we should always be invisible. This means that we should never again be seen in such a form or deed that anyone who sees us might be offended <note>In a religious sense, "offended" (*geärgert*) means to be led into sin or stumble in one's faith by someone else's behavior.</note>.

Dear children, Paul said: The world is crucified to me and I to the world <note>Galatians 6:14.</note>. That the world was crucified to him means this: that all joy, tenderness, and pleasure that all this world might desire was so entirely repulsive and unpleasant to him, and he desired it less than the gallows or the cross. But that he was a cross to the world means that he offered and showed himself—in his morals, in his gestures, in his detachment <term>Gelaß: a technical term in German mysticism referring to a state of being "let go" or released from self-will and worldly attachment.</term>, and in all his works—in such a way that the world desired him as little as it desired the cross. In this part lies the perfection of spiritual people. Whoever finds themselves here should know that they are on the right path to perfection. Unfortunately, there are many of us to whom the world is a cross, in that they do not desire the world; but among thousands, one does not find even one who has entered into this perfection: that they do not desire to please the world. I am not speaking here of sinful things. No, not at all, dear children; rather I say this: the person who reaches such perfection that they may say with St. Paul, "I am a cross to the world," should offer themselves in all deeds, in all matters, and in every gesture and manner, so that they do not desire, nor care, nor think to please anyone at all, except God alone. Such a person might well say: The world is crucified to me, for I offer myself in all things, both inwardly and outwardly against the world, so that the world desires me no more than the gallows or the cross.

## 95.

# On the Fifteenth Sunday after the Holy Trinity.

## The First Sermon.

Concerning a threefold conduct: how a person should live and bear himself toward himself, toward his neighbor, according to the image of Christ’s life, and according to inward waylessness <note>German: *Weisloßigkeit*. A mystical term describing a state where the soul is so lost in God that it no longer follows specific "ways" or methods.</note>, or unknown darkness; all with good instruction, fruitful for all Christians to read.

->If we live in the Spirit, let us also walk in the Spirit. <note>original: "Si spiritu vivimus, spiritu et ambulemus."</note> Galatians VI. v. 1 and 25. *)<-

Brothers, if we live in the Spirit, then we should also walk in the Spirit, and should not act upon or follow the desire for vainglory <note>German: *üppigen Ehre*. Referring to the pursuit of worldly status or prideful recognition.</note>. We should not fight among one another, nor be angry, nor hate. And if anyone should be caught in any sins,

Empty honor is everything for which one wishes to be praised by others. This creeps into all good manners, words, works, and gestures, so that a person needs to stand diligently on his guard, and must pray to God to protect him, for he can do nothing good of himself.

For what costs nothing is worth nothing. No, dear child, those young, healthy, strong, unconquered natures who still live in "flesh and blood" complain that they have so many intrusive thoughts, stirrings, and imaginings.

Where there is a good nature and grace is added to it, progress happens very quickly; as I know more than one person (younger people of 25 years), married and of noble birth, who stand perfectly in this way. Yet when these poor children should be waiting upon **God's work** toward the goal in this way, they are hunted out and told they must go work for bread; thus a great thing can be neglected. It is very delicate to deal with people who walk in this dark way; they may very easily become desolated <gloss>become lost</gloss>.

## On the aforementioned fifteenth Sunday.

### The second sermon.

Regarding the great harm that <term>disorderly temporal worry</term> <note>original: "unordentliche zeitliche Sorgfalt." How one should seek the kingdom of God and His righteousness, and where such things may be found; why God often allows His own people to suffer want here. Finally, concerning a useful care that we should have—that is, to maintain the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.

*Seek first the kingdom of God and His righteousness. Matthew 6:33.* <note>original: "Primum quaerite regnum Dei et justitiam ejus."</note> *Seek first the kingdom of God and His righteousness, and all these things shall be added unto you.*

Here the Son of God gives us a notable sign and a comparison; He points the <term>rational man</term> <note>original: "vernünftigen Menschen." In this context, humans are distinguished from the rest of creation by their "Vernunft" (reason/intellect).</note> to the adornment of the flowers of the earth and to the <term>unreasoning birds</term> <note>original: "unvernünftigen Vögel." Creatures that do not possess human reason but are still cared for by God.</note> of the heavens, and says: Look at the lilies of the field and the flowers of the earth; they neither spin nor sew, yet Solomon in all his wisdom and riches was never clothed as lovely and beautiful as they. Consider the birds of the heaven; they neither reap, nor sow, nor gather into barns with their worrying, and yet your heavenly Father feeds them. Since this is so, are you not much better than these unreasoning creatures? Therefore I say to you, you shall not worry about what you will eat, nor what you will be clothed with, and you shall not say: "What shall we eat?" or "What shall we drink?" or "What shall we wear?" for these are the things the people of the world seek after. But your heavenly Father knows well that you [need them].

## 97.

### On the Sixteenth Sunday after Trinity.

How a person can reach the height of the super-essential <term>super-essential: (German: überwesentlich) a mystical term describing God as being "beyond all being" or "above all essence," exceeding human comprehension</term> Godhead through three noble virtues: detachment <term>Gelassenheit: a core concept in German mysticism meaning a total "letting-go" of the self and worldly desires to be open to God</term>, un-affectedness <term>Unannehmlichkeit: in this context, the state of not being moved or swayed by personal gain or sensory experiences</term>, and inner freedom <term>Ledigkeit: literally "emptiness" or being "unencumbered"; a state where the soul is free from all created things</term>; additionally, the today’s Epistle is subtly and fruitfully explored in all its points, especially what the breadth, length, depth, and height in God may be. How a truly detached, pure, free, and humble person may attain and grasp these things with all the saints. Finally, what the art of Christ is, which we all ought to be able to perform.

->I bow my knees to the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, etc. Ephesians 3:14<- <note>original: "Flecto genua mea ad Patrem Domini nostri Jesu Christi etc. Ad Ephes. III. v. 14."</note>

St. Paul says: I bow my knees to the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, from whom all fatherhood in heaven and earth is named, so that you do not lose heart because of my suffering. May that same Father give you the riches of His glory and strengthen you with virtues, with His Spirit of truth in the inner man; may He grant that Christ dwell in your hearts through holy faith, rooted in the love of God, so that you may truly grasp with all the saints what the breadth, the length, the depth, and the height of God is, so that you may know this. For the highest love of Christ is that you be filled with all the fullness of God.

Children, this speech is so rich and so full of noble meaning that there would be no need for us to search through books for it or need to add anything to it. When St. Paul wrote this Epistle, he was a prisoner, and in it he desired that his friends would not be distressed by this. If I were a prisoner, that would also be a source of suffering for my own children, and I would be especially sorry for that. While St. Paul was in this prison, he truly pointed his dear friends toward the way of detachment <gloss>Gelassenheit</gloss>, so that they should not allow themselves to be troubled by this, nor by any other thing. For such people, the sorrow and suffering of their friends is much closer to their hearts than their own, and with this they wish to excuse—

...[be discouraged], although it is not true detachment <term>Gelassenheit: a core concept in German mysticism meaning a total "letting-go" of the self and worldly desires to be open to God</term>; one should commit all things to God. Therefore St. Paul desired that they should be without any distress <note>Betrübniß: sorrow or affliction of the soul that weighs down the spirit</note>, for distress is a great hindrance to man; it spoils life, darkens light, and extinguishes the divine fire in man’s heart. Thus St. Paul says: Rejoice always in our Lord, and again he says, rejoice.

Now St. Paul speaks further: I bow my knees, not only the outward ones but also the inward ones. For the interior world <note>Inwendigkeit: the inner life or the "ground" of the soul</note> is always a thousand times wider, broader, deeper, and longer than the exterior—the feet and knees, which are our outer support. In the same way, the rational man <note>vernünftiger Mensch: in this mystical tradition, this refers to the higher part of the soul capable of knowing God, rather than simple logic</note> should bow all his capacity under God the Lord; and moreover, everything he is and is capable of, he should bow it all together before the mighty power of God, and should there fundamentally acknowledge his own natural and frail nothingness. Natural nothingness is that we are nothing by nature, and frail nothingness is that which has reduced us to nothing <note>likely referring to the state of sin or the transience of human existence</note>. With these two "nothings" we should lay ourselves humbly at the feet of God. 

This humble bowing truly directs us toward a pure submission to God, with right detachment, toward suffering, and toward un-affectedness <term>Unannehmlichkeit: literally "un-accepting-ness"; here meaning "resignation" or (Latin: Resignatio), the state of not seeking personal satisfaction or "taking" things for oneself</term>. These three are just like three sisters, and are clothed in one garment, which is true humility. For man should stand in a right, ordered equality <note>Gleichheit: a state of equanimity where one is unmoved by external changes</note>, concerning love and sorrow, having and lacking, the hard and the soft; and he should take every thing purely from God and not from creatures. For man is, in a way, as if he were three men. That is, the outer man should be subdued as far as one is able through detachment, and then drawn inward into the other, inner man—into the noble, rational man. This means that the outer man should not act nor run about except according to the instruction of the rational man, and not according to sensuality. <meta>This page continues the sermon for the 16th Sunday after Trinity, based on Ephesians 3:14–21. Tauler's Sermons. Vol. II. 25.

[This love should] be universal, with nothing excluded, in the same way as it is in the love of God. For if this pure, God-formed ground <note>In German mysticism, the "ground" (*Grund*) refers to the spark of the soul where the human spirit and God are united</note> slips away from a person, then the true, pure love of God is not within them; for the universal love of God in a person flows into or draws all things into itself. If this love could share itself with all people—both the evil and the good—it would do so willingly, joyfully, and gladly for God’s sake. It is like the holy father St. Dominic, who once offered to sell himself into slavery to raise money so that he might help poor people in their desperate need <note>An reference to an early legend of St. Dominic, who offered to sell himself to redeem a man held captive by the Moors</note>. A person should act from this divine love at all times.

The "length" refers to one turning inward to the Now of eternity <note>original: "Nu der Ewigkeit." This refers to the *nunc stans*, the "ever-present now" where there is no past or future, only God's presence</note>. This is the length: it is without a "before" or "after," and without any changeability. It is there that the beloved saints in eternity employ, acknowledge, love, and enjoy that which God Himself employs. By this we should understand a cooperative activity and a lovely, sweet feeling—actual and practiced without ceasing—as far as it is possible here in this time of grace.

The "depth" that is in God is such a deep abyss that no created understanding can follow or attain it. Not even the worthy, divine soul of our Lord Jesus Christ can fully fathom it (because of His created, hu<unclear>man</unclear> nature), for it cannot be followed or searched out by anyone except God Himself. A person should encounter this depth in this manner: with depth. This means a bottomless abyss of "annihilating" oneself <note>A technical term in mysticism for letting go of the ego and self-will so completely that the soul feels it has become "nothing" in the face of God's "everything"</note>, without any foundation. For if the soul of a person could here become a total, pure nothingness, that would seem to the soul to be possible, right, and just; from this depth comes the confession of one’s own nothingness. 

The soul also goes among the poor, blinded, and corrupted sinners, feeling a wretched, sensitive, and painful sorrow for them, for it pities them to the very core in their great blindness. This person's depth is so abysmal that, were it possible, it would pull them down to the very bottom of hell—and if the eternal God had so ordered it (which He has not) so that all souls in hell could be redeemed and come out, these people would gladly offer themselves to go in so that the others might all be set free. However, no one should actually do this, nor even think of it in the form of a prayer, for the same...

Rather, what He is, He is of Himself and from no one else. These noble people follow the "height" in this way: they swing their spirit upward into the height above all things, with such great gratitude and magnanimity that it is beyond all measure. Everything that is created is unspeakably far below God—like a pure nothingness compared to the full being of the angels and spirits. Furthermore, everything that God *could* make is as nothing when weighed against the height of God. For this height and this noble, super-essential being draws the person’s spirit so excellently high above itself with divine love, gratitude, and with eager praise; it flees so high and far above itself that all praise of oneself and of all creatures, angels, and saints is outgrown. <meta>This page continues the exploration of the "four dimensions" of spiritual life (height, breadth, length, and depth).
