...passed into life, and moreover they surpass all virtue. Just as a great fire comes from many coals, and then a bright flame leaps up above the coals into the heights, so should a person allow a surpassing manner to penetrate their spirit from all thoughts, imaginings, and actions of their lowest and highest powers; this manner travels high above all their own capacity and the working of themselves and all creatures into the noble height of the super-essential Godhead <note>original: "überwesentlichen Gottheit." This refers to God’s essence which exists beyond all "being" or "substance" as understood by humans.</note>.

A young wife whom I once knew experienced the same thing. This woman’s spirit once soared into the heights, and in that moment her own ground <note>In this context, the "ground" (Grund) is the innermost core of the human soul where it meets God.</note> was uncovered and revealed to her. She saw herself in a surpassing clarity and saw the ground in an unfathomable height; this same height was without end, and was also in an endless length, and moreover broad and deep; and this same depth was without any bottom. Thus, a person comes to understand the height, the breadth, the length, and the depth of God <note>Tauler is referencing Ephesians 3:18 here.</note>, as far as is possible here in this time. Know, children, that those people who enter into this through these noble virtues—that is, releasement <term>Gelassenheit: a central concept in German mysticism meaning a state of letting go, detachment from the self, and surrender to God's will.</term>, emptiness <term>Ledigkeit: a state of being unencumbered or free from worldly and internal distractions.</term>, and non-attachment <term>Unannehmlichkeit: the refusal to "take in" or claim spiritual experiences as one's own possession.</term>—and when these three virtues are clothed with true, deep humility and truly dwell in the "cloister of divine love" in a state of detachment, these are truly people according to all the will of God, for they are one with Him and He with them without ceasing. In these people, God may perform His works as He wills and when He wills, without any hindrance. Therefore, all people who have not truly gone through this with right practice fall back down to the bottom. But if you have entered here with these aforementioned virtues and truly stand within them, and it then slips away from you, this must surely come from the self-satisfaction and the possessiveness <note>original: "Annehmlichkeit und von der Eigenschaft." These terms refer to the soul taking selfish pleasure in its progress or clinging to spiritual gifts as personal property.</note> that you have had within yourself. Guard yourself against this, if you wish to remain in this divine ground. Dear children, here the seed of grace is then born, and it pours itself into the ground, as it is written: 

> Come to me, and be filled with my birth. <note>This is a mystical adaptation of Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 24:19: "Come to me, you who desire me, and eat your fill of my fruits." Tauler identifies the "fruit" with the "Birth of the Word" in the soul.</note>

One must pass over all things. This birth is indeed shown to some people, yet it is not born within them. But the person who, with all their practice, aims outwardly and inwardly at right, true releasement—in that person this birth can happen, provided they have walked through these paths.

Know, children, I find these noble foundations perhaps in young people, but in the elderly it is especially corrupted; for the elderly stand too firmly upon their own opinions and their old ways, with their self-centeredness <note>Original: "Eigenſchaft." Therefore, of necessity, this inward ground must remain hidden from all those people who always remain with all their activity in the external, sensory person; for the outer person is too coarse for this bottomless ground of God.

...like a servant standing ready to wait for what his master would have him do, so that he may do it at all times without any contradiction. Those outer people do not do this; they are always acting externally, according to their sensory ways, and they even pull other people into those same outward ways, which they certainly should not do. One can follow this manfully, for this holy life is established solely by the Holy Spirit in every pure soul that waits upon Him alone and no one else.

[The] Man suffered, so that he might redeem us all from eternal death, if we ourselves are willing. When He was the most forsaken of all people on this earth, He was then most pleasing to His heavenly Father; that was when Jesus Christus cried out with a lamentable voice: <note>original: "Mein Gott, mein Gott, warum hast du mich verlassen?"</note> "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" For the eternal Son of God, Jesus Christus, was more forsaken—and indeed more bitterly so—than any saint was ever forsaken by God the Father. Jesus Christus acknowledged this wretched, painful, and bitter abandonment when He sweated bloody sweat on the Mount of Olives <term>Oelberge: the Mount of Olives, where Christ experienced his agony before his arrest.</term> for the sake of all people; and yet, according to His highest powers, He was a true possessor of that which He now is: the Godhead, which He Himself was. This is the art of Christ, and it surpasses all other arts: that a person holds themselves to be comfortless and forsaken from both without and within, poor and wretched of all refuge, and stands in true, steady releasement <term>Gelassenheit: the mystical state of letting go of one's own will to be filled by God.</term> and detachment <term>Abgeschiedenheit: a state of being "cut off" or detached from worldly desires to focus solely on the divine.</term>, just as our Lord Jesus Christus was forsaken. Whoever truly stands in this state, in misery and comfortlessness, would be most pleasing to God the heavenly Father.

In this empty, pure, and detached person, God truly directs and reigns in the inner ground of the person; there the essential peace of God is born. You should never let this same complete divine peace (which the mild and kind God has given you) be taken from you in this time—neither by angels, nor people, nor devils, nor by all creatures together. In this ground and disposition, the person should always have their outer self under control, and keep it in a humble submission under God and under all creatures. They should always be suspicious of the outer self, not trusting it nor believing it too much, but keeping this outer self in check and pressing it down, so that it may not be a hindrance to the inner person in its noble works and ways, and especially in its sensory, fragile desires. For as long as a person is here in this time, they cannot easily be without all satisfaction or desire; but there, one should let that noble virtue, detachment, be the master, so that all pleasure and satisfaction may be in God alone, or through God. For this reason, one should seek help from God; then God gives them His excellent divine power and strengthens them with His wis[dom]...

<summary>Tauler presents the suffering and abandonment of Christ as the ultimate model for the believer, explaining that the highest spiritual state is reached when one feels most forsaken and detached from worldly comfort. This "inner ground" allows God to reign and brings about a divine peace that should be guarded against all external distractions.</summary>

### 98.

# On the Seventeenth Sunday after the Holy Trinity.

## The First Sermon.

Regarding the calling of God: who it is that calls and invites us so often, to what He calls us, what His call is, and how one should worthily follow this call. Concerning three kinds of people whom God calls to Himself, in three degrees of a true Christian life: namely through the commandments, through counsel <term>Rath: the "evangelical counsels" of perfection, such as voluntary poverty, which go beyond the basic requirements of the law.</term>, and through the internal union of the spirit in the bond of peace, which surpasses all senses. Brothers, I, a prisoner in the Lord, beseech you. To the Ephesians, Chapter 4, verses 1–6. <note>original: "Fratres, obsecro vos ego vinctus in domino. Ad Ephes. IV. v. 1–6."</note>

Brothers, I, a man bound in God, beg you that you walk worthily in the invitation or calling, as you are invited, with all humility, gentleness <term>Sanftmuth: a mild and patient disposition of the soul.</term>, and patience. Bear with one another in love. Be diligent to maintain the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. One body and one Spirit, even as you are called.

In these words, as St. Paul begs us that we should walk worthily in the call, as we are called, there are four things to be noted. The first: who is He that calls and invites us? The second: for what purpose does He wish to have us? The third: what is His call, and in what manner does He perform it? The fourth: how one should worthily follow this call in this invitation.

Now first, regarding who calls us: it is the **Heavenly Father**, who calls us with all that He is, has, and can do. All of this leads and lures us toward Him and into Him; His love, His goodness, His noble essence, all lead us to Him. In truth, God is always in such need of us, as if all His bliss and His very being depended upon us. <note>This provocative idea—that God "needs" humanity—is a central theme in Rhineland mysticism. It suggests that God’s nature as Love requires an object to love, making the soul's return to Him essential to the divine experience.</note> Everything that God the Father has made and created in heaven and on earth, with all His wisdom and goodness, He did all of it so that He might call and invite us back into our **origin**. <term>Ursprung: the "source" or "origin," referring to the state of the soul as it existed eternally in God's mind before it was created in time.</term> A Master says: Everything God ever did, or ever does, He has done so that He might bring the **soul** back to the point where she might hear His call and desire to love Him.

Second, to what He calls us: that is to His most beloved Son, our Lord **Jesus Christ**, so that we should be His brothers and **co-heirs** with His Son. He is the first and the highest among the brothers, and possesses the innate inheritance by nature, while we are to be co-heirs by grace. To this He calls us: that we follow His image, for He is the way through which we should go, and He is the truth that should direct us on the way, and He is the life that should be our end and our possibility—not alone in thoughts, but through a virtuous life and patient suffering.

Third, what His call is, and to whom He calls. The call by which God calls man is manifold. Inwardly in the ground <note>The "ground" (Grund) refers to the deepest, most essential part of the soul where the spark of divinity resides.</note>, God calls man without ceasing, with many an admonition and with inward warnings day and night; and with hard punishments, from within and from without, with all the tribulations that He permits to befall man. These come in many ways—now as love, now as sorrow—and these are the powerful voices with which God calls man. If man followed the gentle, sweet call, he would not need the harsh voice with its many sufferings and many misfortunes.

Fourth is that we should walk worthily with all patience, and with all **humility** and **gentleness**.

This call is much higher and different than the first one regarding the Commandments. So that this Counsel of God in this calling might be followed rightly and well, the holy Christian Church—by the counsel of the Holy Spirit—has established spiritual communities and Orders, so that one may follow the Counsel of God within them. These have many laws, all of which are directed toward that end.

Do not be terrified by this; if you sink deeper into your nothingness and recognize yourself, it will turn out very well. Afterward, you will walk much more truly and worthily in the unity of the spirit, in the **bonds of peace**. <note>A reference to Ephesians 4:3.</note> Whoever walks thus and follows the worthy image of our Lord Christ, in all patience and **gentleness**, and in humility, and in every way as you have heard, there the peace is born which surpasses all senses. It begins here, will last eternally, and will shine upon us in all our life and being. Amen.

### 99.

# On the Same Sunday.

## The Second Sermon.

How one may receive and attain true **patience** and **gentleness**. Likewise, how we may come to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.

> I beseech you, I, a prisoner in the Lord, that you walk worthily of the vocation wherewith you are called, etc. <note>original: "Obsecro vos ego vinctus in domino, ut digne ambuletis vocatione, qua vocati estis etc."</note> Ephesians IV. v. 1—6. *)
> 
> I, a prisoner in God the Lord, beg you, dear brothers, that you would walk wisely in the calling to which you are called, with all **humility** and **gentleness**, with patience, and bear with one another in the love of God, and be diligent to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bonds of peace, and be one body and one spirit, even as you are called to one hope of your calling.

Every person should set these noble words before their mind as a mirror; wherever they might be or whatever they might do, they should always have this patience within themselves, inwardly and outwardly, and humbly bear everyone’s failings in the love of God. They should always diligently perceive their calling within themselves, in all humility and gentleness with patience. Therefore, if I may request anything of you or serve you in any way, I ask that you diligently practice these things and observe this within yourselves with all industriousness. For all the good works you might perform—whether internal or external, or the practice of the high, noble, and worthy **Sacrament**, <note>A reference to the Eucharist or Holy Communion. The author emphasizes that the ritual itself is secondary to the participant's inner spiritual state.</note> or however great the virtue may be that you perform—all of these are unpleasant and worthless to God if you do not possess the aforementioned virtues.

These noble virtues do not come to a person unless he runs to meet the things that are bitter and contrary to him. <note>This reflects a core mystic teaching: spiritual growth is not found in comfort, but in embracing suffering and "bitterness" as a means of breaking the ego.</note>

Therefore, even if a person thinks often and deeply about **humility**, it is of no use unless they have first been completely humbled and despised by others. Likewise, if they reflect much on **patience**, it is again for nothing, unless they have first been severely tested by all created things. Otherwise, it is worthless; it lacks true substance, and it falls away the moment it arises. But when a person is offered insult, dishonor, and even great outrage in words or deeds—whether deserved or undeserved—that person should immediately hasten in humility with **gentleness**, and calmly perform a special, loving service for the very person who has despised and persecuted them. Even if that person were to spit on them during this act of love, they should not stop, as far as they are able; for gentleness and patience are two virtues that must both be won bravely and manfully <note>The original "männlich erkrieget" suggests a "manly" or "courageous" spiritual warfare or conquest to attain these virtues.</note> through struggle, amidst great, bitter, and harsh adversity from both within and without. If nobody did anything adverse to me, how would I then practice this noble virtue? For the virtue of gentleness focuses more on the internal training of the soul <note>original: "Gemüth"; in this context, the deep seat of a person's disposition and inner life.</note>, in which a person has perhaps never truly and fundamentally practiced themselves; whereas patience focuses more on the external practice and the actions of the outer person. 

If I were called a false, wicked man, and my teaching were utterly rejected and destroyed, and I suffered great shame or dishonor—if someone felt sorry for me because of this, they would not be any dearer to me than anyone else. In fact, they would be denying me a blessing <note>original: "Seligkeit"; literally "blessedness" or "salvation." The author views suffering as a spiritual gift.</note>, for I would not be worthy of all this—that I should follow the worthy footsteps of my dear Lord and **Creator**, whose divine teaching and holy, pure, and innocent life were altogether falsified and destroyed in the hearts of men. Therefore, dear children in **Christ Jesus** our Lord, I exhort and ask you, by everything I may ask of you in God, that you practice this noble virtue and diligently keep watch over your soul. I tell you that the greatest help and practice for this is at night after **Matins** <term>Matins: the first of the "canonical hours" or prayer services of the day, traditionally observed in the middle of the night or at dawn.</term>, because the night is long. Therefore, whoever truly wants to attain this unity of the Spirit should go to their rest at a timely hour in the evening, so that they may have the sleep they require for their needs. Then, after Matins, a person should observe their **inner ground** <term>inner ground: "Grund," a central concept in German mysticism referring to the deepest, most essential part of the soul where God and the human spirit meet.</term>, to see what might most stir them, and toward what they feel the most love, grace, and devotion.

It may be the pure, clear, noble, and worthy life and suffering of our dear Lord **Jesus Christ**. However, if a person does not have a specific grace from our Lord, they should begin again in the worthy name of God their specific, good practice without any **self-interest** <note>original: "Eigenschaft"; in this context, it refers to "propiety" or "attachment," the ego's tendency to possess its own actions or spiritual experiences rather than being detached.</note>; or perhaps the worthy, innocent, and sharp suffering of our Lord Jesus Christ; or His bitter, wretched, innocent death; or His many wounds; or His manifold, innocent shedding of blood. By these things, perceive your inner ground, and with them, the devout person should gather all their love together. For just as a great fire comes from many coals and much wood, and the flames thereby press upward into the heights, so should these good practices fervently ignite the person’s soul <note>original: "Gemüth"; the inner seat of a person's disposition, emotions, and will.</note>. 

But the devout person should soon let go of these **images** <note>original: "Bilde"; refers to the mental pictures or concepts used in meditation. The author suggests moving from "meditating" on scenes to a deeper, "imageless" state of contemplation.</note> and should instead press upward longingly with flames of God's love through the "middle man" into the innermost, **God-shaped** man. For that same inner man performs no work of his own; that work belongs to God alone within him, and he keeps himself acting solely in God. Yet there remain within him the insights from the good practices which the person...

...whatever one has practiced previously, whether it be the worthy suffering of our Lord, or his infirmities, or praying for someone, living or dead—through all of this, one should press forward with a single mind, entering into God purely and nakedly <note>original: "blöslich"; in mystical writing, this refers to being "stripped" of all worldly attachments, images, and the self.</note>. If these inward glances are then broken through purely and receptively <note>original: "leidentlich"; this describes a state of "holy passivity" where the soul is not acting, but being acted upon by God.</note>, then the eternal Truth comes and gazes into itself, drawing the mind after it, receptively, into itself. This happens quickly and swiftly, just like a moment, or even less. In the same way that the turning of the angels is swift, back and forth in every moment, so it happens here in this **inner ground** of the soul; for the swifter it is, the nobler it is. Here, one should offer all such insights back into the divine ground and become one spirit with God; for God is a pure spirit, and thus we become one spirit with Him. These are truly the true worshipers of God, who worship the eternal Father in truth. Here, then, the true, essential, divine peace is born, and the noble virtues of which we have spoken also lead into this state. 

When a person stands in this practice, their nature <note>The "natural man" or the ego-driven self, as opposed to the spirit.</note> stands there entirely poor and parched, for it no longer has anything of its own. Thus, it thinks to itself in wonder: "God bless me, where have the **prostrations** <term>prostrations: original "Venien," ritual acts of bowing or kneeling used as penance or prayer in monastic life.</term> gone, and the good exercises? Why do the psalters lie idle?" For nature would dearly love to *have* something, it would dearly love to *know* something, and it would dearly love to *will* something. And before these three "Somethings" die in the natural man, it feels very hard and bitter to nature, until it dies away completely in this ground. 

This does not happen in a single day, nor in a short time; it must be won through a "breaking through" <note>original: "Durchbrechen"; a central concept in German mysticism describing the soul's effort to move beyond the created world into the Godhead.</note>. One must accustom oneself to it with diligent industry and earnestness, and then it will finally become easy and sweet to the person. As one reads of the chosen saints of God in the **Book of Wisdom**, which says: "Having been disciplined a little, they will receive great good." When nature has finally died away (says **St. Bernard**), then the person should speak the most lovely words to our Lord that a human can ever devise or imagine, such as:

> "O, my dearest Creator and Redeemer, if only I were worthy to be one of your dearest friends, and that I might embrace you in my soul, and encompass myself entirely within you, and thus lock you within me, so that I might never lose you for all eternity."

### 100. ª

# On the Eighteenth Sunday after Trinity.

## The First Sermon.

How precarious it is to hear the Word of God fruitlessly; which is the state of the scribes and Pharisees now. Concerning thorough humility and divine love, and concerning false teachers.

> <note>original: "Diliges Dominum Deum tuum ex toto corde tuo, et in tota anima tua, et proximum tuum, sicut te ipsum."</note> You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind, and your neighbor as yourself. Luke 10:27. *)

Dear children, the scribes and Pharisees often tested our Lord, but they could not catch Him in a single word, as the Gospel reports in many places. Now know, that hidden and enclosed within these words is the most noble, most useful, and purest teaching and salvation that one can have in time and in eternity. St. Luke describes to us that our Lord (before He spoke of this commandment of love) had sent His disciples to proclaim the Word of God to certain cities, and wherever it was not received, they were to turn away quickly and go to other cities. Now, there were certain cities that had not received the Word of God for their improvement, to which our Lord said: Woe to you, Capernaum and Bethsaida, and woe to you others, for if the truth that has been proclaimed to you had been proclaimed to those of Sodom and Gomorrah, they would have been much more receptive to it, and their judgment on the last day would also be much more merciful than yours.

Now let us consider the city of Cologne; I do not know in the whole world, from one end to the other, where the Word of God has been so richly, purely, and clearly poured out and revealed—these last 60 years and even to this day—as here in Cologne, through many enlightened teachers and <term>Friends of God</term> <note>original: "Gottes-Freunde"; a 14th-century mystical movement within the Catholic Church, consisting of laypeople and clergy who sought a deeper, more personal inner relationship with God.</note>, whom God has...

...these high things hidden from the great and wise of the world, and hast revealed and discovered them to the little ones. Our Lord also spoke, saying that the eyes of His disciples were blessed. The **Scribes**, however, are those who stand in their natural cleverness and have grown up in their own reason <note>original: "Vernunft"</note>, and who, out of a proud foundation, boast of their high understanding, arts, lofty words, and ways. These people have done, and still do, great damage to the holy Church.

Which, then, are the eyes that are blessed, of which the Lord spoke? These are the few, the little ones, who look upon themselves in their **nothingness**, considering themselves as nothing in their own true ground, and recognizing themselves in the truth: that they are nothing. ...worthy, true, and thorough knowledge goes downward, not with words, nor with <gloss>interpretations of scripture</gloss> <note>original: "Glossen"</note>, but in the truth; just so much does God rise within him. A person should sink from the <term>ground</term> <note>The "ground" (Grund) is a central concept in German mysticism, referring to the deepest, innermost essence of the soul where it meets God.</note> beneath God and beneath all creatures, so that one remains empty under all <term>occurrences</term> <note>original: "Auffälle"; this refers to things that happen to us—events, impulses, or afflictions—whether they originate from within or without.</note>, from wherever they come, and through whom, and in what manner it may be, inward or outward, appearing good or evil (sin always excluded). 

Why do you think that God often permits even good people, who are in His grace, to fall into sin? For no other reason than that they may recognize their smallness in it, and learn humility and <term>nothingness</term> <note>original: "Vernichtigkeit"; a state of mystical self-abnegation where the person recognizes they are nothing without God.</note>, and despise themselves. Who was ever dearer to our Lord than the apostles? Yet He let them all fall into sin for the sake of this foundation! 

If a person finds in this ground that they love God above all things, and intends to do so, then they should not be terrified. Dear child, God has permitted it for your own good. Now, when small failings fall upon such people, they run to confess them so that they might be free of the punishment. Run, you poor blind person, into yourself; flee into your ground and confess to God. Holy Church demands nothing for you to confess but mortal sins. If such people were in my power, they should remain unconfessed for four weeks. 

Press yourself, dear child, into your inability and worthlessness; let yourself go, and keep silent under all occurrences. Remain and keep silent, and press yourself down under all <term>temptations</term> <note>original: "Bekorungen"; trials or spiritual testings.</note>, inward and outward. You cannot overcome all things in a better way. In the same way, if a hundred of the most evil dogs came upon a person from the outside, and the person sat down and pulled themselves inward and did not move, the dogs would do nothing to him and would run away from him; but if they looked back and found that he moved a hand, they would all run over him again. 

By this is meant all the temptations that may ever fall upon you: turn into your ground, remain still, and leave yourself to God, and do not act outwardly; they will all fall away, all of them, and even if all the devils of hell had sworn it, they cannot harm you.

Teach yourself to suffer and to let go, and listen to your Father's voice, which He speaks within you, and your Mother's voice from without—that is the Holy Church. The voice demands: Love God above all things, above all things, above all things, and your neighbor as yourself. <header>100. b</header>

# On the aforementioned Eighteenth Sunday.

## The second sermon (or the 13th; the 3rd sermon).

Concerning three kinds of false opinions held by certain seemingly good people. Concerning three kinds of the love of God, one of which is called sweet, sensual, or figurative love; the second, a rational love; the third, a strong <term>essential love</term> <note>original: "wesentliche Liebe." In mystical theology, this refers to a love that is rooted in the very essence or "being" of the soul, rather than just in emotions or thoughts.</note>, each of which far surpasses the other. Mention is also made of the falsity of the <term>free spirits</term> <note>The "Brethren of the Free Spirit" were a controversial medieval mystical movement often accused of heresy for believing they could achieve a state of perfection where they were no longer bound by moral laws.</note>. Finally, regarding the wonderful properties and effects of essential love. All intended for spiritual people—that is, those who desire to live according to the Spirit of God.

> ->"You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart," etc. Luke 10:27; Matthew 22:37.<- <note>original Latin: "Diliges Dominum Deum tuum ex toto corde tuo etc."</note> *)

A Pharisee wanted to test our Lord and asked him what he should do to obtain eternal life. Our Lord pointed him to his own skill and intellect, and asked him how he had read in the Law? He answered and said: "You shall love your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your <term>mind</term> <note>original: "Gemüth." A difficult term to translate, it encompasses the heart, mind, and soul—the seat of one's inner disposition.</note>." Children, this man did not mean God, nor eternal life, for his intention was false. Oh, how common this Pharisaical way is on earth—that people generally intend outward things in words and works that have a spiritual appearance, yet they actually intend more outward things: wealth, honor, advantage, to be seen and respected, and favor and pleasure. Now, all works that a person does which serve more for appearance, or so that one might be seen and respected, or considered great—God does not accept any of these works, however great or high they are or seem to be. Whoever is the cause of the work, whoever gives birth to the deed, to them the birth belongs, and not to another.

Now, concerning this love which is a commandment, **St. Bernard** <note>St. Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153), a Cistercian abbot and influential mystic who wrote extensively on the "Degrees of Love."</note> speaks and calls it one love, a **sweet love**; and the second, a **wise love**; and the third, a **strong love**. You should take note of these three kinds of love through a comparison of three types of statues. The first is a wooden statue, gilded with gold. The second is a silver statue, also gilded. The third is a statue of pure gold. The wooden statue represents **sweet love**. The silver statue is compared to **wise love**; but the **strong love** is compared to the golden statue.

The first—**sensory, sweet, and image-based love**—is like the wooden statue; one looks upon it with great pleasure when it is well-crafted, shaped, and gilded. But if one were to scrape off the gold, it would hardly be worth twelve pence. So it is with this sweet, image-based love: it is gilded with a "good intention," but if one scrapes that away, what remains would be of little value, though it is very pleasant to the natural senses. God draws and entices a person further with such sweetness, as a starting point, so that true love may finally be formed and born within them through this feeling. Thus, through this "tasting" of God, the taste and desire for nature and all worldly things may be extinguished. 

But a person should not reject this; they should receive it with reverent fear and humility. They should attribute it to their own smallness—that they must be lured and enticed in such a way—and they should move through the **images** into **transcendent forms** <note>original: "Ueberbilde." In mystical theology, this refers to moving beyond mental pictures or concepts toward the direct, unmediated reality of God.</note>, through outward sensory exercises, and deep into themselves—into the **ground** <note>original: "Grund." A central term in German mysticism referring to the deepest "spark" or essence of the soul where the human meets the Divine.</note> where the Kingdom of God exists in truth. This happens to them because of a lack of practice, and also because they remain stuck on these sensory images; they persist there, go no further, and do not "break through" into the **ground** where the living truth dwells. For one cannot serve two masters—that is, the senses and the spirit.

Heaven is the highest, and the earth is the lowest. Now, heaven works nowhere so fruitfully as it does in the lowliness of the earth; and thus the majesty of God works nowhere so fruitfully, nor so kindly, as in the deepest lowliness of man. Just as the sun draws the moisture up from the low earth, so God draws the spirit up into Himself, so that it truly perceives and even imagines itself to be God, and then sinks down into itself and thinks itself less than a human. It is exactly like a large kettle that boils intensely; for a while it boils upward, as if it would overflow at once, but when the fire is pulled out, it sinks deep down. In this way, strong love drives and draws the spirit so that it makes an overflow, and at once wants to go out of itself into an "unknowing" <note>A state of mystical contemplation where the soul lets go of intellectual concepts to experience God directly.</note>; this then keeps the spirit down in an acknowledgment of its nothingness.

Strong love has three properties in itself. 

First, it exalts the spirit of man so exceedingly in that which he loves, and draws him far away from the characteristics, power, and workings of his faculties—memory, and will; this is beyond all manner and senses. 

The second property is that it presses him so deeply down into the "ground" <note>The "Seelengrund" or soul-center.</note>; that is an annihilation that is bottomless. There, humility is unknown to the senses and has lost its very name. 

The third property is that love makes the person so "essential" <note>meaning the person acts from their true inner being rather than superficial desires</note> that it is a wonder; he goes along thus, and he is satisfied with all things, however all things come. He does not have much outward activity, for he stands in a quiet rest and is ready for wherever the Lord wants to lead him or work through him. He is like a servant who stands before his master’s table and does nothing else but look at his master to see what he wants from him, so that he is ready to do it.

### 101.

## On the Nineteenth Sunday after the Holy Trinity.

->How we should be renewed in the spirit of our minds; for which it is necessary that we guard ourselves against lies, anger, and theft, and how these three things should be understood. On the difference between these four things: Soul, Spirit, Mind, and Man, of which one is often mistaken for the other. How a person should dispose and prepare themselves for inner renewal.<-

"Be renewed in the spirit of your mind," etc. <note>original: "Renovamini spiritu mentis vestrae etc."</note> Ephesians 4:23. *)

**B**rothers, be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man, who is created according to God in righteousness and in the holiness of truth. Therefore, cast away lies from yourselves, and speak the truth, each of you to his neighbor, for we are members of one another; you should not be angry, and not sin. The sun should not go down upon your anger. You should not give a place to the angry enemy. Whoever has stolen, let him steal no more, but rather let him work with his hands at what is good, so that he may have something to give to those who suffer in need.

This is the Epistle <note>A selection from the New Testament letters read during a church service.</note> that is read at this time. St. Paul writes it, and it is full of noble meaning and teaching. In particular, we should take heed of the brotherly admonitions that we should be renewed in the spirit of our mind <term>Mind: The original German "Gemüth" refers to the deep seat of a person's thoughts, will, and emotions—the inner disposition.</term>. Now he teaches us how we should come to this renewal, and gives us to understand that we should do certain things and leave certain things behind. We should put on a new man, who is created according to God in righteousness and in the holiness of truth. There are certain things we should leave behind—there are three of them—which we must necessarily leave if we are to come to this renewal. First, we should cast away lies, and each speak the truth to his neighbor. Secondly, we should not be angry. Thirdly, we should not

stealing. These three things a person must necessarily possess <note>The sense here is that one must "possess" the avoidance or the understanding of these three things.</note> if they wish to be renewed.

Now, what is lying? Whatever a person demonstrates—whether by signs or appearances, words or works—that they do not mean in their heart, so that the mouth and the heart are at odds with each other: that is lying. Now there are some people who appear spiritual, but are entirely unlike it, for their hearts are worldly and are possessed by creatures <term>Creatures: In medieval theology, "creatures" refers to anything created (people, objects, status) as opposed to the Creator.</term>, whatever they may be, dead or alive. I am not speaking of worldly people, but of worldly hearts, who take their pleasure entirely in temporal things that do not belong to God, whether it be their clothes or their jewels. If this is said to them, they grow angry and find false excuses <gloss>original: "Glossen" – interpretations or explanations used to justify behavior</gloss>, saying: They are young, they must enjoy themselves; they do it so that they may serve God all the better and more easily. That is a lazy lie. Should you serve God better by drawing into yourself things that, in truth, hinder you from God? Should the dear God not be able to delight you more than corrupted, straying creatures? That is an evil lie. 

There are also other lies that are spiritual; that is, when some perform good spiritual exercises, and in doing so they intend themselves and their own benefit more than God. They go on like this for 30 or 40 years and do not recognize themselves or their own intentions. Ignorance does not excuse them, for they should have examined their intentions so that they might have known themselves, and seen whether their intention was toward God or toward their own—neither reward, nor heaven, nor pleasure, nor profit. Whoever could see how God dwells in that ground would be made blessed by the sight. The closeness that God has there, and the kinship, is so wonderfully great that one cannot, nor may, nor should speak much of it.

In this mind, one shall renew oneself, with a constant entering into the ground, and a turning-toward it with a real love.

# On St. Cordula the Holy Virgin’s Day, or on the Twentieth Sunday after Trinity.

## The First Sermon.

Of the union and marriage <term>Vermählung: In mystical theology, the 'spiritual marriage' represents the highest state of union between the soul and God.</term> of God with the loving soul; how He first washes and strips her, so that He can afterwards rightly clothe and adorn her with Himself.

The kingdom of heaven is like a king who made a marriage for his son <note>original Latin: "Simile factum est regnum coelorum homini regi, qui fecit nuptias filio suo."</note>. Matthew 22:2–14. *)

Today we celebrate the day of the noble virgin St. Cordula, who was left to herself in her own infirmity <note>St. Cordula was one of the companions of St. Ursula. Legend says she hid in fear during the initial massacre but emerged the next day to face martyrdom alone.</note>. There she descended to the lowest degree among all others, in human fear, and wanted to flee. It is also well worth noting that through this she reached the highest degree above all others; for all the bloodshed, clubs, maces, and wounds that St. Ursula and her company suffered—all this passed through her heart and her imagination. She died a distinct death in her mind with every one of them, whereby she died many deaths, while the others died only one death. After all this, she submitted herself to the full power of her enemies and under the sword of death.

Here we should take great note of the wonderful faithfulness of God, and the hidden paths through which God draws a person to Himself, and leads them wonderfully to the highest things through unknown ways and manners. God often leaves a person to themselves—

<summary>This page introduces a sermon on the spiritual marriage of the soul to God, using the martyrdom of St. Cordula as an example of how God uses human fear and "mental death" to lead a soul to the highest spiritual state.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the sermon for St. Cordula’s Day, transitioning from the martyr's physical and mental suffering to a broader discussion of the spiritual marriage between God and the soul. in great distress and oppression, in human infirmity; if man would now follow God in this way, and perceive Him therein, without any doubt He would lead him a thousand degrees higher through the struggle and through the infirmity, if he would be diligent. If he looked upon and perceived divine help, and trusted God, did not despair in Him, and also did not fall into unrighteous freedom <term>unrechte Freyheit: This likely refers to the "Free Spirit" movement, a medieval heresy where individuals claimed that being "one with God" meant they were no longer bound by moral laws or the Church.</term>, then the temptation could never be so evil, so heavy, nor so great that it could harm him in any way. 

Now one reads in today’s Gospel <note>original: "Evangelium"</note> how a wedding was made by a king for his son, and how many people were invited to the feast [the meal]. This Lord is the heavenly Father; the bridegroom of this wedding is our Lord Jesus Christ; the bride is my soul and yours. We are all called and invited, and all things are ready, entirely in the union of God with the loving soul, with His bride; this is so inexpressible, and the love is so near, so inward, so secret, so friendly, that it altogether surpasses all understanding. 

All the skillful masters in Paris <note>The University of Paris was the most prestigious center for scholastic theology in the Middle Ages; the author is contrasting their intellectual "dexterity" with the experiential knowledge of a simple believer.</note> with all their dexterity could not reach this; and if they wanted to speak of it, they would altogether have to fall silent; and the more they wanted to speak of it, the less they could, and the less they would understand it. Not only natural riches, but even all the riches of grace cannot express this, nor can all the saints, nor angels; rather, a simple person who has abandoned himself to God <term>Gelassenheit: A central concept in German mysticism, meaning a total letting go of self-will and "releasement" into God's will.</term> and is humble, he feels something of this in his innermost ground, and yet he cannot comprehend it, nor could he put it into words in any way, for it is far beyond the comprehension of all creatures.

Now one should prepare this spouse as one prepares an earthly spouse: one should wash her, and clothe her with new garments, and adorn her with all finery, and throw away the old clothes, even if they were good.

Understand well what the washing is: it is a purification from all sins and failings; and the stripping away, in a coarse sense, is the "old man," all vice, manners, and habits. The new clothes are new virtues, and a heavenly, divine life, and the "new man" who is formed after Christ; but in a closer sense, when one strips the spouse of the good clothes because they are old, so that one also [strips away] these divine [gifts...] <note>The sentence breaks off mid-word "Ge-" at the end of the page.</note>

<summary>This page uses the parable of the royal wedding feast to illustrate the mystical union between the soul and Christ. The author emphasizes that this inward experience of God's love is inaccessible to the intellectual scholars of Paris and can only be felt by the humble, "abandoned" soul.</summary>

--- Page 431 ---
<meta>This page continues the sermon for St. Cordula’s Day, discussing the union of the soul with God. The previous page ended by noting that even the most learned scholars in Paris cannot fully grasp or describe the secret love between God and the bride-soul.</meta>

...time <note>original: "mahl"</note> [the soul] must put off these old clothes—even the new virtues and ways—because they are old, and He shall put others upon her in a higher way. And if one says that one should be **stripped** of virtues and go **beyond** the virtues, could one not say it was wrongly spoken: that one should go beyond virtue?

One can answer: Yes and no. No one should, nor may, go beyond virtue in such a way that he should not love it, nor practice it, nor possess it. But it is true that when a man is enraptured by God, during that time he does not practice works of virtue—neither patience nor mercy, nor many such things. But as soon as he comes back to himself, he possesses every virtue as the time for it to act arises.

In another sense, too, one can be stripped of virtue. A person might want this or that from God. He would like to be so poor that he does not lie one night where he lies the next <note>This refers to the ideal of radical apostolic poverty, traveling without a fixed home, as practiced by some medieval mendicants.</note>, and would also like to know all truth, and have great earnestness from God, and feel His presence, and have intimacy <note>original: "Heimlichkeit"</note>, and that it might be with him as it is with this person or that. From all of this one should be stripped, and leave oneself in the most pleasing will of God in true abandonment <term>Gelassenheit: A central concept in German mysticism meaning "letting-be" or "releasement"—the state of letting go of one's own will to rest entirely in God's will.</term>, however God wills it, and strip away all that, however good it may seem or be to you. 

For however good it is, man has a hidden un-nature <term>Unart: In this mystical context, it refers to a deep-seated spiritual flaw or "bad habit" of the soul, specifically the ego's tendency to take credit for or cling to its own goodness.</term> within him that corrupts and destroys all the good in him, just like someone who puts noble, good food into an unclean bowl, or good wine into an unclean cask. Faithful God recognizes this, and lets the man fall because of it, so that He may teach him to let go of himself, and thus overcome this evil un-nature. This stripping is often much better for him than if he were clothed with many great things.

Ach, children, if anyone would take heed of his ground <term>Grund: The "spark" or deepest interior part of the soul where the human spirit meets the Divine.</term>, of what is within him and his un-nature, and would let go of himself and follow God—in whatever way and by whatever path He wished to draw him—he would soon get through it; he would take from God everything that fell upon him, internally and externally, and would receive the hidden judgments and decrees of God with gratitude. Also, this sometimes seems so strange and inconsistent, and yet in this you are better clothed than with the highest works, where you imagine you are achieving great things. Thus they say:

> Lord, I would like to be master of myself, and I would like to be inwardly at peace, and that it would be for me as it is for this person or that.

<summary>The author explains that true spiritual progress requires "stripping" away even the desire for virtues and spiritual experiences to achieve "Gelassenheit" (abandonment) to God's will. He warns that a hidden "un-nature" or ego-centeredness can corrupt even good deeds, making God's intervention necessary to humble the soul.</summary>
<keywords>virtue, stripping (Entkleidung), abandonment (Gelassenheit), un-nature (Unart), the soul's ground (Grund), God's will, spiritual humility</keywords>

--- Page 432 ---
<meta>This page continues the sermon on being stripped of the self to find God. The previous page discussed how a soul must move beyond even the practice of outward virtues to reach a state of total abandonment (Gelassenheit) to God’s will.</meta>

No, dear child, it must be otherwise; you must be stripped, you must be pointed toward your **nothingness**, and see what lies hidden and covered within you; stay with yourself.

I asked a high, noble, holy person what his highest focus <note>original: "Vorwurf"; here meaning the primary object of his contemplation or concern</note> was, and he said: "My sin, and thus I come to my God." So let God and every creature point you toward your sin, and judge yourself, so you will not be judged by God, according to St. Paul’s words <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 11:31: "For if we would judge ourselves, we should not be judged."</note>. This should be within you in truth, without any **gloss** <note>original: "Glosse"; meaning without excuses, external interpretations, or softening the truth</note>; it should not be a manufactured humility, for that is a sister of pride. It should be in the **ground** <term>Grund: The "ground of the soul," the deepest interior essence where man meets God.</term>, and not with a storm, as if one wanted to break heads. Present to Him—with a quiet, gentle, composed dejection, in humble fear of God—your evil, possessed ground in heartfelt prayer, and do this in the spirit; seek that in Him, for if you run anywhere else, it helps you nothing. 

Do not model yourself after this person or that one; it is a blindness. As diverse as people are, so also are the ways to God. What would be one person’s life would be another’s death, and as people’s **complexions** <term>Complexionen: A term from medieval medicine referring to a person's physical and psychological temperament or "humors."</term> and natures are, so their grace often directs itself. Therefore, do not look at the *manner* of people, but at their virtue; there you may well look, whether it be gentleness, humility, and the like. But take the *manner* of practicing it according to your **calling**. Observe above all things what your calling is, to which God has called you, and follow that. If you only observed it with diligence, you would find it and recognize it as clearly as your own hand.

But now you do not stay with yourselves, and you do not seek it faithfully and inwardly from God, for you look at everything outwardly; and therefore God remains unknown to you in truth, and you remain unknown to yourself. You run in a race for twenty or thirty years, and though you have appeared to shine in a spiritual outward-show and life, you have ended up just as near and just as far as you were on the first day. That is surely a misery! Therefore, take heed of the root of your vices <note>original: "Untugenden"</note> and kill those, and not your nature; but because you do not do that, you lose in one hour what you have gathered in a year—perhaps in words and deeds that grow out of the evil roots lying in the **ground**. ### 103.

# On the Twentieth Sunday after Trinity <note>Trinity Sunday is a major feast in the Christian calendar; the "Sundays after Trinity" make up the long season of Ordinary Time in the Western church.</note>.

## The Second Sermon.

How the person who is invited to the heavenly wedding must strip and divest himself of his inward, secret failings and evil inclinations, thereafter cast off all useless immoderation and anxious multiplicity, and must clothe himself with divine love, in a true and pure intention toward God in all things.
"Behold, I have prepared my banquet" <note>original: "Ecce prandium meum paravi."</note>. Matthew 22:4. *)

I said yesterday that one reads in the Gospel <note>original: "Evangelio"</note> how our Lord spoke: "Behold, my meal is prepared; come, you who are invited, to the feast and the wedding." As we spoke of this wedding which the King had prepared, it is also said here how the spouse must be stripped of her old clothes if she is to please her Spouse. For the bride or spouse must be entirely clothed in new garments, and be beautiful and well-adorned. God gives and takes, allows and permits all things, so that His spouse may be stripped, so that—

that he may clothe her nobly and gracefully once more, with true divine wedding garments. This spouse of God is the soul of every devout person, whom God desires at all times and every hour, if only we are willing. Now, it would be much more necessary for us to be stripped than to be clothed; for if we were stripped and prepared, the gracious God would undoubtedly clothe us in a wonderful and elegant manner, for all things are fully prepared. Now, I spoke a word yesterday in the **sermon** <note>A formal religious discourse; the preacher is referring to his previous teaching to ensure his audience follows his logic.</note> that perhaps you did not all understand, regarding how the root must come out. This is what I mean: When a field or a garden is cleared of weeds, sometimes a root of the weeds remains deep in the soil, and it goes unnoticed. Then the soil of the garden is well-sown and smoothed over with a harrow, but when the good seed is meant to sprout, the evil weeds emerge—those which rise from the evil roots—and they spoil and crowd out the good plants and the good seed. 

This is what I called a "root": the evil failings that lie hidden in the **ground** <term>Grund: In mystical theology, this refers to the "ground of the soul," the deepest interior essence of a person.</term>, which have not been put to death, nor settled through **confession** <note>The sacramental act of telling one's sins to a priest.</note> and **penance** <note>Acts of devotion or self-denial performed to show sorrow for sins.</note>. Though the plow of good **spiritual exercises** <note>Structured activities like prayer, fasting, or meditation intended to strengthen faith.</note> has passed over them, the inclination of those evil roots has nevertheless remained there in the depths—whether it be **pride** <note>original: "Hoffart." A specific term for haughtiness or spiritual arrogance.</note>, unchastity, hatred, envy, anger, or the like. These same sins and vices then break out just when the divine, blessed, and virtuous life is meant to sprout within you; then the evil fruits of these evil roots arrive and ruin your fruit, your devout and holy life. 

God pursues these vices with everything that He allows to befall a person, both in giving and in taking, so that this harmful root may be recognized and driven out of the person. For as long as these vices are hidden, they will undoubtedly break out when you least expect or intend it. This has clearly appeared in many great people—**Church Fathers** <note>The influential early Christian teachers and scholars.</note>, women, and men—who lived in the wilderness for 30 or 40 years in great exercises and works, and yet they did not perceive these evil roots or seek to drive them out; because of this, they were ultimately ruined and fell away from their strict, devout life. In truth, no one can take this away from you but He alone, through His divine grace; so remain constant in this and do not break out with words or with deeds. Do not do as some people do: as soon as they do not perceive the fruit of their prayer, they give up immediately. Because of this sickly inclination, one should always be suspicious of oneself and diligently guard against everything that might cause or give rise to it; in this way, you are always safe. For if you only intend to flee once you are wounded, it will be impossible for you to recover. Flee while you can—it is necessary for you—and hold yourself in fear of your own nature.

Those people who remain inward and do not break out into worldly distractions—when the terrible storm comes, which we must always expect, and when all things are thrown into confusion, when misery and distress arrive—then God will surely find a **little nest** <note>A metaphor for a place of spiritual refuge or divine protection.</note> where He hides and preserves His own, the chosen ones. 

Know also, that at the time of death, those people who have not paid attention to these vices within themselves will fall into misery and distress. When the **ground** <term>Grund: The deepest, most essential part of the soul where man meets God.</term> is suddenly revealed, they will be judged without any of God's mercy. Therefore, humble yourselves under God and look at your roots in a state of patient suffering; let these temptations be your **purgatory** <note>original: "Fegfeuer" – a place or state of suffering inhabited by the souls of sinners who are expiating their sins before going to heaven.</note>, and regard yourselves for what you truly are. 

Now, there is no spot so small, nor any little image <note>Distracting thoughts or mental attachments to worldly things.</note> with which you have hindered God’s noble work within you—provided you have drawn it into yourself with free will, to say nothing of great, coarse sins—but that you must suffer more pain for it in purgatory than all the **martyrs** have ever suffered for God’s sake. If you must suffer in purgatory for 30 or 40 years, you would much rather lay down your failings here, in a patient and humble manner, and thereby earn a great reward, delight, joy, and eternal glory.

### 104.

# On the Twenty-First Sunday after Trinity.

->On the weapons of spiritual chivalry, especially on humility and gentleness,<-
->through which one may overcome all temptation. On the great benefit that<-
->suffering and temptation bring to man. Also how excellent, spiritual<-
->people should keep themselves guarded in their hidden temptation.<-
> Be strong in the Lord, and in the power of His might. Ephesians 6:10. <note>original: "Confortamini in Domino, et in potentia virtutis ejus. Ad Ephes. VI. v. 10."</note> *)

St. Paul says in the Epistle: Brothers, be strengthened in God the Lord, and in the capability of His power, and put on the armor of God. Now notice, as I spoke yesterday, that the spouse <note>Tauler frequently uses the "Gemahl" (spouse/bride) as a metaphor for the human soul in its relationship with God.</note> of God must be stripped of all things if she is to be truly or perfectly clothed within. Now the spouse sees that her dear Lord Jesus Christ desires and demands such great things of her—to do and to leave undone—and these seem to her to be impossible. Because of this, she falls into great sadness and a natural doubt that she cannot manage what He desires and requires of her. And to this, Saint Paul gives her wise counsel and says: Become strong in God; what you then cannot do in yourself, you can do through Him and with Him. Therefore, sink yourself into nothing but Him, and leave all your doing and non-doing to Him; thus you can do all things. Seek it in His lordship, in His power, and in His humanity <note>Seeking God in His "humanity" refers to the mystical practice of meditating on the life and suffering of Christ as the gateway to the Godhead.</note>; seek it in Him inwardly and fundamentally, and take your strength in God the Lord, in His capability; let all your capability and strength within you be in God the Lord alone. 

But know, there are now many people in spiritual appearance <note>Tauler is likely criticizing those who appear holy on the outside ("spiritual appearance") but are inwardly full of pride.</note> who conduct themselves as if they themselves were God, and otherwise would know nothing of any power or lordship in doing or leaving undone; and yet each wants to be higher and better than the other. This God will not always tolerate, nor remain silent regarding it.

### 105.

# On the Twenty-Second Sunday after the Holy Trinity.

*How the love of man toward his neighbor and God should increase, and overflow in knowledge and perception with good direction and discernment; how far the love of neighbor may extend, and how through this outward love of neighbor, a person should prove, or test, or learn the inward love, which is turned toward God in its origin, and how high that same love may grow above itself.*

> I pray, brothers, that your charity <note>original: "charitas"</note> may abound more and more. Philippians 1:9. *)

St. Paul says: Brothers, I pray you, that your love may grow more and more and overflow, and he says: God is my witness, how I long for you all, in my remembrance of Jesus Christ. And I pray for this, that your love may grow more and more, and overflow in all knowledge <term>Kunst: In this medieval context, this refers to "spiritual skill" or "acquired knowledge" of divine things.</term>, and all perception, and that you take heed of what is best, and that you may be pure and without offense until the day of Jesus Christ, filled with the fear of righteousness, to the praise and honor of Jesus Christ.

Now observe with great diligence, St. Paul said that God was his witness, how he thought of his own in his memory. If we had love, it should draw us wonderfully and deeply toward what God's friends desire for us from the bottom of their hearts—that we do right in this—and we should fulfill their desire. Now St. Paul says: I pray you, that your love may grow more and more, and overflow from a burning love into a perfect love.

The noblest and greatest thing of which one may speak is love; one can learn nothing more useful. God does not demand great reason <term>Vernunft: Human logic or intellectual power, which the mystics often placed below the "simple" experience of love.</term>, nor high intellect, nor great exercise (although one should not abandon good exercise), yet love gives all exercises their worthiness; God demands only love, for it is a bond and a form of all perfection, according to the teaching of St. Paul. Great reason and cleverness is common to the heathens and the Jews. Great works

<meta>This page continues the sermon on Philippians 1:9, shifting from the theological definition of love (caritas) to its practical application. are common to the righteous and the unrighteous. Love alone separates the false from the good, for God is love, and those who dwell in love, they dwell in God and God in them; and therefore, before all skills <note>original: "Künsten"</note>, learn love. Because God first loved us inexpressibly, we should also love him in return, as St. Augustine speaks; and therefore our love does not diminish, nor does it decrease, but rather it grows and increases. For with love one earns love; the more one loves, the more one desires to love and is able to love. 

Now love has two works: an inward and an outward work. For we should not be satisfied with merely doing good, but he admonishes us to strive for the very best, and that we overflow in love. 

Knowledge is the third gift among the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, and it goes directly before love, like a handmaid who serves a lady and walks before her. Divine love makes a person renounce himself and all of his own will. Therefore, in this state, a person falls at the feet of God and desires God's judgment in love, so that God's righteousness may be satisfied in him and in all creatures; so that God's will may be done in him according to His entire will, as He has eternally willed it and pre-ordained it in His eternal will, or still intends to ordain—be it in Purgatory <note>original: "Fegfeuer" — a state of spiritual purification after death</note> or however it pleases Him; what, how, when, or how long, or how soon. Lord, as You will, whether the person be great or small, near or far, everything falls into God's will. And he shall rejoice that God's mercy is fulfilled in his smallness, and grant a worthy person his greatness; and thus, another's grace becomes your own. Children, this would be a true love! Oh, whoever could reach such a turning point at his final end, that he fell entirely into God's will and was found therein—even had he committed all the sins that all the world has committed, he would travel to heaven without any intermediary <note>original: "ohne alles Mittel" — implying immediate entry to heaven without the need for further purgatorial cleansing</note>. No one can give this to you but God alone. Just as there is no safer nor better way of dying than this, so there is no better nor closer life than to live in this at all times, and in this, a person increases wonderfully and without ceasing. Love sinks into the Beloved.

In this, there is a great opposition <term>Gegenwurf: literally a "counter-throw"; a spiritual hurdle or objection encountered in the soul's progress</term>; these are great, heavy trials <note>original: "Anfechtungen" — a central term in German mysticism for spiritual struggles, doubts, or temptations that test the soul’s resolve</note> in many difficult ways, whatever they may be. This should be understood thus: temptation as temptation—that is, the occurrence of failings—one should not want nor choose; rather, the pain in resisting and in overcoming is what a person should choose, placing himself out of love under the weight of the burden. If God wanted him to suffer until the Last Judgment, he would gladly suffer it out of love, for God's praise and honor. Everything that one might earn from this—purification or salvation—if it pleased God and He wanted to give the reward to a Heathen <note>original: "Heiden" — a non-Christian</note>, or a Jew, or someone across the sea whom you never saw, you should grant it to them from the bottom of your heart for God's sake just as much as to yourself.

# On the Twenty-Third Sunday after Trinity.

How we should purify and prepare the temple of our soul (in which the image of God lies) through a thorough renunciation of ourselves and all things, through a constant turning inward and perception of ourselves, and a shutting in of our senses, with a living following of Christ.

*Whose image and inscription is this? Matthew 22:20.* <note>original Latin: "Cujus est imago haec, et superscriptio?"</note>

**O**ur Lord God has placed His own image and inscription into our soul, as He created the soul according to His image and likeness. Therefore, it is necessary for all people that they often turn inward to themselves, and explore all the corners of their soul (wherein the

Those who wander about and travel through the whole world with their senses, seeking transitory comfort and burdening themselves with worldly care, love, and pleasure in creatures <note>In medieval theology, "creatures" (Creaturen) refers to any created thing—people, animals, or objects—as opposed to the uncreated God.</note>, and with things that are not commanded of them, cannot do this. <meta>This page continues the sermon for the 23rd Sunday after Trinity. The previous page discussed the soul as a "penny" bearing God’s image; here, the text transitions into a discussion of the Neoplatonic "exitus-reditus" (flow out and return) of all things from the Father through the Son, and the mystical union of the soul with the "One."</meta>

— 451 —

Father created all things, as John speaks: All things are made through him. Just as all things have flowed out from the origin of the Godhead, which the eternal Word brings forth from God the Father, so all creatures <note>In this context, "creatures" refers to any created being—human, animal, or inanimate—as distinct from the uncreated God.</note> remain in their essence through that same birth of the Son from the Father, and all creatures must also return again to their first origin through the Son into God the Father. In this eternal birth of the Son from the Father, a flaming love often breaks forth from God the Father toward His divine Son, and from the Son toward the Father; that is then the Holy Spirit, which is a true bond that binds the Father and the Son together with eternal love. Although the holy Trinity <note>original: "Dreyfaltigkeit"</note> consists of three persons, personally distinct, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are nonetheless a single, pure, essential One. That they are a single One is proven to us by the divine masters and even the pagan masters themselves. Aristotle said: There is only one prince who judges all things. Moses says: "Hear, O Israel, the Lord your God is one God."

Therefore, beloved children in Christ, whoever now wishes to have a true and pure union <note>original: "Vereinigung"</note> with God must devote and unite the penny of his soul <note>An allegory for the soul as the "tribute penny" from the Gospel of Matthew, which must be returned to its rightful owner, God.</note> with all his powers and senses to God alone; for if the highest single One (which is God) is to be united with the soul, this must happen through unity. And therefore, when the soul has renounced and turned away from itself and everything that is of a created nature, and stands especially free and bare of all multiplicity <note>A common term in German mysticism referring to the distraction caused by many worldly thoughts versus the "oneness" of God.</note> in truth, then the single One (which is God Himself) answers the unity of the soul, where nothing is in the soul but pure God alone. Therefore, when a person is so purely ordered, or properly directed, that his heart and soul are concerned with and inscribed by nothing but God alone—and all that he must have for the body’s necessity, he can name as ordered through God and with God—then such a union occurs between God and the pure soul that they become truly one with each other. As St. Paul says: "He who clings to God becomes one spirit with Him," and thus the pure soul is united in unity with the single One, which is God Himself.

<meta>This page continues the sermon for the 23rd Sunday after Trinity. While the previous page focused on the philosophical and mystical union of the soul with the "One," this page shifts to a practical warning: one cannot reach the heights of God’s divinity without first passing through the humility of Christ’s human life and suffering.</meta>

Now there are some people who wish to fly before they have grown feathers, or who wish to pluck fruit before it is ripe. These are "beginners" <note>original: "anhebende Menschen" — a term for those in the first stage of spiritual development, often criticized by mystics for trying to skip basic discipline for high ecstasy.</note>; as soon as they have started a good life, they immediately want to fly high through the contemplation of divine and eternal things, chasing after that which they cannot grasp. For such people, it is very difficult and bitter to contemplate the perfect, pure life of Jesus Christ, and they do not wish to concern themselves with it. The life of such people is quite precarious and almost unsafe, for a person must be firmly established upon the strong rock and cornerstone, which is Christ himself, if anything is to come of them. And he must follow the humble Lord Jesus, in the pure footsteps of his holy life, which he practiced and fulfilled in human nature <note>original: "menschlicher Natur"</note>, as much as is possible for him. A person must also eagerly and diligently contemplate the bitter passion and the pain of his martyrdom, and his despised death; and this should be valued above all virtue, for one never comes to a perfect life except through this way of truth. Therefore, Christ said:

> I am a door; whoever enters through me shall be saved and find joy and pasture in me; <note>John 10:9</note>

as if he meant to say:

> Whoever does not go through the humility of my humanity <term>Humanity: The physical, suffering human life of Jesus, seen as a necessary bridge to the divine.</term> shall never reach the height of my divinity <term>Divinity: The eternal, godlike essence of Christ that exists beyond time and space.</term>.

It happened to a priest who did not want to concern himself with the noble humanity of our Lord; it was bitter for him to contemplate his suffering, and he wanted only to deal with the high divinity, which he nonetheless could not grasp. When he thought he was standing quite securely, he fell, and in that fall he came to a profound self-awareness, and began to speak:

> Oh, eternal and merciful God, I now truly confess that I have done wrong, because I did not want to go through your humanity; therefore, I could not and might not come to the height of your divinity. For had I truly directed my way through you, and followed the pure image of your holy life, I would not have fallen so.

For this reason, it is the very best thing a devout person can have or do: to be in constant, diligent contemplation of the shameful, painful suffering and bitter death of our Lord.

So that you may understand this better, take note of this teaching that I wish to present to you. Dear child, hold fast to this teaching: if you desire a blessed, good life, you must perform many inward retreats <term>Inward retreat: (German: Einkehr) The practice of pulling one's attention away from the world to focus on the presence of God within the soul.</term> into yourself; let this be a most useful lesson for you. For when a person turns toward outward things and becomes fragmented among created things <note>original: "vermannigfaltiget mit creatürlichen Sachen" — the state of being "multiplied" or distracted by the diversity of the physical world rather than the "oneness" of God.</note>, he can neither achieve nor accomplish anything good in his inwardness <note>original: "Inwendigkeit"</note> as long as he stands in disorder within this multiplicity, and his heart and mind <note>original: "Gemüth" — a term encompassing the soul's disposition, will, and emotional state.</note> remain distracted and restless.

Now there are many people who complain, saying: "Dear Lord, I am burdened with so many duties <note>original: "Aemtern" — likely referring to administrative or domestic roles within a monastic community.</note> and with outward matters that I must perform out of obedience, so that I cannot and may not come to myself because of them; and though I would gladly make an inward retreat into myself, the outward work distracts me." 

Dear child, complain of this to no one but yourself, for it is your own fault and no one else’s, because no one distracts you more than you distract yourself. If you truly took heed of yourself, so that when you took six steps in total obedience, you then took the seventh step in a true inward retreat, then certainly no outward thing could harm you, provided you kept yourself in constant watchfulness. Without doubt, the fault lies only in the fact that the person keeps neither watch nor heed over himself, as he rightly should do at all times. 

And when a person must attend to something outward, he sets his heart and mind too much upon it and dwells on these things, either with excessive worry or with a self-satisfaction in his office (where he looks more at the office than at the obedience), or with some pleasure that he seeks in such outward things, or with a reluctant resentment, so that he does unwillingly what obedience requires—though he would be willing enough if only obedience were not involved—and this is, among many spirit[ual]— <note>The text cuts off here at "geiſt-", likely "geiſtlichen Menschen" or "spiritual people."</note>

Your mouth should be so completely closed that it speaks of nothing else but necessity <note>original: "Nothdurft"</note>, God's praise, and your neighbor's benefit. Your heart should be so prepared for the Eternal One that He may constantly have His dwelling therein. Your will should also be so freed from all desire for temporal, created things that everything is bitter to you which is not God; and your reason should be freed from all subtle speculation <note>original: "subtilen Speculiren" — over-intellectualizing spiritual matters rather than experiencing them in the heart.</note> and worldly things, and your confidence and memory from all useless thoughts, so that you offer your will and all your life at all times pure and clear to your only...

Just as the grain of wheat <note>original: "Weißenkorn," an older spelling of Weizenkorn</note> must first wither, die, and perish when it is cast into the earth before it can bring forth fruit, so too must all worldly things in your heart be in a state of diligent dying and perishing. ### 107.

# On the Twenty-fourth Sunday after Trinity.

How the Holy Spirit draws his own through many degrees of his divine love, which is strong as death; and concerning the heavy fall and error of those who do not follow such a drawing, although some of them are miraculously called back by God to their first grace.

-> Love is strong as death. Song of Solomon 8:6 <note>original Latin: "Fortis ut mors dilectio. Canticor. VIII. v. 6."</note> <-
