<meta>This page continues the sermon for the Twenty-fourth Sunday after Trinity, which began on the previous page with the theme "Love is strong as death." It explores the practical steps a soul must take to ascend toward divine grace.</meta>

— 460 —

...is as powerful as death. Whoever wishes to reach this point, so that this love may manifest in him, should first observe the degrees or steps <note>original: "Grade oder Staffeln," terms often used in mystical literature to describe the "ladder of ascent" toward God</note> upon which he may learn to climb little by little, until reaching the height of this noble grace. For there are many degrees of love through which the Holy Spirit draws his own, and in each one, love is as strong as death—that is, if love is to stand rightly, a person must suffer much before he can essentially obtain it <note>original: "wesentlich erkriegen," meaning to acquire it so deeply that it becomes part of one's being</note>, each [form of] love in its own degree.

The first love that God gives to his friends is **godly fear**, and this is the first gift of the Holy Spirit, for the Holy Spirit is love. And this gift leads a person to disdain all sins that are against the commandments of God and the holy Church, and does not let the person part from this fear until his end. This fear is mixed with bitterness, for penitence <term>Bußfertigkeit: the state of being truly sorry for one's sins and willing to change</term> is at first very bitter to perform for those who are just beginning. And when God sees that this person is willing to convert (however painful it may be for him) and does not cease because of it, He takes mercy on the person and puts honey in his mouth—that is, **merciful sweetness**.

And therefore this second love is called **gentle love**, and it makes the penance and repentance a person has suffered so sweet that it is no longer difficult for him, and he is ready to follow the commandments of God and the holy Church without any resistance from his nature, and thus he lives in joyfulness. And when God sees that the person has a cheerful spirit in this, out of willing devotion and love, and [yet] believes that he has never yet been perfect, then God demonstrates to him **artful love** <note>original: "künstliche Liebe," referring here to a more refined, spiritually skillful, or wise form of love</note>. And that is the third love, in which the person understands that one must also turn inward toward understanding and overcome the desire for sin <term>Begierlichkeit: concupiscence, or the innate human tendency toward selfish or worldly desires</term>, which is now as difficult for him as if he were to produce the first, innate angelic love <note>original: "anerschaffene englische Liebe," referring to the pure, effortless love shared by the angels at their creation</note>. See, thus love is sweet, and yet difficult in its practice, and that is what it means to be **strong as death**. Now, when some people become aware of this pain—outwardly in sins and inwardly according to desire—they do things rightly and abandon all vice, outwardly and inwardly, and die to what they should die to, and leave it, for no one's sake, nor for their [own]...

And if the work cannot be performed by the person, yet he would gladly do it, the intention and the will are enough, no matter how late he begins or starts.

He later arrives at a state of false peace within and does not practice inward gratitude or the repentance of his sins. 

Eventually, he comes to trust in himself and hopes in the penance he previously endured; he often reflects on his good works and esteems them greatly. If he is then occasionally mocked by people, or if he displeases them in some of his disorderly ways, he consoles himself with trust in his good works, thereby driving away the mockery and shame. Therefore, within him there is neither true repentance for sin nor a truly good confession; for the person who performs good works of penance and yet seeks pride <term>Hoffart: spiritual arrogance or a haughty vanity</term> and empty honor in them becomes blinded in his conscience. Thus, he still wishes to teach and rule, and to be busy with many things, and to concern himself with spiritual matters, yet he improves nothing in himself nor in other people. Because of this, an accusing conscience is given to him, so that he is in a bad state afterward, and in a poor condition regarding the salvation of his soul <term>Seelen Seligkeit: the eternal blessedness or "happiness" of the soul in God</term>. He then takes courage from the Scripture <term>Schrift: the Holy Bible</term> that suits his purpose, drives away all those admonitions, and then returns to his old ways, and is then satisfied again. 

He then receives enlightenment in his understanding from the Scripture, or in his prayer, or some other inwardness <term>Innigkeit: deep, heartfelt devotion or spiritual intimacy</term>, and while he is of good cheer and joyful, suddenly the conscience returns, and he does not know where he stands. Then the fleshly trials come, such as unchastity and greed, sloth and the like. He then believes that God sends these to him so that he may earn more crowns <note>A reference to the "crown of life" or "crown of righteousness" mentioned in the New Testament as a reward for enduring trials.</note>, and he wants to resist the trials with this thought; immediately they attack him even more harshly, and he no longer knows what to do, for he has run out of his own wisdom. Thus he then falls into bodily sensory rest, and begins his...

<summary>This page describes the psychological and spiritual trap of a person who performs outward religious acts and penance to maintain a "good name" while failing to transform their inner soul. It warns that relying on one's own wisdom and reputation leads to a cycle of guilt, false comfort from Scripture, and eventual surrender to sensory desires.</summary>
<keywords>penance, spiritual trials, conscience, pride, reputation, inwardness, soul's salvation, Scripture, temptation</keywords>

--- Page 470 ---
<meta>This page continues the description of the "modest person" who, while maintaining a pious facade, has internally strayed from a disciplined spiritual life. The previous page ended with the observation that such a person lacks true repentance because they are preoccupied with their public reputation.</meta>

[He begins] to take his ease in a disorderly way—in sleeping, in eating, in drinking, in walking and amusements, and in all such things—and becomes almost entirely like a worldly person, except that he commits no outward mortal sin <term>Todsünde: a grave sin committed with full knowledge and intent that "kills" the life of grace in the soul</term>. Consequently, trials <term>Anfechtungen: internal spiritual struggles, temptations, or crises of faith</term> come upon him even more heavily than ever before; he cannot defend himself against them and thus falls in many ways before he even realizes it himself, yet he is still ashamed to lose his reputation. He has a bad conscience within, and his good exercises <term>Uebungen: disciplined spiritual practices like prayer or meditation</term> no longer taste good to him but become bitter. It vexes him to be in the service of God, unless he can derive some sweet pleasure from it.

Now, things have gone so far with this person that either he must fall into outward sins, or God must send him a new conversion <term>Bekehrung: a "turning back" or spiritual re-awakening</term> which he might understand better than he understood the admonition <term>Vermahnung: a spiritual warning or divine nudge</term> he encountered previously, as has been said of this. For all of that was given to him so that he might turn away from his erring <term>Verirrung: a state of being spiritually lost or wandering from the path</term>; but since he would not acknowledge that he erred and turn toward a better life, it has come to this: he must either turn back to a new conversion or fall into great sin. 

Therefore God comes and often lets such people fall into great public shame, or into great suffering of the body and heart, so that they do not know where to turn and thus place their comfort in God. Only then does God begin to look upon them again, giving them acknowledgment <term>Bekenntniß: here, a private or internal admission of one's faults</term> of their sins, and trust in forgiveness <term>Vergebung: the release from the guilt of sin</term>, and the will to begin anew to improve themselves in all their disorderly works and desires. They are no longer ashamed before people—neither regarding the works in which they displeased God, nor regarding the understanding God now gives them; they do not resist it. 

But there are some who pay no heed to any admonition, and when the suffering is over, they return again to their sins. Although their conscience <term>Gewissen: the internal sense of right and wrong</term> pricks them, they nevertheless follow their desires and persist in them. Ultimately, things go very well for these people according to the flesh and according to their possessions, and they seem as if they are quite well off, for God allows them their way according to all their desires. But know now, as you have heard before, that before God [takes] the people...

<summary>This page describes the spiritual decline of a person into worldly habits and the two possible outcomes: a "new conversion" often triggered by God through suffering and shame, or a total lapse into sin where God allows the person to prosper materially while they perish spiritually.</summary>
<keywords>spiritual decline, hypocrisy, conversion, trials, conscience, divine discipline, repentance, worldliness</keywords>

### Tauler’s Sermons. Vol. II. 30.

...to perish, He gives them such manifold admonition <term>Vermahnung: a divine warning or internal nudge toward the right path</term>, both outwardly and inwardly, that they should convert, so that it is sufficient for every person’s conversion, provided they are willing to turn toward it.

But the good person, who turns toward this through the admonition of God, is first seized with ashamed anxiety; he looks upon his own ingratitude and now pays attention only to himself and to his sin. He realizes how he has internally erred with bad intentions even in his good works, and how he has grossly displeased God in all his deeds and sins—things he previously did not want to admit <note>original: "nicht Wort haben wollte"</note>. Out of gratitude, he does not know what penance he should perform for this; instead, just as he did when he first attained spiritual awareness, he does now: he begins to become like a young child in the Holy Church once again <note>This metaphor suggests a total spiritual reset, returning to the fundamentals of faith with a beginner's humility</note>. He learns to fast and keep watch with discretion, and to perform all his works and exercises in submissiveness, humility, and obedience, according to the order and arrangement of the Holy Church and according to the station in life in which he finds himself. He practices and looks through and through the life of our Lord *Jesus Christ*; to this he gives himself with all his might, guided by divine counsel, according to the Scriptures, his spiritual advisor, and his own conscience. 

He learns to order his spirit according to the spirit of *Christ*, as best as he is able. He learns to die to all defects, both outward and inward, and to all disorderly things; from day to day, he desires to learn this better. He is especially more terrified of "coldness" in the spiritual state than of all other defects, for it was through such coldness <note>In mystical theology, "coldness" refers to a state of spiritual apathy or listlessness where the soul loses its fire for God</note> that he had fallen into all his previous faults and errors. This person had indeed fallen into a great pit of sins from which he could not emerge by his own power, but God has delivered him from it—even while God allows so many others to remain there without their consciences being troubled. 

Thus, the soul cannot easily carry this grace within itself in silence, but reveals it to all people through many signs, for love cannot remain idle. First, the person possesses a genuine love that does not spare itself; he gives his very limbs to all good works of penance where he knows it is pleasing to God, keeping it as secret as he can. Thereafter, he is also persistent and steadfast in his works; he...

<summary>This page describes the process of spiritual re-awakening, where a person, moved by divine admonition, returns to a state of humble obedience and disciplined practice. Tauler emphasizes the "imitation of Christ" and the danger of spiritual coldness as the root of all sin.</summary>
<keywords>conversion, repentance, spiritual coldness, imitation of Christ, humility, penance, Johannes Tauler, spiritual exercises</keywords>

--- Page 472 ---
<meta>This page continues the sermon from the previous page, completing the description of the soul's commitment to God and detailing the progressive stages of divine love.</meta>

...vows until the end of his life never to fall away from God again into lukewarmness <term>Lauheit: a state of spiritual apathy, indifference, or "going through the motions" without heart</term>. In this soul, there is also an intelligent and discerning love, which seeks not to kill nature, but to overcome the sin that reigns within nature and the soul. Then, a free love also enters this soul, which does not love any creature alongside God <note>meaning the soul no longer loves worldly things as ends in themselves or as rivals to God</note>, but rather holds all things within God. Then comes a calling love, for the soul cannot be still, but calls out to all things that have been driven away; then comes a welling love <note>original: "quellende Liebe," imagery suggesting a spring of water bursting forth</note>, where she does not know what she ought to do for the honor of God, and [she grieves] because people do not turn to God as they should; then comes a burning love, which out of love cannot maintain any moderation in morality <note>the soul becomes so overwhelmed by divine fervor that it surpasses conventional, "measured" religious practice</note>; then comes a foolish love, which now disdains, now honors, and all its diligence and will are like unto folly. Then comes a joyful love in the delights of the heart; then a love united with God, both here and hereafter. This may well be the love of which the words of the Bridegroom <note>The "Bridegroom" refers to Christ, here quoting the Song of Solomon 8:6: "Love is strong as death"</note> speak: *Love is strong as death.* To attain this divine love is to love with great pain, and therefore it is compared to a painful death, which is bitter to the taste. And since no one can serve the world or sin without great pain, why should one not then be willing to suffer so that they might attain divine love, which is never-ending? When earthly love comes to an end, this love is not yet diminished.

->May God help us that we may thus attain the love of God and not die the eternal death. Amen.<-

<summary>This page concludes the sermon by detailing the ascending stages of love—from discerning and free love to a "foolish" and "burning" fervor—eventually reaching a state of union with God. Tauler emphasizes that the pain required to achieve this love is far more meaningful than the pain of serving the world.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the sermon from the previous page, finishing the description of the soul’s commitment to God and transitioning to the 25th Sunday after Trinity. It defines the nature of divine love as an active, restless force centered in the heart.</meta>

### 108.

## For the Twenty-Fifth Sunday after
## Trinity.

->On the difference between true and false love, through several signs and qualities that a true lover of Christ should possess, and how one should or can rightly use and love both temporal and spiritual things.<-
->I sleep, but my heart watches. <note>original Latin: "Ego dormio, et cor meum vigilat." From the Song of Solomon 5:2.</note><-

The more the loving soul is loved by God, the more restless she becomes; and that is the nature of love, that it cannot be idle. It works great things wherever it exists within a person, and if it does not work, then there is no love there. The noblest part of a human being is the heart, which possesses this love and desires no rest there, but rather to love God, to honor God, and to thank God, and to perform His praise at all times; that is its delight, for love loves the Beloved more than it loves itself.

So that one may distinguish between good and false love, one should know that three parts belong to a wakeful and living love, or rather, love consists of three things: the will, the intention, and the desire. This means that a person wills, intends, or desires nothing else in all things—both outward and inward—than that he might purely and solely love God, and refer all his things and works to God and toward God. This is because God is good, and out of goodness He created us, and redeemed us with His blood. The soul thanks God for various other special virtues and blessings that He has bestowed upon us, and still bestows every day, and intends to bestow upon us hereafter, which is even better. See, love cannot take a holiday <term>feyern: to rest from labor or be idle; here meaning love never stops its spiritual activity</term>, nor can it rest, but it watches constantly to thank and praise God in this, and to respond even a little to His love.

<summary>This page explores the restless and active nature of divine love, explaining that true love for God is seated in the heart and manifests through the will, intention, and desire to honor the Creator.</summary>

--- Page 474 ---
<meta>This page continues the sermon for the Twenty-Fifth Sunday after Trinity, further exploring the theme of "true love" versus "false love." It specifically addresses the need for the soul to detach itself not only from worldly pleasures but also from the emotional "rewards" of spiritual practice, such as feelings of sweetness or consolation.</meta>

Thus, the loving servant does not intend to mean or love God alone, but also to love all creatures <note>In this context, "creatures" refers to all created things, including people, animals, and the natural world.</note> for His sake; and for His sake, he is willing to suffer all annoyance and adversity, and to abandon all disorder for the eternal glory of God, seeking nothing of his own in any thing, whether in temporal or eternal matters. By "temporality," one understands here all sinful desires that pull a person toward all sensual pleasures; for by nature, a human being loves beautiful, clean, and pleasing things, and everything that brings delight and joy to our nature. Behold, to all of these things the loving soul is bound to die <note>The term "die to" (German: *abzuſterben*) is a common mystical expression meaning to become indifferent or detached from worldly desires.</note>, and to overcome them through desire [for God], which a person shall easily learn to recognize if he would closely observe and examine his temporal and outward senses to see where he might lose his way.

The lover of Christ should also seek nothing temporal for himself or for his own sake, even in a spiritual form and manner. Such seeking seems to be permitted to the beginning and imperfect servants of Christ, but is in no way permitted to the perfect; and that is: consolation, sweetness, savor, inwardness, and good progress in all spiritual exercises. Pure, sincere love must not seek these things, nor anything like them, for their own sake—to rest upon them, to cling to them, or to place one's confidence in them. For that would be to trust more in the gifts of God than in God Himself, and that is against right, pure, and perfect love. Because some people love in such a disordered way, God often withdraws all these spiritual gifts from them and makes them dry and sluggish, poor and wretched, so that they might learn to flee to God in a state of total abandonment <term>Verlaſſenheit: a state of spiritual "desertion" or dryness where one feels distant from God's presence</term> of spiritual delight, and serve God alone in faith, hope, and love. They must learn to "kill" themselves and suffer all spiritual disgrace out of love, resting only in trust in God, in His goodness and bottomless mercy, from which everything comes—both His giving and our taking or receiving of virtue.

It belongs to pure love that one maintains as faithful a love for God in a state of total abandonment as in a time of grace. If this does not happen, it is obvious that one places more trust in the gift than in God Himself, and thus we commit spiritual unchastity <note>original: "geiſtliche Unkeuſchheit." A metaphor for spiritual infidelity, where the soul "cheats" on God by loving His gifts more than His person.</note> with the grace of God. It is always a gain, which we herein...

<summary>This page exhorts the believer to practice "pure love," which requires detaching from both worldly pleasures and spiritual "sweetness" to trust God alone during times of spiritual dryness. It warns against "spiritual unchastity," which is the error of loving God's gifts more than God Himself.</summary>
<keywords>pure love, detachment, spiritual dryness, abandonment, spiritual unchastity, grace, temporal vs eternal, mysticism</keywords>

--- Page 475 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of spiritual love. It focuses on the dangers of becoming attached to the "sweetness" or emotional rewards of religious devotion, distinguishing between the needs of a spiritual beginner and the requirements of those seeking deeper union with God.</meta>

seek for our own sake, only we do not recognize this.
We should rather seek and desire spiritual grace, solely to learn all the better how to recognize God and to taste how good and how sweet He is, so that we might better learn to reach the inward spiritual Good, which is God Himself, who dwells in our innermost ground <note>The "ground" (German: *Grund*) is a central concept in German mysticism, referring to the deepest part of the soul where the human meets the divine.</note>, so that we might then fully practice true virtue inwardly, through detachment <term>Gelassenheit: a state of letting go, yielding to God's will, or being free from worldly attachment</term> and the practice of virtue, by which one first attains God.

A good person may indeed desire to "taste" or experience other forms of inwardness <term>Innigkeit: a deep, emotional sense of intimacy with God</term>, for themselves or for other people, as necessity requires, or as inwardness demands for the glory of God and the salvation <note>German: *Seligkeit* can mean both "blessedness" and "salvation" in an eternal sense.</note> of humanity, so that through this sweetness, while working earnestly for virtue, they might sooner and better obtain from God what is necessary for the glory of God and the salvation of humanity; for in all such forms and ways it is permitted to love oneself and to use what is good, whether it be temporal, physical, or spiritual. You should know that it is indeed permitted for a beginning lover to seek spiritual goodness <gloss>delight</gloss>, even if it is temporal, so that they may learn therein to die to the fleeting taste of sin, and so they may learn to taste how good and sweet it is to cling to God, and to seek nothing else but Jesus <note>original Latin: "Jesum"</note>, so that they might thus drive away all sin, all vanity, and all attachment to earthly desire and imagination, so that they desire only to cling to God in good practice. Once God has gifted them with this good spiritual taste, and the temporal taste has diminished, then it is time to turn to the path that has been revealed a little here. For if one remains stuck in the first stage, as if it were the highest good, they can never arrive at the true highest good, and they will no longer advance in virtues, and they deceive themselves and can never arrive at true virtue and at the right confession of themselves and their sins, and cannot know what is permitted to them or not; and thus they also cannot recognize the temptation that occurs in the spiritual life, and some even fall at last into great sin without resistance. Behold, this is called temporal spiritual good, in which wakeful and pure love must not seek itself.

<summary>This page explains that while beginners are allowed to enjoy the "sweetness" of spiritual feelings to help them turn away from sin, they must eventually move past these feelings to find God in the soul's "innermost ground." Failure to move beyond emotional devotion can lead to self-deception and an inability to resist deeper temptations.</summary>

--- Page 476 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of spiritual love, moving from the "sweetness" felt by beginners to the "pure love" required for deeper union. It emphasizes that true virtue acts without regard for reward or punishment.</meta>

Now listen also a little to where pure love must not seek itself: in the eternal Good, such as glory, honor, and the great reward to be received in the Kingdom of Heaven for our good works. That, and things of that nature, do not belong to pure love or to perfect virtue—to seek something for one's own sake. Instead, one should love all things and desire to act, to refrain, and to suffer simply and purely for the sake of God’s glory alone. Whether He gives the Kingdom of Heaven or takes it away, whether He preserves or condemns, true, pure love has nothing to do with that. For love loves God’s glory and God’s will, and God knows well what He wants; and what He wants, that is His love, and His love is the best love. Indeed, the loving soul who stands rightly in this would not cease seeking God’s glory and practicing the highest virtue, even if it seemed to her that God would condemn her and punish her virtue, or never forgive her sins. She would practice virtue all the more, for she does not seek her own interest, but intends the eternal glory of God in all things; and these people truly keep the first commandment of God.

But self-love, which is servile <note>German: *knechtisch*, meaning the love of a servant or slave who acts only out of fear or for pay, rather than the free love of a child.</note> and only beginning, is mixed with fear. It says: "If I did not hope to receive a reward for my labor and <term>Penance: acts of atonement or self-punishment for sin (from the Latin *poenitentia*)</term>, I would not do it." This is certainly permitted for a person just beginning their spiritual journey, but not for the true lover. For the first commandment says: to love God above all things, and above oneself. Whoever wishes to reach this state should examine their inner ground <note>As noted previously, the "ground" is the deepest essence of the soul where the human meets the Divine.</note> and their outward conduct to see where they are unlike this love, and turn their heart toward improvement and true love. In this way, you shall bear much fruit in your days and attain much virtue. If you do otherwise, you remain in your false love, from which God must lead us, so that we may turn toward a living and waking love, lest we fall asleep in false ignorance. May God help us in this. Amen.

<summary>This page defines "pure love" as a state of total devotion to God's glory, independent of the hope for heaven or fear of hell. It distinguishes this from "servile love," which is motivated by rewards or penance.</summary>
<keywords>pure love, Kingdom of Heaven, virtue, glory of God, first commandment, penance, self-love, spiritual maturity</keywords>
